Just as ancient Israel's temple was set apart from profane space, Bethel (as a place of false worship) is designated as spiritually off-limits. The man of God's refusal to participate in normal hospitality within that space mirrors the way temple worship requires separation from the profane. His dietary refusal also echoes later temple practices of ritual purity and sanctification—one prepares for sacred work by maintaining separation from that which is contaminated.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern court system, the acceptance and refusal of hospitality carried profound political significance. A monarch's invitation to his home was an honor; refusal was a public insult. Jeroboam, having just witnessed the altar split and experienced divine rebuke (his hand dried up at verse 6), is attempting to recover political and religious authority through the offer of royal hospitality. By contrast, the man of God's refusal is a clear assertion that he operates under a different authority—not the king's, but God's. The radical separation the prophet maintains (refusing even to eat or drink in Bethel) reflects ancient concepts of ritual purity and sacred space. A place dedicated to false worship was considered spiritually contaminated, and a faithful servant of the true God would avoid eating there not out of suspicion of poisoned food, but out of theological conviction that the place itself was off-limits. The three-fold refusal (not going, not eating, not drinking) is comprehensive enough to rule out any possibility of social integration or the establishment of normal diplomatic relations. Jeroboam would have recognized this as a devastating refusal, not merely of a meal, but of any future relationship or negotiation.
commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's refusal to accept the king's offer, 'no matter what the condition,' prefigures Jesus' categorical rejection of Satan's temptations. When Satan offers Jesus 'all the kingdoms of the world' (Matthew 4:8-9), Jesus responds with the absolute statement: 'Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve' (Matthew 4:10). Like the man of God, Jesus refuses to negotiate or consider compromise, even when offered something that might seem beneficial or necessary (turning stones to bread when hungry, gaining authority over all earthly kingdoms). Both the man of God and Jesus demonstrate that fidelity to God's word is non-negotiable, even in the face of extreme offers or pressure.

text_kjv: For so it was charged me by the word of the LORD, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.

commentary.narrative: The man of God now reveals the source of his uncompromising stance: he has received a direct command from God through the word of the LORD. This verse is the theological foundation for everything he has just said. He is not being difficult or proud; he is being obedient. The divine command has three components, each with distinct significance. First, 'eat no bread'—a complete prohibition of eating in Bethel. Second, 'drink no water'—a prohibition of drinking there. Third, 'nor turn again by the same way that thou camest'—do not return to Judah via the same road. The first two prohibitions address social participation (no eating, no drinking, no fellowship). The third addresses the prophet's exit strategy. Together, they create a mission profile that is surgical in its precision: arrive in Bethel, deliver the word, refuse all social engagement, and depart via an alternate route.
commentary.narrative_continued: What is striking about this verse is how it transforms the man of God's refusal from a personal choice into an act of obedience. In the previous verse, the king might have dismissed the prophet's answer as stubbornness or pride. Now it becomes clear: this man is not choosing to be difficult; he is choosing to obey. The Covenant Rendering notes that the divine command 'must not' (rather than 'shall not') emphasizes obligation and necessity. These are not suggestions or preferences; they are non-negotiable commandments from the God of Israel. The fact that the man of God immediately cites his divine commission suggests that he understands something crucial: when a prophet has received a word from God, that word is final. It does not require the prophet's personal understanding of why the command exists. It does not require consultation with the king or negotiation with human authority. The command stands because it comes from God.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The prohibition against returning 'by the same way' deserves particular attention. The Covenant Rendering notes that this may serve a practical purpose (avoiding pursuit or ambush) but also functions symbolically: the prophet's path must be one-directional, delivering God's word and departing without backward entanglement. There is something theologically profound here. The man of God cannot look back. He cannot return to the place where he has prophesied. He cannot recreate fellowship with Jeroboam. He cannot be tempted to soften his message or negotiate with the king. The alternate route is not just physical geography; it is spiritual severance. Once God's word has been spoken, the prophet is done with that place. He moves forward, never returning to the scene of his ministry in Bethel. This principle will become critical in the narrative that follows: when the old prophet later invites him to return to Bethel for hospitality, the man of God will have already been told not to return by the same way. The reader will understand that the subsequent reversal of this command (when the old prophet claims divine authorization) is suspect.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern disciples to examine the quality of their obedience to God's word. When you receive a divine command—through scripture, through the promptings of the Holy Ghost, or through God's appointed servants—do you obey it with the same absoluteness the man of God demonstrates? Or do you negotiate, seeking exceptions or compromises? The man of God's citation of the command shows that he has internalized God's word. He can repeat it exactly, showing that he has truly heard it and received it into his heart. A practical question: can you cite the commandments and promises God has given you? Do you know them well enough to reference them when tempted to deviate? Additionally, the prohibition against 'turning again by the same way' speaks to the principle of spiritual momentum. Once you have taken a stand on behalf of God's truth, you cannot afford to reverse direction. You cannot return to the place of compromise or softening. The man of God's refusal to take an alternate route back to Judah is not just practical; it is symbolic of his commitment to move forward in God's work, never looking back at Bethel or its false worship. What 'same way' are you tempted to return by? What place or person or compromise are you being called to leave behind, without possibility of return?

cross_references.connection: Later in this chapter, when the old prophet invites the man of God to return with him to Bethel for food, the man of God will initially cite this very command as his reason for refusing. This establishes that he remembers and takes seriously the prohibition against returning.

Moses establishes the test for a true prophet: if what the prophet says comes to pass, he is true; if not, he is false. The man of God's obedience to God's word (as stated here in verse 9) establishes his credentials as a true prophet and validates his earlier prophecy against the altar.

God commands Lot and his family fleeing Sodom: 'Look not behind thee...lest thou be consumed.' Like the man of God's prohibition against returning by the same way, Lot is forbidden to look back at the place of judgment. Both commands create a spiritual severance from the place of God's judgment.

Jesus tells a potential disciple, 'No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.' The principle of not turning back, which the man of God embodies in this verse, reflects the deeper gospel principle of undivided commitment to God's word.

Alma asks whether the people have been 'born of God' and 'received his image in your countenances,' and then asks: 'Can you feel so now?' The man of God's ability to cite his divine command with such clarity reflects the reality of having received the word of the LORD—it is something that can be cited, recalled, and relied upon with complete confidence.

word_study.meaning: Tzivvah is the third-person masculine singular past of tzavah ('to command,' 'to charge,' 'to give command'). Oti is the direct object marker with first-person singular pronoun ('me'). The full phrase means 'he commanded me' with the subject being God (implied from context and the following phrase 'by the word of the LORD').
word_study.significance: The verb tzavah carries the weight of royal or divine authority. When God tzavah (commands), the subject is obligated. There is no room for negotiation or personal interpretation. The man of God uses this term to assert that he is under a binding obligation that transcends any earthly consideration. This is not advice; this is command.

word_study.term_english: by the word of the LORD
word_study.meaning: Bi- is the preposition 'by' or 'through.' Debar is 'word' or 'thing' (from davar, meaning 'word,' 'matter,' 'thing'). YHWH is the divine name (Yahweh). The phrase means 'by the word of Yahweh' or 'through the word of the LORD.'
word_study.significance: The phrase 'by the word of the LORD' asserts that the command does not originate with the man of God or with any human authority; it comes directly from God. This formula appears throughout the prophetic literature to assert divine authorization. By citing this phrase, the man of God establishes that his refusal is not based on his personal judgment but on God's explicit will. There is no higher authority to appeal to.

word_study.term_english: nor turn again by the same way that thou camest
word_study.term_original: וְלֹא תָשׁוּב בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר הָלָכְתָּ (velo tashuv baderekh asher halakhta)
word_study.meaning: Velo is 've + lo' ('and not'). Tashuv is the second-person masculine singular imperfect of shuv ('to return,' 'to turn back,' 'to turn aside'). Baderekh is 'by the road' or 'on the path' (with the definite article). Asher is 'which,' the relative particle. Halakhta is the second-person masculine singular perfect of halakh ('to go,' 'to walk').
word_study.significance: The prohibition against returning 'by the same way' is absolute. Tashuv carries not just the sense of retracing one's steps but of turning back or turning aside—any backward motion is forbidden. The Covenant Rendering's 'you must not return by the road you came on' captures this precisely. The prophet's journey is one-directional. This creates a spiritual boundary that cannot be crossed without direct violation of God's command. This detail becomes critical for understanding the temptation the man of God will face in the following verses.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, angels and divine messengers consistently cite their divine commission when giving instructions. Alma the Younger, after his conversion, understands that he has received a 'charge from God' to preach (Alma 36:24). Like the man of God in 1 Kings 13:9, Alma bases his authority and his obedience on the fact that he has been commissioned by God, not by any human organization or authority. This principle runs throughout the Book of Mormon: those who hold divine authority are answerable first to God, not to earthly kings or institutions.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 establishes the principle that the Lord's servant 'shall be given all the desires of his heart' if he relies on God's word. The man of God's complete reliance on the word of the LORD, as stated in verse 9, exemplifies this principle. Additionally, D&C 1:37-38 teaches: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled...For his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth.' The man of God treats God's command in the same way—as something that comes directly from God's mouth and therefore cannot be modified or negotiated.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The man of God's dietary restrictions (no bread, no water in Bethel) anticipate temple concepts of fasting and separation from the profane. In later temple practice, those who partake of sacred ordinances are understood to be separating themselves from worldly sustenance and entering a realm where God provides spiritual nourishment instead. The man of God's refusal to eat ordinary food while in the spiritually contaminated space of Bethel reflects a high view of sacred separation that becomes fully developed in temple theology.

commentary.historical_context: The formulation 'by the word of the LORD' was the standard way an Israelite prophet asserted divine authorization for his message or command. This phrase appears frequently in prophetic literature (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and others) to distinguish between the prophet's personal opinion and God's actual word. In the context of 1 Kings 13, the man of God's citation of this formula establishes that he is not merely a religious eccentric or a political agitator; he is an official messenger of God. The specific nature of the command—no eating, no drinking, no returning by the same way—reflects practices that would have been recognizable to an ancient Israelite audience. Prophets in the ancient world sometimes practiced ritual fasting or abstinence as a means of spiritual preparation or as a sign of grave seriousness. The prophet Elijah, who appears later in 1 Kings 17, will similarly separate himself from normal social patterns. The prohibition against returning by the same route also reflects ancient travel protocols—a messenger or prophet might take alternate routes for security reasons, but in this case, the alternate route also carries spiritual significance. It demonstrates the prophet's complete severance from Bethel and from any temptation to reconsider or soften his message.
commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's absolute obedience to God's word, even when the full consequences are not yet apparent, prefigures Christ's obedience in Gethsemane. Jesus, too, has received a command from God that requires him to walk a path from which there is no turning back. 'Let this cup pass from me,' he prays, 'nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39). Like the man of God, Jesus must proceed along the path God has set before him, without deviation or return. The principle of trusting God's word over one's own desire or understanding is central to both figures.

text_kjv: So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Bethel.

commentary.narrative: The man of God now demonstrates the obedience he has just proclaimed. He leaves Bethel by an alternate route, fulfilling the third component of God's command. This verse is deceptively simple, but it carries profound theological weight. The man of God's actions match his words. He has told the king 'no,' he has cited God's command, and now he walks away. There is a kind of finality here. The narrative has established that the prophet has successfully completed his mission: he has delivered the word of the LORD against Jeroboam's altar, he has refused the king's offer of hospitality, and he has now separated himself physically from Bethel by taking an alternate route. At this point in the narrative, the man of God is still walking in perfect obedience. He has not yet been tempted, manipulated, or deceived. He is still doing exactly what God told him to do.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering notes that this verse 'establishes his faithfulness at the start, which makes his subsequent failure all the more devastating.' This is a crucial narrative function. By showing the man of God's obedience at the outset, the author prepares the reader for the shocking reversal that comes in verses 11-19. We will see this faithful man—who refused a king, cited God's word with clarity, and took an alternate route in obedience—become confused, wavering, and ultimately disobedient. The narrative contrast makes the tragedy all the more poignant. He was so faithful at the beginning. What went wrong? The answer will unfold as we see how the old prophet deceives him.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: There is also a subtle psychological element here. The man of God has successfully completed the hardest part of his mission: delivering the word to the king's face, refusing royal pressure, and maintaining his boundary. Now he is heading home. His mission is accomplished. His resolve might naturally begin to relax. He has done the hard thing. He has obeyed the difficult command. Might not a more subtle temptation—the old prophet's claim to have divine authorization—seem less threatening than the king's direct pressure? The man of God is now tired, hungry (he has eaten nothing since arriving in Bethel), and on the road. He is vulnerable in ways he was not when adrenaline and the confrontation with the king kept him sharp. This sets the stage psychologically for what follows.
commentary.application: This verse calls modern disciples to examine their own obedience. When God gives you a command, do you follow it with the same deliberateness the man of God demonstrates? He does not merely depart Bethel; he consciously takes an alternate route, showing that he has truly heard and internalized the command. The second application concerns the principle of moving forward without looking back. Once you have taken a stand for truth, once you have separated yourself from a spiritually compromised situation, you cannot afford to remain in that place or retrace your steps. The man of God's deliberate choice of an alternate route demonstrates this clearly: he is not lingering near Bethel. He is not tempted to reconsider. He is moving forward decisively. What 'alternate path' is God calling you to take? What compromise or temptation are you being called to move away from? The principle here is that obedience is often about movement, about actively choosing God's way and moving forward along it with intention and consciousness. Passive obedience—merely avoiding the prohibited path—is not enough. Active obedience involves deliberately walking the way God has shown you.

cross_references.connection: The old prophet will discover which road the man of God took and will pursue him on that alternate road. This shows that the specific detail of taking 'another way' becomes the means by which the man of God is eventually found and tempted. The obedience that protects him initially becomes, through deception, the mechanism of his undoing.

Lot's wife looks back at Sodom and becomes a pillar of salt, while Lot is commanded to flee and 'look not behind thee.' Like Lot's obedience (verses 15-17), the man of God's obedience to not return by the same way reflects the principle of leaving the place of judgment behind without looking back.

Joshua is told to 'observe to do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest.' The man of God's obedience to follow the exact route God has commanded him reflects this principle of careful adherence to God's word.

The proverb warns: 'There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.' The man of God, by following God's specific command about the route, avoids the way that 'seemeth right' to human reasoning and instead follows God's way.

word_study.term_english: went another way / went by a different road
word_study.meaning: Vayyelekh is the third-person masculine singular consecutive perfect ('and he went') of halakh. Bederekh is 'by the road' or 'on the path' (be- is the preposition 'in/on,' derekh is 'way' or 'path'). Acher is 'another' or 'different.'
word_study.significance: The specific choice of 'another way' (derekh acher) fulfills the command of verse 9 exactly. The man of God does not merely leave Bethel; he deliberately takes a different route. This shows his conscious obedience. He is not passively leaving; he is actively choosing a different path, demonstrating that he has heard and internalized God's command.

word_study.term_english: returned not by the way that he came
word_study.term_original: וְלֹא־שָׁב בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר בָּא בָּהּ אֶל־בֵּית־אֵל (velo shav baderekh asher ba bah el Bethel)
word_study.transliteration: ve-lo / shav / ba-derekh / asher / ba / bah / el
word_study.meaning: Velo is 've + lo' ('and not'). Shav is the third-person masculine singular perfect of shuv ('to return,' 'to turn back'). Baderekh is 'by the way.' Asher ba bah is 'which he went in it' (a relative construction with asher + ba + bah, where bah is the locative pronoun 'in it'). El is 'to,' and Bethel is the destination.
word_study.significance: The double emphasis on not returning ('returned not') and the specification of 'the way that he came' shows the deliberate nature of the man of God's obedience. He is actively choosing not to retrace his steps. This is not an accident; it is an intentional obedience that requires him to remember God's command and consciously walk a different path.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: When Nephi is directed by the Holy Ghost to do all things, he says 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them' (1 Nephi 3:7). The man of God's obedience in verse 10 reflects this same understanding: having received a command, he trusts that God will provide a way to fulfill it. He goes another way because God has commanded it, trusting that this too is part of God's provision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:8-10 establishes that 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The man of God's obedience to take an alternate route places him squarely in the category of those who do 'what I say,' and thus he remains bound by God's promises—at least for the moment. This will change when his obedience falters in the coming verses.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of following a specific, prescribed path (rather than taking one's own way) connects to temple theology, where the endowment involves progressing along a specific covenantal pathway that cannot be deviated from without consequence. The man of God's adherence to the specific route God has commanded foreshadows this temple principle.

commentary.historical_context: The emphasis on taking a different route (derekh acher) reflects the realities of ancient travel. Major roads in the Levant were well-established and relatively easy to follow, but alternate routes existed for those who knew the terrain or for those seeking to avoid detection or pursuit. A prophet traveling from Bethel back to Judah would have natural routes through the hill country, and an alternate route would not be difficult to find for someone familiar with the geography. The Covenant Rendering notes that the alternate route may serve a practical purpose (avoiding pursuit) but also functions symbolically. In ancient Near Eastern narrative, the choice of path often carries theological meaning. To choose a different way is to demonstrate separation from the place one has left. The man of God's deliberate choice of an alternate route would have been understood by an ancient Israelite audience as a clear statement: this prophet is finished with Bethel. He is not lingering. He is not tempted to return. He has completed his mission and is moving forward.
commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's obedience in walking the path God has set before him, without deviation, prefigures Christ's obedience in 'the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). Jesus consistently emphasizes that he does not follow his own will but the will of the Father who sent him. Like the man of God taking the alternate route in obedience, Jesus follows the path God has set before him, even when it leads to Calvary. The principle of trusting God's direction and following it faithfully, rather than choosing one's own way, is central to both.

text_kjv: Now there dwelt an old prophet in Bethel; and his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel: the words which he had spoken unto the king, them they told also to their father.

commentary.narrative: The narrative now introduces a new character: the old prophet in Bethel. The description 'old prophet' (navi zaqen) is deliberately ambiguous. We are not told whether he is a true prophet or a false one. We are simply told that he lives in Bethel and that his sons witnessed the confrontation between the man of God and King Jeroboam. The sons come home excited, full of news about the dramatic events of the day: a prophet has challenged the king, the altar has split, the king's hand has dried up and then been restored. They tell their father everything—the works (the miracles), the words (the prophecy), and the interaction with the king. The old prophet hears this account with keen interest. What might he be thinking? Is he moved by the sign? Is he concerned about Jeroboam's religious program? Or is he calculating something else? The text does not say. It merely sets the stage: an old prophet in Bethel, living in (and presumably complicit with) Jeroboam's false religious system, has just learned that a prophet from Judah has delivered God's judgment against it.
commentary.narrative_continued: The introduction of the old prophet is crucial to understanding the structure of this entire passage. The man of God has successfully completed his mission: he has refused the king, cited God's word, and taken an alternate route in obedience. He is walking away safely. But now we learn that there is another actor in the drama—someone who lives in Bethel and presumably knows its topography and its inhabitants. The old prophet's knowledge of 'which way' the man of God took (verse 12) suggests that he has connections in Bethel, people who would have noticed which road the stranger prophet took. The fact that he is willing to pursue the man of God raises questions about his motives. Is he seeking to reconcile the two prophets? Is he offended that the man of God refused Jeroboam's hospitality? Is he acting out of pride—jealous that a young prophet from Judah has come to his city and delivered such a powerful word? The text does not explicitly state his motives, but his actions will reveal them.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The detail that the old prophet's sons reported to him 'all the works' and 'all the words' is significant. These are the two categories of prophetic witness: signs (works) and words (prophecy). The sons have given their father a complete account of both. An old prophet living in Bethel, hearing such an account, would have understood the gravity of the situation. Something extraordinary has happened. The question is: what would a true prophet do with this information? Would he repent? Would he warn Jeroboam? Or would he do something else? The fact that the old prophet immediately becomes interested in which way the man of God went (verse 12) suggests that he has decided to pursue him. But why? This is the central mystery that will drive the rest of the narrative.
commentary.application: This verse introduces a critical principle for modern disciples: proximity to spiritual deception does not automatically corrupt you, but it can cloud your judgment. The old prophet lives in Bethel, a place of false worship. We do not know if he is complicit or merely silent, but his residence there raises questions. Modern application: What 'Bethel'—what place or community or institution—are you living in that might be compromised spiritually? Are you becoming so accustomed to spiritual error that you no longer recognize it? The second application concerns discernment. The old prophet's sons report the truth—they witnessed a genuine prophetic encounter and report it accurately. But their father's response to this true report will be calculated and deceptive. The lesson: just because someone correctly understands and reports what has happened does not mean their subsequent actions will be righteous. The old prophet will use his accurate knowledge of events as the basis for his deception. This is a sophisticated form of spiritual trap: using true information to establish credibility, then using that credibility to lead someone astray. What information about your testimony or commitments could be used by others to manipulate you into compromise?

cross_references.connection: The old prophet will use his age and his prophetic status to convince the man of God that the divine command has been reversed. The introduction here establishes his position and authority in Bethel, which he will later weaponize through deception.

Moses warns that a prophet may perform signs and wonders, yet if he leads people away from God, he is a false prophet who 'shall be put to death.' This passage becomes relevant as we learn more about the old prophet's character and motives. The Covenant Rendering notes that his prophetic status is ambiguous—he may be false.

Paul warns that false apostles can 'transform themselves into the apostles of Christ' and that 'Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.' The old prophet's ability to present himself as a man of God, despite his compromised relationship with Bethel's false worship, reflects this principle of deceptive appearance.

John advises to 'believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.' The man of God will face exactly this test when the old prophet appears, claiming divine authorization. The reader, like the man of God, must attempt to discern truth from falsehood.

word_study.meaning: Navi is 'prophet.' Echad is 'one,' creating the construct 'an old prophet.' Zaqen is 'old,' 'elder,' or 'aged.' The phrase is literally 'one prophet, old/an old one prophet.'
word_study.significance: The designation 'old prophet' carries ambiguity. In scripture, age can connote wisdom and authority, but it can also connote being out of touch or displaced. The fact that he is described as 'old' and living in Bethel, the site of Jeroboam's false worship, raises the question: is he a remnant of true prophecy, or has he been compromised by his long residence in this place of illegitimate worship? The Covenant Rendering does not specify his spiritual status, leaving the reader to draw conclusions from his subsequent actions.

word_study.meaning: Yoshev is the masculine singular participle of yashav ('to sit,' 'to dwell,' 'to remain,' 'to settle'). The participle form suggests a continuous state: he was dwelling, had been dwelling, lived there continuously.
word_study.significance: The choice of yoshev (dwell, settle) rather than a temporary verb suggests that the old prophet has made his home in Bethel. He is not a visiting prophet; he is a resident. This raises questions about his relationship to Jeroboam's religious establishment. How long has he been there? Has he witnessed the creation of Jeroboam's cult and remained silent? The Covenant Rendering's 'was living' captures the sense of settled, continuous residence.

word_study.term_english: his sons came and told him
word_study.term_original: וַיָּבוֹא בְנוֹ וַיְסַפֶּר־לוֹ (vayavo beno vayesaper lo)
word_study.transliteration: va- + yavo / beno / va- + yesaper / lo
word_study.meaning: Vayavo is 'and he came' (third-person masculine singular). Beno is 'his son' (constructed with possessive suffix, though the plural 'his sons' appears in the KJV rendering). Vayesaper is 'and he told' (third-person masculine singular of siper, 'to tell,' 'to recount,' 'to narrate'). Lo is 'him.'
word_study.significance: The verb siper ('to tell,' 'to recount') suggests a detailed narration. The sons are not merely informing their father; they are recounting, narrating, giving him a full account. This is how news travels in ancient societies—through eyewitnesses who come to trusted figures and give detailed accounts. The fact that it is the sons who bring the news suggests they were present at the confrontation in Bethel and are now reporting what they saw.

word_study.meaning: Et is the direct object marker. Kol is 'all,' 'everything.' Maaseh is 'work,' 'deed,' 'action,' or 'thing done.' The phrase means 'all the deeds/works.'
word_study.significance: The term maaseh (works) refers to the spectacular signs—the altar splitting, the king's hand drying up and being healed. These are the visible, miraculous works that demonstrate divine power. By reporting these 'works,' the sons are attesting to the supernatural dimension of the encounter.

word_study.term_english: the words which he had spoken unto the king
word_study.term_original: אֶת־הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ (et haddevarim asher diber el hammelek)
word_study.transliteration: et / haddevarim / asher / diber / el / hammelek
word_study.meaning: Et is the direct object marker. Haddevarim is 'the words' (plural of davar, 'word'). Asher is the relative particle 'which.' Diber is the third-person masculine singular perfect of davar ('to speak,' 'to say'). El is 'to.' Hammelek is 'the king.'
word_study.significance: The term devarim ('words') refers to the verbal prophecy—the man of God's condemnation of Jeroboam's altar and the prediction of future judgment. The sons report both the visible signs (works) and the spoken message (words), giving their father a complete prophetic picture.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains numerous accounts of prophets being deceived or confused by those who speak with apparent authority. Korihor, described as 'an anti-Christ,' confuses some of the people through persuasive speech despite his lack of true authority (Alma 30). The principle of discerning true from false prophetic authority becomes critical. The introduction of the old prophet here sets up a test of spiritual discernment—can the man of God distinguish between the old prophet's claim of divine authorization and the actual word of God he has received?
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 46:7-8 teaches that one gift of the Holy Ghost is the ability 'to know the differences of administration, as it will be pleasing unto the same Lord, to do the work of Christ according to the direction of his Church...another great and important gift is to know the diversities of operations of the same Spirit.' The man of God needs this gift—the ability to discern true prophetic authority from false—to navigate the encounter with the old prophet that follows.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of discerning true from false authority, and the importance of verifying claimed divine communications, became central to Restoration understanding of priesthood. Joseph Smith emphasized that claims to divine authority must be verified against the doctrines of Christ and the actual teachings of God. This episode prefigures that principle: a claimed prophetic message must be tested against the direct word of God the prophet has already received.

commentary.historical_context: The existence of prophets living in towns and cities throughout Israel (both north and south) is attested in biblical narratives. These prophets had varying relationships to the political establishment. Some were loyal to the king, others were critical. By 1 Kings 13, Jeroboam has been on the throne for a generation (approximately 20 years). A prophet living in Bethel would have witnessed the entire development of Jeroboam's religious program. The fact that the old prophet is described as 'old' might suggest he was already established in Bethel before or during Jeroboam's religious reforms. His choice to remain in Bethel rather than flee to Judah (where the legitimate temple stood) raises the question of whether he had accommodated himself to Jeroboam's program or whether he had been silenced by the king's religious establishment. The detail that his sons witnessed the confrontation and reported it to him suggests that they were free to move about in Bethel and observe public events. This would be consistent with a prophet's household being a known entity in the town.
commentary.christological_typology: The old prophet's ambiguous status—potentially a voice of God, but also potentially compromised by his proximity to false worship—reflects the broader scriptural pattern of testing prophetic authority. Jesus was constantly challenged to prove his authority. In John 5, Jesus points to multiple witnesses to his authority: John the Baptist, his works, the Father's voice, and scripture. The principle that genuine prophetic authority must be tested and verified runs throughout scripture and reaches its apex in the incarnate Word of God himself, whose authority is contested and must be proven through works and teachings.

text_kjv: And their father said unto them, What way went he? For his sons had seen what way the man of God went, which came from Judah.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet's first and immediate question is revealing: 'Which way did he go?' This is not a question of casual curiosity about the day's events. It is a question of urgent pursuit. The old prophet has heard about the confrontation, the miracles, and the prophecy, and his first instinct is to find out which direction the man of God took. He does not ask, 'What did he say?' or 'What did he prophesy?' His priority is to discover the route, the direction, the location. This reveals that the old prophet has already decided to pursue the man of God. His sons, having witnessed the event, know the answer: they saw which way the stranger from Judah departed. The Covenant Rendering notes that the old prophet's 'interest is pursuit, not curiosity.' This is the moment the reader understands that something ominous is beginning. The man of God, who has walked away in faithful obedience to God's command, does not yet know that he is being tracked.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'which came from Judah' (asher ba mi-Yehudah) is significant. It identifies the man of God not by his name (which we are never given) but by his geographical origin. He is a prophet from Judah, sent to confront the religious center of the northern kingdom. This identification is important for the old prophet's subsequent strategy. A prophet from Judah represents the authority of the south, of Jerusalem, of the true temple. To deceive such a prophet and get him to violate God's command would be a significant victory for the old prophet and, by extension, for Jeroboam's false religious system. The old prophet's pursuit of the man of God is not a neutral act; it is an attempt to neutralize the threat that this Judean prophet represents.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What we are witnessing is the setup for a trap. The man of God has been faithful. He has completed his mission. He has taken an alternate route in obedience. But now, unknown to him, an old man who lives in the very place he has just condemned is deliberately seeking him out. The old prophet knows something crucial that the man of God does not: the location, the approximate direction, and the fact that the prophet is on the road. The old prophet is not a king with an army; he is not an obvious threat. He is an elderly prophet, potentially presenting himself as a brother in the prophetic calling. This makes him a far more dangerous threat than Jeroboam ever was, because the man of God will lower his guard with him. He will assume that an old prophet would be a voice of truth and godliness, not deception.
commentary.application: This verse serves as a warning about the nature of spiritual danger. The most dangerous threats often come not from obvious opposition (like Jeroboam's direct pressure) but from those who appear to share your faith and authority. The old prophet is about to approach the man of God not as an enemy, but as a brother prophet. This should raise a question for modern disciples: Who in your life is pursuing you with seemingly righteous intentions but might actually be trying to lead you away from God's word? It could be a family member who loves you, a friend who seems wise and caring, a church member who appears righteous. The warning is not to be suspicious of everyone, but to be clear: if someone is pressuring you (however gently) to deviate from a direct command from God, they are working against you, no matter how righteous they appear. Additionally, the old prophet's immediate focus on 'which way did he go?' rather than engagement with the prophecy or its content suggests something important: people who are not genuinely concerned with truth will often focus on practical details (location, isolation, opportunity) rather than on the actual message. If someone seems more interested in where you are going and how isolated you are than in the actual content of your faith, that is a red flag. What 'old prophets' in your life might be pursuing you with intentions other than your spiritual welfare?

cross_references.connection: Later in this chapter, after the man of God dies (killed by a lion as judgment for his disobedience), the old prophet goes to mourn him and brings him back to Bethel for burial. This shows the old prophet's continued interest in the man of God and his fate throughout the narrative.

The proverb states: 'A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.' The man of God, despite his earlier faithfulness, will fail to foresee the trap the old prophet is setting. This represents a failure of prudence and discernment.

Jesus tells his disciples: 'Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.' The man of God needs this balance—the spiritual innocence to obey God's word, but also the discernment (wisdom as serpents) to recognize danger when it appears in a deceptive form.

Peter warns: 'Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.' The old prophet, though not the devil himself, becomes an instrument through which deception and temptation approach the man of God. The man of God's failure to maintain vigilance will be his undoing.

word_study.term_original: אֵי־זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ הָלָךְ (ei zeh haderekh halakh)
word_study.meaning: Ei is an interrogative particle 'where,' 'which,' or 'what.' Zeh is the demonstrative 'this,' 'that,' or 'which.' Haderekh is 'the road,' 'the way,' or 'the path' (with the definite article). Halakh is the third-person masculine singular perfect of halakh ('to walk,' 'to go,' 'to travel').
word_study.significance: The question 'ei zeh haderekh' is intensely focused on the route. The old prophet is not asking about the prophecy or the events; he is asking about the direction. This reveals his intent: he wants to know where to find the man of God. The Covenant Rendering's rendering of this as 'Which road did he take?' captures the urgency and specificity of the inquiry.

word_study.meaning: Vayiru is the third-person masculine plural perfect of ra'ah ('to see,' 'to perceive,' 'to observe'). Banav is 'his sons' (constructed with possessive suffix).
word_study.significance: The verb ra'ah ('to see') carries the weight of eyewitness testimony. The sons did not hear about the man of God's departure; they saw it with their own eyes. This is firsthand testimony, which makes their answer to their father reliable. However, it also makes the old prophet's pursuit more informed and therefore more calculated.

word_study.meaning: Asher is the relative particle 'who,' 'which,' 'that.' Ba is 'came' (the third-person masculine singular perfect of ba', 'to come,' 'to go,' 'to arrive'). Mi is the preposition 'from.' Yehudah is 'Judah.'
word_study.significance: The identification 'which came from Judah' (asher ba mi-Yehudah) is crucial. It marks the man of God as an outsider and as a representative of the southern kingdom and the legitimate temple worship. For the old prophet, living in Bethel and presumably accommodating himself to Jeroboam's cult, this southern prophet represents a threat to the religious status quo. The Covenant Rendering notes: 'His sons had seen the road the man of God from Judah had taken,' emphasizing both the geographical origin and the specific knowledge the sons possess.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Alma is pursued and confronted by various individuals and groups who seek to either destroy him or redirect him from his mission. The principle of being pursued or tracked by those with less than righteous intent appears several times (e.g., Alma 8:9-10, where Alma is beaten by those who oppose him). The man of God's situation here—being tracked by an old prophet who appears outwardly righteous but is actually pursuing him for questionable motives—represents a more subtle form of this kind of opposition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:31-32 teaches that 'Beware of false prophets, which come unto you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Ye shall know them by their fruits.' The old prophet, in his outward appearance (old, established in Bethel, apparently righteous), wears 'sheep's clothing.' The man of God must learn to test prophetic claims against the actual word of God he has received—the only reliable basis for discernment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of maintaining sacred boundaries and not being drawn outside the covenantal path by those who present themselves as authorities parallels temple theology. The endowment teaches the principle that we must learn to recognize and resist the subtle temptations and deceptions that seek to divert us from the covenant path. The old prophet's pursuit of the man of God becomes an enactment of how such temptation often comes—not as an obvious evil, but as something that appears righteous and authoritative.

commentary.historical_context: The question 'Which way went he?' reflects the practical geography of the land. Ancient Palestine had established roads and also lesser-known routes. A prophet departing from Bethel could have taken several possible paths heading south toward Judah. The fact that the old prophet's sons can report the specific direction shows that they were observant and that the departure was notable enough to be observed and remembered. In a town like Bethel, a foreign prophet's arrival and departure would have been an event of some moment. The old prophet's immediate pursuit suggests both his mobility (despite his age, he is capable of travel) and his determination. The identification of the man of God 'which came from Judah' is also geographically specific. Bethel lies just north of the Judah-Israel border, making it a natural point of contact between the northern and southern kingdoms. A prophet from Judah traveling to Bethel would have crossed a border and entered foreign (and, from his perspective, religiously hostile) territory. The old prophet's awareness of this geographical and political distinction ('which came from Judah') shows that he understands the significance of this southern prophet's appearance in his town.
commentary.christological_typology: Jesus repeatedly warned his disciples about false prophets and deceptive authorities who would appear righteous but lead people astray. The principle that internal deception is more dangerous than external opposition runs throughout Jesus' teachings. The old prophet, by virtue of his age and his prophetic status, presents himself with an appearance of authority that the man of God will find difficult to resist. Jesus himself faced this: the Pharisees and Sadducees appealed to their authority as teachers of the law and representatives of the religious establishment. Jesus' response was to appeal to a higher authority—the Father's word—and to test all teachings against it. The man of God, in theory, should do the same, but he will fail where Jesus succeeds.

text_kjv: And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon,

commentary.narrative: The old prophet has heard the man of God's prophecy against the altar and Jeroboam's idolatrous worship. Now he takes action—not to intercept the man of God immediately, but to prepare his donkey for pursuit. The command is simple and practical: chavash li ha-chamor ('saddle the donkey for me'). His sons obey without question, and he mounts the animal. Yet this mundane act of preparation is loaded with narrative significance. The Covenant Rendering notes that the verb chavash (to saddle, bind, harness) will recur throughout the chapter, creating a rhythmic pattern: departure frames both the old prophet's deceptive chase and the man of God's final, fatal journey.

word_study.meaning: To saddle, bind, gird, harness an animal for riding or work. The root carries the sense of binding or securing something firmly.
word_study.significance: The repetition of chavash in verses 13, 23, and 27 creates a narrative refrain: each departure (the old prophet's, the man of God's) is marked by the act of saddling a donkey. This verbal repetition subtly links the old prophet's pursuit to the man of God's doom. By verse 27, when the man of God is saddled onto a donkey again—this time lifeless—the verb carries ironic weight.

word_study.meaning: Male children, descendants. In this context, the old prophet's literal sons, who serve his household.
word_study.significance: The old prophet's sons appear here as obedient servants, unaware of their father's deceptive intention. They will not reappear in the narrative, but their presence underscores the domestic setting from which deception springs. The man of God has no household to witness his departure or mourn his death.

cross_references.connection: The same verb chavash (saddle) appears again when the old prophet saddles his donkey to retrieve the man of God's corpse, completing the narrative rhythm begun here.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death—the old prophet's path of deception leads both himself and the man of God toward judgment.

False prophets and teachers arise among the people, even as there shall be false prophets among you—the old prophet exemplifies the type of corrupted prophet who uses the language of revelation to deceive.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, donkeys were the primary means of long-distance travel for non-military figures. The act of saddling a donkey was quick and routine. The old prophet's decision to pursue the man of God immediately—rather than waiting or sending a messenger—suggests urgency and personal investment. The household structure (commanding sons) reflects the patriarchal authority typical of the period, with obedience expected and given without explanation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 30:20-30, Korihor, a false prophet, deceives many by claiming angelic authority and speaking flattering words. Like the old prophet, he uses the appearance of prophetic credentials to contradict true messengers. Both narratives warn against accepting contradictory spiritual claims, even when voiced with apparent authority.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 teaches that Church leaders should 'give unto [the] servants... every good thing; and labor with your hands.' The old prophet labors to catch the man of God through deception rather than honest persuasion, inverting the principle of righteous work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The man of God was sent to the altar with a covenant word from the Lord—a solemn charge. The old prophet's pursuit and deception represent a violation of covenantal boundaries. Covenant keepers do not deceive fellow servants, even if they disagree with their message.

commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's obedience to divine instruction (which he will shortly abandon) prefigures Christ's willing obedience to the Father's will, even unto death. The old prophet's deceptive use of angelic authority inverts the heavenly realm's role: where angels serve truth, the old prophet invokes their authority in service of a lie.
commentary.application: This verse establishes the old prophet's agency and premeditation. He does not stumble into deception; he actively prepares and pursues it. Modern disciples must recognize that spiritual deception rarely arrives unannounced. It is usually preceded by deliberate choices, planning, and a willingness to misuse the language and credentials of faith. We ought to examine our own motivations when we are tempted to override someone else's revealed direction or to claim authority we do not have.

text_kjv: And went after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak: and he said unto him, Art thou the man of God that camest from Judah? And he said, I am.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet's pursuit succeeds. He finds the man of God yoshev tachat ha-elah—sitting under a terebinth tree, a large shade tree associated with sacred sites and rest. The man of God has stopped his journey rather than pressing forward to his destination. This is the first sign of his vulnerability. He responds to the old prophet's identification question with simple affirmation: ani ('I am'). The tone is neutral—no suspicion, no guarded response, only acknowledgment. Yet in this moment of fatigue and repose, before the old prophet has spoken his lie, the man of God is already susceptible to deception because he has already violated the command to avoid delay and fellowship.

word_study.meaning: Sitting, dwelling, remaining in a place. The participle conveys an ongoing or habitual state.
word_study.significance: The man of God is not merely resting momentarily; he is actively sitting, settled under the tree. This suggests he has made a deliberate stop—contradicting the urgency of his divine commission. The very posture indicates a departure from his mission.

word_study.meaning: A large, long-lived tree (likely Pistacia lentiscus or Quercus calliprinos), valued for its shade and associated with sacred covenant sites in the Hebrew Bible.
word_study.significance: The elah is not arbitrary. Sacred trees mark theophanic sites: Abraham met the Lord under the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 18:1). Joshua erected a pillar under an oak as a witness to covenant (Joshua 24:26). The man of God sits under a tree that evokes sacred encounter, yet he encounters deception instead. The sacred geography becomes ironic—a place of shade and rest becomes a trap.

word_study.meaning: I, myself. A simple first-person pronoun affirming identity.
word_study.significance: The man of God's response is stark and undefended. He does not ask who the old prophet is, does not inquire about his purpose, does not invoke God's name. His simple ani ('I am') confirms his identity without any protective question or invocation. This openness will be exploited immediately.

cross_references.connection: Abraham sits in the tent door and is visited by the LORD under the oaks of Mamre—a covenant encounter. The man of God sits under the terebinth but encounters deception instead of divine presence.

Joshua sets up a stone under an oak tree as a witness to the covenant. The tree marks a place of covenant renewal. Here, the man of God sits where covenants are marked, yet violates his own covenant word.

Jesus retreats to Gethsemane to pray and finds his disciples sleeping when he returns; he is vulnerable to betrayal while his companions rest. Similarly, the man of God's rest and fatigue leave him open to the old prophet's approach.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: the man of God should have tested the old prophet's claim with spiritual discernment but does not.

commentary.historical_context: The terebinth tree (elah) was a real and significant feature of the Palestinian landscape. Large shade trees provided refuge from the heat of the day—critical for travelers in an arid region. The man of God's stop under the elah is physically sensible but spiritually dangerous. In the ancient Near East, hospitality was a sacred obligation, and refusing an invitation to eat and drink could be seen as insulting. The old prophet exploits both the man of God's fatigue and the cultural expectation of hospitality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 1:1-8, false priests arise and lead people away from righteousness by claiming authority and speaking pleasing words. The old prophet is a corrupted priesthood figure who uses the apparatus of prophetic calling to undermine truth. Alma 5:41-42 warns against false teachers who cry 'Peace, peace' but lack the Spirit.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:5 teaches that those who are sealed by the Spirit receive a promise of eternal life. The man of God has received a sealing word from the Lord (his covenant instruction), yet he begins to break faith through fatigue and lack of vigilance. D&C 121:1-6 shows that prophets are not exempt from trials and tests.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sacred tree evokes temple imagery—a place of divine encounter and covenant. The man of God's willingness to be drawn into conversation under the sacred tree, though already bound by covenant, represents the vulnerability of covenant keepers to subtle temptations. The tree itself remains sacred, but the man of God's presence there becomes compromised by his disobedience.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ withdrew to places of solitude to pray (Luke 5:16), but he remained vigilant and never deviated from his mission. The man of God's rest prefigures the temptations Christ faced—weariness, hunger, and offers of fellowship—but unlike the man of God, Christ did not waver from his covenant purpose.
commentary.application: Rest is necessary and good, but rest can become a vulnerability if it disconnects us from our sacred responsibilities. The man of God has left his post to sit in ease. Similarly, modern disciples must guard against the spiritual fatigue that comes from the demands of covenant keeping, recognizing that in moments of weariness, we are most susceptible to compromises that seem reasonable, even hospitable. The simplicity of his answer—'I am'—also warns against careless openness. We should not confirm our identity or position to those we do not know, without first understanding their intent.

text_kjv: Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet's first assault is the most disarming: a simple invitation to hospitality. Lekhah itti habbaytah ve-ekhol lachem—'come with me to the house and eat food.' This echoes the offer that Jeroboam made in verse 7, but without the incentive of a gift or reward. The old prophet presents himself not as a king but as a peer, a fellow prophet extending neighborly hospitality. The invitation is framed in language that appears natural and innocent. No mention is made of the prohibition the man of God must keep. The old prophet does not need to argue or cajole; he simply opens his home. This is the genius of the deception: it does not immediately contradict the covenant word; it simply invites the man of God to step outside the boundaries of obedience before speaking the false revelation.

word_study.meaning: Come, go. An imperative form of halak (to walk, go, proceed).
word_study.significance: Lekhah is a direction, an invitation to journey. It echoes the command the man of God received: 'Go' and deliver the prophecy. Now he is invited to 'come'—a different direction, away from his mission. The subtle shift in direction (away from Jeroboam and toward the old prophet's home) mirrors the spiritual diversion that is occurring.

word_study.meaning: House, household, dwelling, family. Can also mean temple or sanctuary.
word_study.significance: The bayit ('house') is a place of intimacy and trust. It is where covenant is practiced in the daily life of a family. By inviting the man of God into his bayit, the old prophet creates a false sense of kinship and safety. The man of God is drawn into a domestic space where social bonds make refusal more difficult.

word_study.meaning: Bread, food, sustenance. More broadly, the staff of life or covenant meal.
word_study.significance: Lechem is not merely nutrition; shared bread is covenant food. To eat together is to enter into fellowship. By refusing, the man of God would signal a breach in fellowship. The old prophet uses the most basic human need—hunger and hospitality—to create social pressure against the covenant command.

cross_references.connection: Jeroboam offered the man of God a reward and invitation to his house; the man of God refused. Now a different figure (the old prophet) makes a similar offer, and the refusal will be repeated—but ultimately overturned.
Lot's visitors are urged to come to his house and eat. The shared meal becomes a place of covenant blessing—but when misused, it can also be a place of exposure and violation.

In the parable of the prodigal son, the father calls for bread and celebration. Shared bread and meal signify reconciliation and entry into the household. The old prophet uses this same cultural vocabulary deceptively.

Paul discusses eating food offered in temples and homes: 'Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat.' The principle is that not all eating is spiritual, but eating shared in defiance of covenant is.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Levantine culture, the refusal of bread and hospitality was a grave insult. To accept someone's invitation was to enter a bond of mutual protection and respect. The old prophet's offer is therefore doubly cunning: it offers the man of God what he physically needs (food after travel) while placing him in a social debt. Refusing would require explicit breach of cultural protocol. The old prophet's home would be a place where the man of God's isolation from his divine commission would become complete—surrounded by the old prophet's family and servants, he would lack witnesses to his covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 28:7-8, false prophets say 'eat, drink, and be merry.' They use the language of hospitality and ease to draw people from truth. Similarly, the old prophet's offer of bread is framed as harmless kindness, yet it leads to covenant violation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 112:28 warns against being 'deceived by fine-sounding doctrines.' The old prophet's invitation sounds fine and reasonable—simple hospitality. D&C 46:7-8 teaches the importance of discerning spirits and knowing true prophets from false.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, bread is broken and water is taken as a covenant renewal. The man of God's refusal of bread and water in verse 16-17 is a refusal to enter into covenant with the old prophet. When he later accepts the old prophet's food, he breaks covenant with the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ was tempted in the wilderness to turn stones into bread (Matthew 4:3-4), yet he responded that man does not live by bread alone but by every word from God's mouth. The man of God faces a similar test: will he prioritize the hospitality of bread, or the word of the Lord? Unlike Christ, he will fail this test.
commentary.application: Hospitality is a virtue, and rejecting genuine kindness can be wrong. Yet there are moments when accepting hospitality means breaking a higher covenant. The test for modern disciples is to develop the discernment to recognize when an offer of human kindness—however genuine it may seem—would compromise our sacred obligations. This verse teaches us to ask: Whose table am I sitting at? What fellowship does it represent? Does accepting this meal commit me to something that violates my covenant with God?

text_kjv: And he said, I may not return with thee, nor go in with thee: neither will I eat bread nor drink water with thee in this place:

commentary.narrative: The man of God holds firm—at least at first. His refusal is complete and direct: lo ukhal lashuv ittekhah ve-lavo ittekhah ve-lo okhal lechem ve-lo eshteh ittekhah mayim ba-maqom ha-zeh. 'I cannot go back with you or come with you, and I will not eat food or drink water with you in this place.' The verb lo ukhal does not express mere unwillingness; it expresses inability rooted in divine constraint. The repetition of the refusal (first negating his return and entry, then negating food and water) creates a verbal wall of resistance. The phrase 'in this place' (ba-maqom ha-zeh) is critical: he has not decided to break his covenant yet; he is still defending its boundaries. His refusal mirrors his response to Jeroboam in verse 7, showing that at this point, the man of God still recalls and honors his original commission.

word_study.meaning: To be able, to have the power or capacity to do something. The negative lo ukhal ('I cannot') expresses inability, not mere unwillingness.
word_study.significance: The man of God does not say 'I will not' (lo aveh) but 'I cannot' (lo ukhal). This is crucial: he presents his refusal not as personal preference but as a constraint imposed from outside—the constraint of the divine word. By using ukhal, he is asserting that the command from God has made him unable to comply with the old prophet's request, no matter how reasonable it sounds.

word_study.meaning: In this place, in this location. Specifies a geographic boundary to the prohibition.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'ba-maqom ha-zeh' is more specific than the divine instruction itself (which does not mention a specific place). By adding it, the man of God is building a fence around the covenant—a common Jewish practice of adding protective stipulations. He is saying: not just anywhere, but especially not here, in the territory where Jeroboam's false altar stands and where my message must be delivered.

cross_references.connection: The man of God uses nearly identical language to refuse Jeroboam: 'I may not go with thee.' His consistency shows that at this point, he has not yet begun to waver.

Peter refuses to eat unclean food, saying 'Not so, Lord.' His refusal is based on a divine command he believes he received. Like the man of God, he initially will not violate what he believes God has commanded.
In Gethsemane, Jesus says 'Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.' The man of God should have said something similar to resist the old prophet, but he does not.

Moses teaches detailed laws about where Israelites may eat and drink in covenant obedience. The man of God's specificity about 'this place' echoes the concern for proper locations and proper conditions in covenant observance.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, to refuse food was to refuse covenant fellowship. Yet there were legitimate reasons for such refusal. Priests and those under vows of separation often had dietary restrictions. The man of God's invocation of a divine prohibition would have been understood as analogous to priestly restrictions or Nazirite vows. The old prophet, hearing this refusal, would have recognized that the man of God was claiming a special status—a direct divine commission that superseded ordinary social obligation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 42:1-3, Alma explains the law of restoration and the importance of strictly adhering to divine law. The man of God's strict adherence here (before his wavering) mirrors the principle that covenant must be kept precisely and completely.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 98:11-12 teaches that keeping covenants should take priority over all other concerns. The man of God's refusal exemplifies this principle—he prioritizes the divine word over hospitality, comfort, and social obligation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the principle that the Lord's word must be honored above all else. The man of God's firm refusal to eat or drink 'in this place' reflects the solemnity with which he has taken his covenant commission.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's fasting in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-4) demonstrates a refusal to prioritize physical sustenance over spiritual obedience. The man of God's refusal here parallels Christ's principle, though the man of God will later contradict it when he accepts the old prophet's food.
commentary.application: This verse stands as a moment of strength before failure—a reminder of what the man of God once knew with certainty. For modern disciples, this is instructive: the man of God's initial refusal shows that he possessed the clarity and strength to resist. The question then becomes: what changed? Why did he later accept what he so firmly refused here? The answer lies not in the old prophet's credentials but in the man of God's own weariness, loneliness, and loss of vigilance. This teaches us that our initial convictions—however firm—must be actively maintained through continued prayer, remembrance, and resistance to fatigue and isolation.

text_kjv: For it was said to me by the word of the LORD, Thou shalt eat no bread nor drink water there; nor turn again to go by the way that thou camest.

commentary.narrative: The man of God now recites his covenant obligation in full, articulating the three-fold prohibition that constrains him. Ki davar elai be-dvar YHWH—'For the word came to me by the word of the LORD.' He repeats the command with precision: lo tochal lechem ve-lo tishte sham mayim lo tashub lalekhet ba-derekh asher halakhta bah. 'You must not eat food or drink water there. You must not go back the way you came.' The repetition is exhaustive and explicit. By reciting the command aloud, the man of God does multiple things simultaneously: (1) he reminds himself of the strictness of the prohibition; (2) he informs the old prophet of exactly what God has commanded; and (3) he places the command on record, so that there can be no later claim of ignorance or ambiguity. The reader hears the divine law clearly stated—no eating, no drinking (there), no returning by the same route. This will make the man of God's subsequent violation all the more tragic and inexcusable.

word_study.meaning: The word/utterance of the LORD. Davar ('word') is the fundamental unit of divine speech—not merely linguistic but performative, carrying authority and creative force.
word_study.significance: The man of God does not say 'I was told' or 'I understand.' He says davar elai be-dvar YHWH—'a word came to me by the word of YHWH.' Davar is the same term used for God's creative speech ('Let there be light'—vayomer YHWH yehi or). By using davar, the man of God elevates his commission beyond mere instruction; it is a performative utterance that has shaped reality and obligation. It is irrevocable.

word_study.meaning: You shall eat, you shall drink. Second-person singular imperative negatives, creating strict prohibitions.
word_study.significance: The doubling of the prohibition—no eating and no drinking—eliminates any loophole or partial compliance. The man of God cannot argue that he can eat without drinking, or drink water even if he abstains from food. Both are forbidden. This completeness of the prohibition should foreclose any possibility of compromise.

word_study.meaning: You shall not return, the way you came. Tashub ('return') and halakhta ('walked') emphasize the physical path and the need for a different return route.
word_study.significance: The third prohibition is not merely about abstinence from food; it is about a change of route. The man of God is not simply prohibited from staying; he is directed to depart by a different way. This suggests an element of secrecy or safety—he must leave and not retrace his steps. Perhaps the different route prevents him from encountering Jeroboam again, or being pursued, or falling into the old prophet's trap on his return. The prohibition is protective as well as prohibitive.

cross_references.connection: The LORD commanded Adam: 'Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat.' Both commands are stark, complete, and unambiguous. Both will be violated by the hearer.

Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it. The man of God's accurate recitation of the command exemplifies the principle that God's word must be kept exactly, without addition or diminution.

The old prophet will later reveal (or claim to reveal) a countermanding word. This verse makes clear that any subsequent command to violate the original word would be a test of obedience to the first word.
Paul warns: though an angel from heaven preach any other gospel unto you, let him be accursed. A different instruction, even from an angelic source, cannot override a prior word from God.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the recitation of a command was a formal act—it placed the command in the hearing of witnesses (in this case, the old prophet), and it created accountability. By reciting the full prohibition, the man of God was not merely reminding himself; he was establishing a legal and spiritual record. The three-fold nature of the prohibition (food, water, return route) shows the meticulous specificity of the divine commission. This was not a vague spiritual intuition but a detailed instruction with concrete behavioral expectations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 3:7, Nephi says 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them.' The man of God has received a clear command and should trust in the Lord's provision. He does not yet understand how the prohibition will protect him.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 82:10 teaches: 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The man of God will soon break the promise by violating the word, and the promise of protection will fail.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony emphasizes the taking of covenants and the necessity of keeping them strictly. The man of God's articulation of his covenant obligation mirrors the solemn nature of temple covenants—they must be remembered, honored, and kept.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ recited and honored God's word perfectly. When tempted by Satan to break his covenant by turning stones into bread (Matthew 4:3-4), Christ responded with Scripture: 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.' Christ's obedience is the inverse of the man of God's coming failure.
commentary.application: This verse is a moment of perfect clarity. The man of God knows exactly what he is commanded to do, and he articulates it with precision. For modern disciples, this is a profound teaching: we should regularly recite and remember our covenants. When tempted to compromise, we should speak aloud what we have promised the Lord. The act of articulation creates clarity and accountability. The tragedy is that the man of God will soon violate what he has just clearly stated. This teaches us that knowing the covenant is not enough; we must actively defend it, remain vigilant, and not allow fatigue, loneliness, or the appeal of false authority to erode our obedience.

text_kjv: He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him.

commentary.narrative: This is the pivot of the entire chapter—the moment where deception becomes explicit and the man of God's fate is sealed. The old prophet speaks with measured authority: gam ani navi kamokha—'I too am a prophet, just like you.' By claiming equality of prophetic status, he positions himself as a peer, not an inferior or a false claimant. Then comes the claim of angelic authority: umal'akh dibber elai bi-dvar YHWH—'an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD.' He uses the exact same formula of authority that the man of God used to describe his original commission. The angel's supposed message is direct and countermanding: 'Bring him back with you to your house so that he may eat food and drink water.' The instruction directly contradicts the man of God's original covenant. It nullifies the prohibition. It invites him to fellowship and hospitality. Every term is designed to exploit the man of God's fatigue and isolation. And then comes the narrator's verdict, delivered with devastating finality: kikhesh lo—'He lied to him.' This is the only moment in the chapter where the narrator breaks from reported speech to deliver a direct editorial judgment. The verb kikhesh means to deceive, to speak falsely, to deny truth. The narrator does not allow ambiguity: the old prophet is a liar, his claim of angelic authority is false, and his countermanding instruction is deceptive.

word_study.meaning: A prophet, one who speaks for God. The root may be related to 'fountain' or 'spokesman'—one through whom divine speech flows.
word_study.significance: The old prophet claims to be a navi kamokha ('a prophet like you'). The claim may be true or false—the text does not disclose his actual prophetic status. But what matters is that he uses prophetic credentials falsely, to speak a message that contradicts the true word of God. His claim of prophetic status gives him standing to be heard; it lowers the man of God's guard.

word_study.meaning: Also, likewise, even. An inclusive conjunction that asserts solidarity or equality.
word_study.significance: Gam ani navi kamokha—'I too am a prophet like you.' The word gam ('also') establishes kinship. It says: we are the same kind of person, we share the same calling, we stand on equal ground. This rhetorical move is crucial to the deception. It makes the man of God feel less isolated and more likely to listen.

word_study.meaning: Messenger, angel. A term for a heavenly being sent with God's message, or sometimes a human messenger.
word_study.significance: By claiming that a mal'akh spoke to him, the old prophet invokes not just human prophecy but heavenly authority. Angels carry divine messages; they have direct access to God's throne. The claim of angelic visitation would be stunning and would demand attention. Yet the 'word' the angel delivered contradicts God's actual word. This is the deepest irony: the apparatus of truth (angelic authority, divine word) is deployed in service of a lie.

word_study.meaning: He lied, he deceived, he denied truth. To speak falsely, to deny what is true, to lead astray.
word_study.significance: Kikhesh lo is placed after the old prophet's speech, not before it. The reader first hears the lie, then learns that it is a lie.
