This narrative technique implicates the reader in the dilemma: for a moment, we experience the uncertainty the man of God felt. But there is no ambiguity in the narrator's judgment. The verdict is flat and unqualified: he lied. Not 'he may have lied' or 'he claimed to speak for God.' He lied. The use of kikhesh, rather than a softer term, emphasizes the gravity of the deception. He did not misunderstand or err; he deliberately spoke falsely.

cross_references.connection: If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder... thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet. The law explicitly warns against false prophets, even those who perform signs. The man of God should have invoked this principle and refused the old prophet's contradictory claim.
Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. The old prophet's claim of angelic authority echoes the strategy Paul warns against: deception cloaked in the language of heavenly authority.

Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. The man of God fails to 'try' the old prophet's claim; he does not test it against his original word from God.

Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. Paul explicitly warns that even an angelic messenger cannot overturn a prior revelation. The man of God should have held this principle firm.

Earlier in the chapter, the narrator describes the old prophet as dwelling in Bethel, the center of Jeroboam's false religion. His proximity to idolatry suggests his spiritual corruption and his vulnerability to serving false ends.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, prophetic authority was powerful and rare. A prophet who could claim angelic visitation would command extraordinary respect. False prophets typically imitated the language and apparatus of true prophecy to gain credibility. The old prophet's claims (prophetic status, angelic authority, word of the LORD) mirror the exact vocabulary of legitimate prophecy. An observer without access to the narrator's judgment might have believed him. This is the tragedy: in a world where true prophets and false prophets could both claim the same credentials, how is the disciple to know? The answer, implied by the text, is that the original word from God must be the measure of all subsequent claims. If a new revelation contradicts an established divine word, the new revelation is false—regardless of the credentials of the one who delivers it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mormon 8:32-34, Moroni warns that 'because of pride, and because of false teachers, and false doctrine, their churches have become corrupted... Because of priestcraft and iniquities, they have become corrupt.' The old prophet exemplifies priestcraft—the use of prophetic office for personal ends. In Alma 39:11, Alma warns Corianton that some false priests 'lead many astray after their own foolish doctrines.' The old prophet leads the man of God astray by claiming authority he does not truly possess.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 teaches that Church leaders 'shall be with [you], inasmuch as [you] contend against the adversary in prayer always.' The man of God failed to pray before accepting the old prophet's offer; he did not contend against the adversary in prayer. D&C 46:8 teaches: 'The Spirit of Christ is given to every man, that he may know good from evil; wherefore, I show unto you the way to judge.' The man of God possessed the Spirit and should have used it to judge the old prophet's claim.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, the endowee learns that Satan will attempt to deceive even the elect through the use of language and forms that mimic the true. The old prophet's deception foreshadows Satan's strategy: the use of familiar prophetic language to lead the faithful astray. Temple covenants include the promise to discern and reject false spirits and false claims.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ faced a similar test in the wilderness when Satan quoted Scripture (Matthew 4:5-7), attempting to use the very word of God to lead him into sin. Christ recognized the deception and refused it, saying 'It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.' The man of God, unlike Christ, does not discern the deception. Christ's victory over this temptation makes him the true pattern of prophetic obedience that the man of God failed to follow.
commentary.application: This verse presents a test that modern disciples will face in various forms: contradictory instructions from those who claim authority. The principle is absolute and clear from the text: if a new instruction contradicts an established word from God, the new instruction is false—no matter how credible the source, no matter what credentials are claimed, no matter how reasonable the new instruction sounds. The man of God's failure was not in hearing the lie; it was in not remembering to test it against the original covenant word. Modern disciples must cultivate the habit of returning to God's established word as the measure of all subsequent claims. Prayer, fasting, and testimony become essential tools for discerning true from false authority. We must also recognize that isolation and fatigue make us vulnerable. The man of God was sitting alone under a tree, away from witnesses and support, when he was approached. We ought to remain connected to community, counsel, and established sources of truth when our faith is being tested.

text_kjv: So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water.

commentary.narrative:
This deceptively simple verse chronicles a catastrophic spiritual failure in three rapid-fire verbs, each one a direct violation of the explicit command given in verse 9. The man of God from Judah—who has just successfully completed his prophetic mission in Bethel, confronting Jeroboam and the corrupted altar—turns around and capitulates to the old prophet's deception. The brevity of the verse is telling: there is no internal struggle narrated, no moment of doubt or conscience wrestling. He simply complied. As the TCR translator notes indicate, 'The silence about his reasoning is part of the chapter's unsettling power.' This is not a moment of temptation overcome through prayer or spiritual discernment. It is immediate, unthinking obedience to a false prophet's lie.

The three verbs—vayyashav ('he returned'), vayyokhal ('he ate'), vayyesht ('he drank')—correspond precisely to the three prohibitions: 'thou shalt not eat bread nor drink water' (verse 9). The man of God was commanded not to return the same way, not to eat, and not to drink. He has now broken all three. The covenant violation is complete and unambiguous. What makes this moment particularly tragic is that the man of God possessed the very gift that should have protected him: prophetic discernment. He had just demonstrated the power to call down judgment and then restore it (verses 4–6). Yet he could not distinguish truth from falsehood when it came from another who claimed prophetic authority.

word_study.meaning: To turn, return, turn back; also to repent or restore. In this context, the physical reversal of direction becomes a spiritual reversal—a turning away from obedience.
word_study.significance: The verb shuv is used for repentance throughout the Hebrew Bible (Jeremiah 3:1, Malachi 3:7). Here it is used for the opposite: a turning toward disobedience. The irony is devastating—he 'returns' (shuv) but not in repentance; rather, he retraces his steps in violation of his orders.

word_study.meaning: To eat bread; in Hebrew idiom, bread is often the primary sustenance, metonymically representing all food. Eating also implies fellowship and covenant acceptance.
word_study.significance: By eating bread in the old prophet's house, the man of God not only violates a direct command but also enters into a covenant meal—a sign of fellowship and acceptance. In ancient Near Eastern practice, sharing a meal was a bond-forming act. He is communing with the very one who lied to him.

word_study.meaning: To drink water; water is essential sustenance in desert regions. The pairing of bread and water represents basic hospitality and covenant meal.
word_study.significance: Water, like bread, represents sustenance. In the covenant of silence and separation that the man of God was meant to maintain, both food and drink were forbidden. Accepting them meant accepting the hospitality and relationship offered by the old prophet—a false fellowship with a false messenger.

cross_references.connection: The explicit command against eating bread or drinking water, which the man of God now violates completely. These verses form a tragic envelope structure—command and violation.

Jesus would later quote this verse (Matthew 4:4) to resist temptation: 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.' The man of God's failure is the inverse of this principle—he chooses bread over God's word.

Peter's later reference to those who 'have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray' recalls this pattern of prophetic compromise. The man of God is a cautionary figure for spiritual vulnerability.

The prudent person 'foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself'; the simple person 'passeth on, and suffereth for it.' The man of God's naive acceptance of the old prophet's story makes him a cautionary example of spiritual naïveté.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite culture, refusing food and drink was an act of ritual separation and spiritual consecration. Prophets sometimes performed symbolic fasts or abstinence acts to mark their dedication to a divine mission (see Elijah's subsequent wilderness experience in 1 Kings 17). The man of God's abstinence was meant to signal that he came on the LORD's business, not for personal comfort or community participation. Accepting hospitality—especially from a resident elder prophet—would have seemed natural and courteous in the culture, which makes the violation all the more insidious. The old prophet was exploiting exactly this cultural norm: it would be rude and socially awkward to refuse food from an established religious figure. But the man of God had been given an explicit counter-cultural instruction, and he failed to honor it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains several warnings against false prophets who come with plausible claims and signs. In 2 Nephi 28, Nephi sees that 'false churches' will arise, and in Alma 30, Korihor is able to deceive many with smooth words. The man of God's failure parallels the vulnerability of the people of Nephi to false teachers who come with credentials. The principle is that even those with spiritual gifts can be deceived when they lower their guard.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 52:14 teaches that the faithful are to 'go forth saying none but Jesus Christ' and that they are to 'keep mine commandments continually.' The man of God's violation mirrors the specific warning in D&C 89 about the importance of adhering to commandments—not for the sake of the rule itself, but because the commandment is a covenant test of obedience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant emphasizes the importance of personal obedience to specific instructions and the danger of accepting plausible-sounding redirections from one's path. Just as a temple participant is instructed in specific covenants and ceremonies, the man of God was given specific instructions. Accepting a false narrative—even from someone who appears to have authority—violates the sacred nature of the covenant made.

commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's vulnerability to deception, despite his prophetic gift, points to the necessity of the Atonement. He possesses power (he called down fire from heaven) but lacks the steadfast obedience to God's word that only comes through Christ. In Matthew 4, Jesus faces similar temptation—to accept sustenance (bread from stones) and earthly authority—but refuses, declaring, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.' The man of God needed what only Christ could provide: the power to say 'no' to legitimate-seeming voices when they contradict God's explicit word.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern believers with a sobering reality: spiritual gift and prior obedience do not guarantee present faithfulness. The man of God had just performed a stunning miracle (healing the altar, calling down judgment, then reversing it), yet this very success may have bred confidence in his own judgment. The application is uncomfortable: do we lower our guard after a spiritual victory? Do we become more open to 'helpful suggestions' and 'new information' from religious voices we respect? Do we rationalize small violations of personal commitments we've made to God? The verse teaches that the test of faithfulness often comes not in a moment of obvious temptation, but in accepting what seems reasonable and hospitable from a trusted-seeming source. Each believer must ask: What specific commitments have I made to God that I am tempted to rationalize away? Where am I vulnerable to accepting a plausible lie from someone who appears to have authority?

text_kjv: And it came to pass, as they sat at the table, that the word of the LORD came unto the prophet that brought him back:

commentary.narrative:
The dramatic irony of this verse is perhaps the most staggering in the chapter. While the man of God and the old prophet sit at table in fellowship—a meal that seals a covenant violation—the word of the LORD comes to the very prophet who fabricated a lie. The man who told a false story about an angel now receives a genuine divine message. The text makes no attempt to justify this, explain it, or soften the blow. The narrator simply states the fact: dvar YHWH ('the word of the LORD') came to 'the prophet asher heshivo' ('who had brought him back')—ensuring that the reader cannot forget, even for a moment, that this is the one who deceived.

This verse shatters any neat theological framework for understanding how God speaks through prophets. The old prophet is not righteous. He lied deliberately, using a fabricated revelation to manipulate a visitor. Yet God chooses this compromised vessel to deliver a genuine word of judgment. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly presents this unsettling reality: prophetic function is not contingent on moral character. God can use a pagan king's seer (Balaam in Numbers 22–24), a deceived prophet (here), or even a donkey (Numbers 22:28) to deliver his word. What matters is the message, not the moral standing of the messenger in that moment. The old prophet becomes, in this instant, a genuine conduit of God's judgment, even as he remains culpable for his earlier deception.

word_study.meaning: The utterance, decree, or message of the LORD. Dvar means 'word' or 'thing' (sometimes indistinguishable); YHWH is the covenant name of God. Together, it indicates God's authoritative speech or command.
word_study.significance: The phrase dvar YHWH occurs over 240 times in the Hebrew Bible and is the standard formula for genuine prophetic utterance. Its appearance here—directed through the lying prophet—emphasizes that authenticity is determined not by the prophet's character but by the origin and nature of the message itself.

word_study.meaning: To come upon, to happen to, to occur; when used with the subject of divine speech, it indicates God's agency in bringing the word to a prophet.
word_study.significance: The verb hayah (literally 'to be, to become') combined with el ('to, toward') indicates that the word of the LORD came TO the prophet—divine initiative, not human invention. This is the language of genuine prophecy, in sharp contrast to the old prophet's fabrication.

cross_references.connection: God speaks through a donkey to rebuke the false prophet Balaam. Like the old prophet in 1 Kings 13, this demonstrates that God can use unexpected or compromised vessels to deliver truth, though the agents themselves may not be righteous.

Jeremiah condemns false prophets who 'dream dreams' and claim divine words falsely, in contrast to those who truly have the 'word' from the LORD. The old prophet's fabrication fits Jeremiah's definition of false prophecy, yet he now receives a genuine word.

Peter references Balaam as an example of a false prophet, but acknowledges that even through compromised vessels, God can rebuke sin. The old prophet's situation parallels Balaam's: both deceive, yet both are used by God to deliver judgment.

Paul writes that 'the foolishness of God is wiser than men.' The shocking use of a lying prophet to deliver judgment illustrates this principle—God's ways are not constrained by human categories of virtue and vice.

Alma testifies that he was 'wrought upon by the word [of the Lord],' indicating that in Latter-day Saint theology, the word of the Lord operates through divine agency regardless of the personal standing of the messenger at that moment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite religious culture, prophetic credentials were often ambiguous. There were schools of prophets, lone prophetic figures, and court prophets—and no institutional mechanism to definitively distinguish a true prophet from a false one (that only came with the canon of Scripture itself). The old prophet presumably had some standing in his community—he was elder, established, and lived where he could expect hospitality from traveling religious figures. His lie about the angel was plausible precisely because prophecy by angelic report was a known phenomenon (1 Kings 13:18 claims an angel spoke to him). The culture had no foolproof test except verification by other prophets or the fulfillment of the prophecy (see Deuteronomy 18:22). This verse reveals the genuine vulnerability of ancient Israelite prophetic culture to deception—a vulnerability that would become acute in the later monarchy as conflicting prophets offered contradictory advice (as in 1 Kings 22, where over 400 prophets tell Ahab one thing and Micaiah tells him another).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 30, Korihor is described as 'an anti-Christ' who comes with plausible arguments and deceives many. Like the old prophet, Korihor has a kind of authority and persuasiveness that leads people astray. Yet even Korihor is used by the LORD to deliver a judgment—he is struck dumb and becomes a beggar, a living sign. The principle recurs: God can use even false prophets or deceived figures to accomplish his purposes and deliver his judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 teaches that the President of the Church will be 'supported by the confidence, faith, and prayers of the church.' Yet D&C 28:2-7 addresses false prophets and the necessity of seeking divine confirmation. The old prophet's situation illustrates why members must not blindly follow even established religious figures without seeking personal confirmation—the old prophet was established and seemingly credible, yet he lied.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology emphasizes direct communion with God and personal confirmation of truth. The man of God's failure to rely on his own direct connection to God, instead accepting the old prophet's story, illustrates why temple covenant recipients are counseled to develop personal spiritual discernment rather than relying solely on others' reports.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate authority on prophecy and revelation. In Matthew 7:15-20, Jesus teaches, 'By their fruits ye shall know them'—a criterion that transcends the mere claim to prophetic authority. The old prophet's mouth later speaks a genuine word, but his earlier deception 'bears bad fruit.' Christ's teaching implies that the ultimate test is not momentary access to divine speech but consistent alignment of life with truth. The man of God's vulnerability to deception points to humanity's need for Christ as the steady, unchanging Word and Light—not dependent on discerning which prophet is speaking truthfully in any given moment.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the modern believer's relationship to authority and discernment. We live in an age of many voices claiming divine inspiration—not only in religious spheres but in politics, wellness, and ideology. The verse teaches that we cannot rely on external credentials alone (the old prophet's age, his establishment, his claim of a revelation) to verify truth. Even a false prophet can occasionally speak truth (or be used by God to deliver judgment). The application is to develop personal revelation and discernment. Ask: How do I verify truth claims, even from established religious figures? Do I seek personal confirmation from the Holy Ghost, or do I defer entirely to authority? Have I experienced moments when someone credible told me something that conflicted with my own sense of God's will? How did I handle that conflict? The verse suggests that the test of faithfulness is not whether we accept the majority opinion or the most credible authority, but whether we remain obedient to the specific word God has given us personally.

text_kjv: And he cried unto the man of God that came from Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD, and hast not kept the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee,

commentary.narrative:
The old prophet now speaks in his genuine prophetic capacity, and his message is a formal, legal pronouncement of judgment. The verb 'cried' (qara) suggests urgency and solemnity—this is not conversational but declarative. The formula 'Thus saith the LORD' introduces the actual word of the LORD that has come upon him. The judgment falls on the man of God with crushing specificity, because the old prophet has just witnessed the violation and now understands its gravity.

The content of the judgment is devastating precisely because it names the exact nature of the failure. The man of God is accused of defying—marita—'the mouth of the LORD' (pi YHWH). The use of 'mouth' is vivid and anthropomorphic; he did not merely disobey an impersonal rule, but rebelled against the very organ of divine speech, the place where God's word originates. The accusation is personal and direct: 'the mouth of the LORD' is God himself speaking. To defy the mouth of the LORD is to defy the LORD himself. The phrase 'the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee' shifts to second-person singular—'thy God.' This is not abstract theology. It is intimate: the man of God had a personal covenant relationship with the LORD his God, and he betrayed it. The repetition of 'LORD' (YHWH) three times in this verse emphasizes the covenantal relationship that has been broken.

word_study.meaning: To rebel, to be contentious, to defy authority. The verb implies not mere accidental transgression but deliberate opposition to authority.
word_study.significance: Marah is a strong verb, used for serious rebellion against God (Numbers 20:24, where Moses 'rebelled against my commandment'; 1 Samuel 15:23, where Saul's presumption is 'rebellion'). By using marah rather than a weaker verb, the text emphasizes that the man of God's violation was not a slip or weakness, but a defiance of authority. As The Covenant Rendering notes, 'defied' better captures the sense of intentional opposition.

word_study.meaning: The mouth, the utterance, the decree of the LORD. Mouth is an anthropomorphic image representing God's personal will and spoken word.
word_study.significance: To defy the 'mouth' is to defy God's immediate, personal communication. It is not violating a law written in stone, but rejecting what God has said directly to you. This intimacy makes the violation more serious, not less.

word_study.meaning: To guard, preserve, keep, maintain. Shamar implies active preservation and protection, not mere passive obedience.
word_study.significance: To 'keep' a commandment means to actively guard it, to protect it from violation. The man of God failed not only to obey but to actively preserve the commandment he was given. This suggests that obedience requires vigilance and effort.

cross_references.connection: The choice between blessing (for keeping commandments) and curse (for not keeping them) echoes here. The man of God's violation of the commandment brings not blessing but death.

Samuel tells Saul, 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' The man of God had offered sacrifice (the altar demonstration in verse 5), but his disobedience to the subsequent commandment negates any credit for prior faithfulness.

Moses gathers Israel and says, 'Keep silence... Thou hast this day become the people of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt therefore obey the voice of the LORD.' The covenantal language mirrors the old prophet's accusation.

Jesus teaches, 'If ye love me, keep my commandments.' The violation of the man of God is not merely technical disobedience but a failure of love toward God. Keeping the commandment is an expression of covenant devotion.

commentary.historical_context: The language of defying 'the mouth of the LORD' reflects ancient Near Eastern covenant language. A vassal who defied the mouth of the suzerain was in breach of covenant. The use of this language in verse 21 puts the man of God in the position of a covenant-breaker, subject to covenant sanctions (curses). In Hittite and other ancient Near Eastern treaties, the breach of a specific command by the vassal resulted in specified curses—often including loss of proper burial (as we will see in verse 22). The old prophet's judgment echoes this legal framework. The man of God is being judged not as a common criminal but as a covenant-breaker who has violated the terms of his relationship with God. This was the most serious charge in the ancient Near Eastern political and religious world.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 12:24-25, Alma teaches that 'it is requisite with the justice of God that men should be judged according to their works.' The man of God is being judged—by a genuine prophet—according to his works. His previous obedience (the prophecy against the altar) does not exempt him from judgment for his present disobedience. The principle is absolute.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 82:3 states, 'I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say; but when ye do not what I say, ye have no promise.' The man of God violated the specific word of the Lord given to him, and therefore he has 'no promise'—no protection, no blessing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants include specific promises and specific conditions. A covenant is not open-ended; it requires adherence to terms. The man of God was given a specific covenant with specific terms (no bread, no water, do not return the same way), and he violated it. Temple-goers are similarly bound by their covenants; deviation is a serious matter with serious consequences.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse points to Christ as the one who perfectly kept the commandment of his Father. While the man of God defied 'the mouth of the LORD,' Christ declares, 'I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me' (John 6:38). In the Garden of Gethsemane, Christ faces a true test of obedience—'Let this cup pass from me'—but ultimately submits: 'Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39). Christ's absolute obedience to the Father's mouth and will is the antithesis of the man of God's defiance, and it makes possible redemption for those who, like the man of God, have defied the LORD.
commentary.application: This verse challenges believers to examine their covenant obedience. It is not enough to have done great things in God's name in the past. The test is present obedience to the specific word God has given you now. Ask yourself: What specific instruction has God given me—through scripture, through the Spirit, through a servant of God—that I am tempted to rationalize or ignore? Do I think that past faithfulness excuses present compromise? Do I understand the difference between general Christian principles and the specific covenant or command that God has placed on me? The verse teaches that defying the mouth of the LORD—treating lightly a direct command from God to you—is the gravest possible violation, regardless of your standing, gifts, or prior obedience. This is uncomfortable, which is precisely why it needs to be heard.

text_kjv: But camest back, and hast eaten bread and drunk water in the place, of the which the LORD did say to thee, Eat no bread, and drink no water; thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.

commentary.narrative:
The judgment moves from accusation to consequence. The old prophet pronounces a curse that names the specific violation and the specific punishment. The man of God 'came back' and ate bread and drank water 'in the place' where the LORD said 'Eat no bread, and drink no water.' The parallelism is perfect: the violation mirrors the command inverted. And for this violation, the man of God will suffer a fate that was, in Israelite thought, worse than death itself: his body will not come to the tomb of his fathers.

This curse strikes at the deepest anxiety of ancient Israelite identity. To be buried in the family tomb was not merely a matter of comfort; it was the final act of belonging to the covenant people, to one's family, to one's inheritance in the land. The Prophet Amos condemns Israel by denying proper burial (Amos 2:1). Jacob's anxiety to be buried in Canaan (Genesis 49:29-50:5) shows how central this was to covenant identity. To die in a foreign land with no one to give you proper burial was to be cut off from your people and your God. The Hebrew word for 'carcase' (nivlah) is deliberately degrading—this is the word used for a dead animal, not the respectful term 'dead body' (met). The corpse of the man of God will be treated like carrion, left unburied, belonging to no one, integrated into no ancestral line. This is desolation. And the curse will be fulfilled, as we will see in verse 24.

word_study.meaning: A corpse, carcass, dead body; often used specifically for animal remains or corpses that have been desecrated or left unburied.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes: 'The use of nivlah rather than the more dignified met ('dead person') is deliberately degrading.' This word choice denies the man of God even the dignity of being called 'dead'—he is a carcass, treated as carrion. The same word appears in verse 24, confirming the curse's fulfillment.

word_study.meaning: The tomb, burial place of your ancestors. Qever is the grave or burial cave; avotekha is 'your fathers.' Together, it indicates the family burial site where ancestral identity and covenant continuity are affirmed.
word_study.significance: The family tomb represented covenant belonging, ancestral identity, and continuity with the promise to Abraham. To be denied burial there was to be severed from the covenantal line. Modern believers may not share this anxiety, which is why the curse's weight is easily underestimated.

word_study.meaning: To return, go back, turn back; the same root as in verse 19 where the man of God 'went back.'
word_study.significance: The recurrence of shuv creates verbal connection between the violation (verse 19: 'he returned') and the judgment (verse 22: 'but camest back'). Every time the word appears, it highlights the reversal—the man of God turned back from obedience.

cross_references.connection: Jacob insists on being buried in the cave of Machpelah with his fathers, and Joseph honors this request. Burial with one's fathers is a fundamental covenant priority. The man of God is denied this.
Part of the covenant curse list: 'Thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth.' The denial of proper burial is one of the covenantal curses for disobedience.

Amos condemns Moab: 'Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; Because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime.' The desecration of bones and denial of burial is a grave sin and a severe curse.
The Preacher notes that a man might live many years but 'have no burial'—suggesting that proper burial is central to human dignity and completion of life.

Alma teaches that the restoration of all things includes 'the restoration of the body from the grave,' affirming that the body's disposition matters in God's economy. The denial of burial is a genuine curse.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite practice, burial in the family tomb was not optional but obligatory. The tomb was typically a natural cave or rock-cut chamber in which multiple family members were interred over generations, often for centuries. These tombs have been excavated by archaeologists throughout the Levant and reveal the practice of layering new bodies among the bones of ancestors, integrating the deceased into the ancestral collective. The practice affirmed kinship, inheritance, and covenant continuity. To be denied such burial—whether through death in foreign land, execution, or deliberate desecration—was to be cut off from one's people and one's God. This was considered a fate worse than death. The curse in verse 22 uses this cultural institution as the instrument of judgment. The man of God will not be integrated into his family's ancestral presence; he will be severed from them permanently. Archaeological evidence suggests that proper burial was so important that families would sometimes go to great expense and risk to recover and properly bury a relative who had died far from home.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 8, Nephi sees in vision a tree of life and a strait and narrow path. Those who fall off the path are lost and lost their way—cut off from the covenant people. The man of God's denial of burial parallels being cut off from the covenant community. In Mormon 9:1-2, Mormon warns against turning away from God, suggesting that such turning results in being 'cast out' from God's presence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76 describes the heavenly inheritance and places of glory—a profound Book of Mormon-era expansion of the afterlife. The curse on the man of God is the inverse: no place of honor, no inheritance, no family continuation. The restoration emphasizes that all things, including family relationships, continue in the eternities. The man of God's curse denies him that continuation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Latter-day Saint temple theology emphasizes that through covenants, we are sealed to our families and to the patriarchal line leading to Abraham. The ordinance of sealing affirms family continuity and inheritance. The curse on the man of God denies him precisely this—no sealing to fathers, no ancestral continuity, no inheritance with the covenant people. The temple makes clear what the man of God loses.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ experienced the ultimate denial of burial 'among the righteous' when he was crucified between two thieves and buried in Joseph's tomb—a borrowed grave, not a family inheritance. Yet Christ's burial was temporary and redemptive. His resurrection from the grave opens the way for all believers to inherit eternal family relationships and restoration, even when earthly circumstances seem to deny them. The man of God's curse points to the human need for Christ's redemptive work: only through Christ's Resurrection can the curse of death—including the loss of ancestral continuity—be overcome.
commentary.application: Modern believers may not share the ancient Israelite anxiety about burial practice, but the principle remains: we are bound to our families and to the covenant community, and violation of God's word can sever us from these bonds. The verse teaches that covenant violation has consequences that extend beyond the moment of disobedience. Ask yourself: What covenants have I made—not just in the temple, but in my personal relationship with God? What are the consequences if I break those covenants? Do I understand that some violations, if persistent, can result in real spiritual severing from God's people and God's promise? The verse does not suggest that momentary weakness or failure is unforgivable, but rather that deliberate, knowing violation of a direct command from God carries serious consequences. The warning is not meant to terrify but to clarify what is at stake: your covenant relationship with God and your place among his people.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, after he had eaten bread, and after he had drunk, that he saddled for him the ass, to wit, for the prophet whom he had brought back.

commentary.narrative:
After the old prophet pronounces judgment—while the man of God is still processing the devastating curse—the old prophet performs an act of hospitality that is utterly incongruous with what has just been said. He saddles the donkey for his guest. It is a moment of almost unbearable tension in the narrative: he has just pronounced that the man of God will die unburied, that his corpse will be left in foreign soil, severed from his fathers forever. And then, matter-of-factly, as though nothing terrible has been announced, the old prophet saddles the donkey. This is preparation for journey—preparation for death, though the man of God may not yet fully comprehend it.

The text identifies the old prophet again by his act: 'for the prophet asher heshivo'—'whom he had brought back.' The narrator will not let the reader forget the deception. And the verb 'saddled' (chavash) appears in verse 13 as well, where the old prophet saddles his own donkey to begin the deception. The repetition of the verb creates a grim bracket: first, he saddled to begin the lie; now, he saddles to send the man of God to his death. The man of God departs from the house, leaving behind a prophecy of his own death but carrying none of the understanding of what is about to happen. He sets out on the road that has become, unknowingly, his path to death.

word_study.meaning: To saddle, to put a saddle on a donkey; to harness an animal for riding or burden-bearing.
word_study.significance: The same verb appears in verse 13, where the old prophet first saddled his donkey to ride out and deceive the man of God. The repetition is deliberate: the same action that initiated the deception now initiates the consequence. Hospitality and preparation become the precursor to judgment.

cross_references.connection: The first occurrence of chavash ('saddled'), where the old prophet prepares his donkey to pursue and deceive the man of God. The second saddling mirrors the first, closing a circle of judgment.

Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein.' The old prophet's deception, intended to trap the man of God, results in setting in motion the events that lead to the man of God's death—and, as later tradition understood it, the old prophet's own accountability before God.

Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood... His mischief shall return upon his own head.' The old prophet's deception initiates a chain of consequences that will reach him as well.

commentary.historical_context: Saddling a donkey for a guest was a duty of hospitality in ancient Near Eastern culture, especially when the guest was a traveling prophet or dignitary. The act would have been performed by the host or a servant. The ease and normalcy with which the old prophet saddles the donkey stands in sharp contrast to the terrible judgment he has just pronounced. This may suggest either callousness (he speaks judgment while performing kindness, compartmentalizing his actions) or a kind of compulsive, ritual hospitality that continues even as doom is sealed. In either case, the hospitality itself becomes ironic: the saddled donkey is both a service to the guest and a step toward the guest's death. The animal will stand beside the man of God's corpse, as we will see in verse 24.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, there are several instances of false hospitality preceding judgment. In 1 Nephi 16:34-35, Laman and Lemuel bind Nephi 'with fine cords,' and Nephi is bound throughout the night, a perversion of care into captivity. The old prophet's courteous saddling, while genuine as hospitality, becomes entanglement in judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:37 teaches that love and gentleness should accompany reproof. The old prophet pronounces a death sentence but then saddles a donkey—a disconnect between word and action that illustrates the difficulty of maintaining genuine spiritual authority when one has used deception.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The irony of the old prophet's action reflects a principle of temple covenant: what appears to be a blessing or service can have hidden consequences if it facilitates violation of covenant. True service and true hospitality must be rooted in truth, not deception.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ was also prepared for his journey to death—the disciples prepared a colt for his entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2-6), and preparations were made for his burial (Matthew 27:57-60). Yet Christ's death was redemptive, not a curse. The man of God's journey is a shadow of a darker kind of ending, pointing to the necessity of Christ's Resurrection and redemption for those under curse.
commentary.application: This verse reveals an uncomfortable truth: we can perform external acts of kindness and hospitality while remaining complicit in injustice or judgment. The old prophet saddled the donkey—a good action—but only after pronouncing a death sentence based on a truth he himself had obscured through deception. Modern believers should ask: Am I performing good works while ignoring the consequences of my past words or actions? Do I offer help to others while remaining responsible for deceptions or harms I have caused? Is my kindness genuine, or is it a way of avoiding accountability? The verse teaches that external actions do not redeem internal complicity. The deeper application is to align actions, words, and heart in truth.

text_kjv: And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him: and his carcase was cast in the way, and the ass stood by it, the lion also stood by the carcase.

commentary.narrative:
The judgment is executed. The man of God departs from the old prophet's house and encounters a lion on the road. The lion 'found him' (matsa)—a verb suggesting purposefulness rather than accident. The lion kills him (vayyemitehu—'and it put him to death'), and then an extraordinary tableau unfolds: the corpse lies on the road, the donkey stands beside it without fleeing, and the lion stands beside the corpse without eating it or attacking the donkey. All three figures remain motionless in this eerie, unnatural configuration. This is not a predator's meal; this is a sign, a manifest judgment. The word 'carcase' (nivlah) appears again, fulfilling the curse from verse 22 with devastating literalness: the man of God's corpse is left unburied on the road, a carcass exposed to view. Passersby will see this impossible sight—a lion, a donkey, and a dead prophet, all stationary as though frozen—and they will understand that something transcendent has happened.

The theological significance of this moment is profound. The man of God, who called down fire from heaven in verse 5, who possessed genuine prophetic power, is now struck dead by a beast for violation of a command that seemed minor compared to his greater mission. There is no reprieve, no miraculous intervention, no angel sent to stay the judgment as the angel might have stayed the hand of Abraham in Genesis 22. The judgment falls, swift and absolute. The creature of God (the lion) becomes the instrument of God's judgment. The contrast with Elijah, who will later in this chapter escape the wrath of Jezebel and be carried to heaven by chariots of fire (1 Kings 19:11), underscores how thoroughly the man of God has forfeited divine protection through his covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: To find, to encounter, to discover, to meet; when used with divine agency or judgment, it implies purposeful encounter.
word_study.significance: The verb matsa suggests that the lion's encounter with the man of God was not random but directed. The lion 'found' him on the road, as though sent. This is not merely animal behavior but divine agency working through the creature.

word_study.meaning: To die, to be put to death, to be killed; vayyemitehu is 'and it put him to death,' the lion as agent.
word_study.significance: The active voice ('the lion slew him') makes clear that this is execution, not accident. The lion is the agent of judgment, doing what God has decreed.

word_study.meaning: Corpse, carcass, dead body; used for desecrated or unburied remains, often animal carrion.
word_study.significance: The word nivlah recurs from verse 22, confirming that the curse is being executed literally. The man of God is reduced to a 'carcass'—denied the dignity of proper burial, treated as carrion, left exposed on the road. As The Covenant Rendering notes, the 'triple image of corpse, donkey, and lion all stationary on the road defies natural explanation: lions kill to eat, donkeys flee from lions. The supernatural restraint of both animals marks this as divine judgment rather than natural disaster.'

word_study.meaning: To stand, to stand beside, to remain in place; etzel means 'beside, next to.'
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'stood' (amad) three times—the donkey stood, the lion stood—creates a parallelism that emphasizes the stillness and the unnatural character of the scene. Nothing moves. Both animals remain as though in grief or witness, neither fleeing nor attacking.

cross_references.connection: Abraham raises the knife to slay Isaac, but an angel stays his hand. In contrast, there is no angelic intervention for the man of God; the judgment falls without reprieve. The contrast highlights how completely he has forfeited divine protection.

David arranges for Uriah to be killed in battle. A human instrument executes a just judgment; here, a beast (the lion) is the instrument. The principle is that God uses whatever means are necessary to execute judgment.
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.' The man of God is under judgment, but the judgment itself comes from God's hand, even if mediated through a lion.

Death rides a pale horse; 'power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.' The beasts of the earth are instruments of divine judgment.
Alma teaches that 'it is requisite with the justice of God that men should be judged according to their works.' The man of God is judged according to his works—his violation of the covenant command.

commentary.historical_context: Lions were present in the Levant during the Iron Age (the period of the monarchy), though they were becoming less common by the time of the late monarchy. Archaeological evidence suggests that lions inhabited the Jordan Valley and the eastern regions. A prophet or traveler on the road could genuinely encounter a lion, making this account plausible within its ancient context. However, the specific behavior described here—a lion killing a human but then standing guard over the corpse without eating it, while a donkey remains beside the body without fleeing—would have been recognized by ancient readers as extraordinarily unusual, even impossible from a naturalistic standpoint. This unnaturalness is precisely the point: the scene announces itself as a divine sign. The combination of a dead man, a calm donkey, and a sentinel lion would have been unmistakable as judgment to anyone who witnessed it or heard the report. In the ancient Near Eastern context, such tableaux were understood as theophanic signs—visible manifestations of divine will.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 19:10, Nephi sees in vision that Christ will be 'lifted up upon the cross and slain for the sins of the world,' then later references are made to prophets who 'have been slain.' The man of God's fate—slain for violation of God's word—parallels the fate of many Nephite prophets. In Helaman 13-16, the prophet Samuel the Lamanite is rejected and killed by those he warns. The pattern recurs: prophets who speak truth but fall into violation face severe judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14 states, 'Behold, I am God and have spoken it; these commandments are of me, and were given unto my servants in their weakness, by me.' Every commandment is from God; violation of any of them is serious. D&C 101:78 teaches that 'all things are obedient to [God]'—including lions. The lion in 1 Kings 13:24 is as much a servant of God as any prophet.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple emphasizes that covenants are binding and have real consequences. Breaking a covenant in the temple—whether through the specific violations of secrecy oaths, or through violation of the spirit of the covenants—is serious. The man of God's death teaches that covenant violation is not merely ritualistic disobedience but a severing of the bond with God that can result in real consequences in this life.

commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's death on the road points forward to Christ's death—also on a road, as it were, on the way to a place of judgment (Golgotha). Yet Christ's death is redemptive and resurrectional, where the man of God's is not. The two deaths contrast: the man of God is left unburied and severed; Christ rises on the third day and opens the way for all to transcend death. The man of God's fate is what would be ours without Christ's Atonement—final separation from covenant belonging, final judgment. Yet Christ's victory makes possible restoration, resurrection, and reconciliation to the covenant family even for those who have violated it.
commentary.application: This verse confronts believers with the ultimate seriousness of covenant violation. The man of God did not merely break a rule; he severed himself from God's protection and fell under judgment. The verse does not suggest that every violation of God's word results in immediate death, but it does establish that covenant violation has real consequences in God's economy. Modern believers should ask: Do I take my covenants seriously? Do I understand that a covenant with God is not a suggestion but a binding agreement with consequences? Have I rationalized violations of specific commitments I made to God, thinking them minor compared to the 'larger mission' I believe I'm on? The verse teaches that God judges not by the scale of the violation relative to past achievements, but by the nature of the violation itself. The man of God's spiritual gifts and prior obedience did not exempt him from judgment. Neither will ours. The application is to repent of any covenant violation now, to renew commitment to specific commandments and covenants, and to understand that faithfulness to God's word—even in small things—is the measure of genuine discipleship. The verse also offers a final warning: those who deliberately and knowingly reject God's word, who prefer their own judgment to God's clear command, cut themselves off from God's protecting hand. The 'good death' of Elijah (who will ascend in chariots of fire in chapter 19) stands in terrible contrast to the death of the man of God. Which death will we choose?

text_kjv: And, behold, men passed by, and saw the carcase cast in the way, and the lion standing by the carcase: and they came and told it in the city where the old prophet dwelt.

commentary.narrative: The narrative shifts its viewpoint to ordinary travelers who become the first witnesses to the tragedy. These unnamed men pass by the road and observe exactly what the narrator has already described to us: the corpse of the man of God lying in the path, and the lion standing motionless beside it. The detail that they "came and told it in the city where the old prophet dwelt" is narratively significant—the travelers somehow know to carry this report to the old prophet's city, which suggests that the connection between the two prophets was already known in the region. The news does not remain a hidden tragedy; it spreads through the community with precision, reaching the one person most implicated in the man of God's death.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering's rendering "People passing by saw the body lying on the road with the lion standing beside the body" emphasizes the stark visual clarity of the scene—there is no ambiguity about what has occurred. The travelers are unwitting messengers, carrying information that will trigger the old prophet's confession and grief. This moment marks a shift from the private tragedy (the man of God's deception and death) to public knowledge and interpretation. The old prophet will now have to respond not to his own private knowledge, but to the verified report of multiple witnesses.

word_study.meaning: Those who cross over, travelers, passers-by; from ʿavar (to pass, to cross over). Emphasizes movement and transition.
word_study.significance: These are ordinary people in motion—not prophets, not officials, but everyday travelers who happen upon the scene. Their status as mere passersby underscores the randomness (from human perspective) of how the truth is disclosed.

word_study.meaning: A dead body, corpse, or carcass; from nabel (to wilt, to shrivel). Carries connotation of something that has lost its vitality and dignity.
word_study.significance: The term nĕbēlāh is used consistently throughout this passage (verses 25, 28, 29) to describe the man of God's body. It strips away his prophetic identity and reduces him to flesh—a stark reminder of the physical consequences of disobedience.

word_study.meaning: Standing, remaining in place; from ʿamad (to stand, to stand firm). Suggests stillness, presence, and stationary position.
word_study.significance: The lion's standing beside the body (not devouring it, not moving away) indicates supernatural constraint. A natural lion would either consume its kill or depart; this lion's stillness is a sign of divine purpose.

cross_references.connection: The previous verse narrates the lion meeting and killing the man of God; verse 25 shows how the eyewitness account corroborates what the narrator told us, establishing the factuality of the judgment.
Instructions that news of covenant-breaking is to be made known throughout the community; here the travelers naturally spread the report, creating public knowledge of divine judgment.

The emphasis on God's word being spoken and then enacted echoes the principle that God's spoken word is performative—the word declared by the old prophet at verse 17 now stands fulfilled before witnesses.
News travels through community networks; similarly here, the death of a notable person (a man of God) is communicated through normal social channels to the relevant city.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, the death of a prophet or holy person would have been noteworthy enough to report, especially if accompanied by unusual circumstances (a lion standing motionless beside the body). The travelers' decision to carry the report to the old prophet's city reflects the social reality that prophets were known figures with established locations and constituencies. The road itself would have been a traveled commercial or pilgrim route where merchants, shepherds, and other travelers routinely passed. The fact that multiple people witnessed the scene and corroborated it would have given the report social weight and credibility in an oral culture dependent on eyewitness testimony.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 14:7-11, the righteous Abinadi's death by fire is witnessed by those who did not repent, and the account of his martyrdom spreads among the people. Like the travelers in 1 Kings 13, witnesses carry reports of divine judgment, and these accounts become part of the community's understanding of God's power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 emphasizes that the Lord's word will be fulfilled: 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The old prophet spoke the Lord's word, and now witnesses verify its fulfillment, demonstrating the binding nature of divine speech regardless of the vessel.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The careful burial and honoring of the man of God's body (which these verses lead toward) parallels the dignity shown to priesthood holders in temple context—even in death, those who held God's authority are treated with sacred respect.

commentary.christological_typology: The man of God's body being discovered and reported parallels the discovery and report of Christ's resurrection—eyewitnesses carry accounts of a divinely significant event that transforms understanding of God's power. The lion as an instrument of judgment foreshadows the Lamb of God whose word judges all things.
commentary.application: This verse reminds us that our choices do not remain hidden; they are observed and reported within community networks. The travelers had no particular stake in the man of God's fate, yet they witnessed and testified to what occurred. We live in an age of transparency where truth spreads rapidly. More importantly, when we receive warnings from God's servants, we should take them seriously—the man of God paid the ultimate price for disregarding such a warning. Our obedience or disobedience to prophetic counsel has real consequences that others will witness and interpret.

text_kjv: And when the prophet that brought him back from the way heard thereof, he said, It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the LORD: therefore the LORD hath delivered him unto the lion, which hath torn him, and slain him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake unto him.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet hears the report and immediately provides the correct interpretation of events. His response, "It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the LORD," demonstrates that he recognizes the death as a direct consequence of the man of God's violation of the boundary-condition (not to eat or drink in Jeroboam's territory). What is striking is that the old prophet interprets the death correctly—he has already received the word that the LORD would slay the man of God (verse 17), so this fulfillment comes as no surprise to him, only as confirmation. He is the one person in the narrative who understands the full causal chain: he conveyed the false message, the man of God believed it, and now the man of God lies dead.
commentary.narrative_continued: The old prophet's statement uses precise theological language: "disobedient unto the word of the LORD" (marah et pi YHWH—literally 'defied the mouth of the LORD'). The Covenant Rendering notes that this exact phrase echoes the divine oracle he himself delivered, creating a ring structure around the tragedy. He does not blame himself or his own deception; instead, he frames the death as the consequence of the man of God's choice to break his covenant with the LORD. The verb 'torn him' (shavar) describes the lion's physical destruction with visceral precision. The old prophet's interpretation is theologically correct, but his own role in precipitating the disobedience remains unexamined—at least, not in his words. His subsequent actions (verses 27-29) suggest a deeper reckoning.

word_study.meaning: To rebel, to be rebellious, to defy; from marah (to be refractory, to resist authority). Carries the sense of active defiance rather than mere neglect.
word_study.significance: The verb mārāh is strong language—it describes not accidental failure but willful resistance to God's expressed will. The old prophet's choice of this term emphasizes that the man of God actively chose to disobey, not passively stumbled.

word_study.meaning: To give, to deliver, to put into the hand of; the most common verb for transferring possession or control from one agent to another.
word_study.significance: The verb nātan places responsibility squarely with the LORD. The old prophet acknowledges that God Himself gave the man of God over to the lion—this is not random tragedy but divine action in response to covenant violation.

word_study.meaning: To break, to shatter, to maul; originally physical destruction, but also used metaphorically for breaking in spirit or will.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'mauled,' capturing the physical violence of the lion's attack. The verb suggests not quick death but violent physical destruction—the body itself has been broken.

word_study.meaning: According to the word, as the word was spoken; the phrase emphasizes alignment between what was said and what came to pass.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears at the beginning and end of verse 26 (ki dibar YHWH asher dibber lo), creating emphasis on the perfect correspondence between divine speech and its fulfillment. The double reference frames the entire interpretation in terms of the binding nature of the LORD's word.

cross_references.connection: The old prophet's interpretation directly references the oracle he himself delivered—the same LORD who spoke judgment through him has now executed it, confirming the word's power.

The test of a true prophet is whether his word comes to pass; here the old prophet's word (delivered from the LORD) is confirmed in the man of God's death, validating his prophetic authority even as it demonstrates the cost of disobedience.

Samuel rebukes Saul for partial obedience, stating that rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft; here the man of God's selective disobedience (obeying the letter of the law by not eating, but violating its spirit by returning) likewise results in severe judgment.
The New Testament warns that neglecting the word spoken through the LORD's servants brings just recompense; the man of God's experience exemplifies this principle of covenant accountability.

The doctrine that the LORD's word is binding and will be fulfilled whether spoken directly or through servants resonates with the old prophet's interpretation that the word he conveyed is now being executed.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite theology, a prophet's word was understood as performative—once spoken, especially when framed as the word of the LORD, it would come to pass. The old prophet's immediate recognition of the death as fulfillment of his own oracle reflects this worldview. The concept of the 'mouth of the LORD' (pi YHWH) was a central motif in Near Eastern royal and prophetic ideology: the king or God's representative's word was a force that accomplished what it said. The old prophet's interpretation would have been immediately comprehensible to his audience—they would understand the death as proof of the word's power, not as random misfortune.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 14:2-8, Samuel the Lamanite prophecies of Christ's death and resurrection, and his words are fulfilled exactly. The principle that prophetic utterance is binding and performative is central to Book of Mormon theology of prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 establishes that the Lord will speak through His servants, and His word will stand whether by their own voice or the Lord's. The old prophet's situation illustrates this principle: he spoke the Lord's judgment, and it was executed, even though his own role in creating the circumstances was deceptive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant violation of breaking the boundary-condition set by the LORD parallels violations of covenant in the temple—there are specific conditions attached to divine blessings, and breaking them has consequences. The old prophet's interpretation emphasizes that such violations are not overlooked.

commentary.christological_typology: The old prophet's correct interpretation of judgment parallels the High Priest's authority to interpret and execute God's will. More broadly, the man of God's willingness to break his covenant echoes temptation in the wilderness—Christ was tested to break His commitment to the Father's will, but unlike the man of God, He remained steadfast.
commentary.application: The old prophet's interpretation teaches us to read our circumstances through the lens of God's word. When we face consequences for our choices, the question is not whether God is fair (He is), but whether we recognize the word we violated. The old prophet did not excuse the man of God's disobedience; he named it directly. In our own lives, when we face difficulties, we should ask: What word have I failed to keep? What boundary has the LORD set that I have crossed? This verse is a call to take covenant seriously and to interpret our circumstances in light of the covenants we have made.

text_kjv: And he spake to his sons, saying, Saddle me the ass. And they saddled him.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet now moves from interpretation to action. He commands his sons to saddle the donkey so that he can travel out to where the man of God's body lies. This verse is deceptively simple on the surface—a straightforward command and its execution—but the Covenant Rendering's note points to something crucial: the command "Saddle the donkey for me" is linguistically identical to verse 13, where the old prophet deceived the man of God into mounting a donkey to return to the old prophet's table. The repetition of this exact command creates a structural parallel that binds the old prophet's two journeys into a single arc: the first journey was driven by deception and resulted in tragedy; the second journey is driven by the need to retrieve and honor the body.
commentary.narrative_continued: The command is immediate and authoritative—no explanation is given to the sons about why the donkey is needed. The old prophet is clearly accustomed to being obeyed. His sons execute the command without question or delay. The brevity of this verse contrasts sharply with the coming verses, where the old prophet will engage in elaborate mourning rituals. Here we see only the machinery of travel being set in motion. The old prophet's journey to retrieve the body is driven by something—whether it is guilt, grief, duty, or some combination remains unstated. What is clear is that he moves quickly once he understands what has occurred.

word_study.meaning: To saddle, to gird about, to bind; from chebesh (to bind, to tie, to saddle). The word carries the sense of securing and preparing something for use.
word_study.significance: The verb hibshu is active and practical—it denotes the physical preparation of the animal for travel. The old prophet is preparing for immediate action, not reflection or delay.

word_study.meaning: Donkey, ass; a beasts of burden used for travel and transport. In biblical narratives, donkeys are associated with both ordinary travel and significant journeys.
word_study.significance: The use of the same word (chamor) for the old prophet's own donkey emphasizes the structural parallel. The donkey carried the man of God to his death; now it will carry the old prophet to retrieve the body.

cross_references.connection: The exact repetition of the saddling command creates a narrative echo that binds the first and second journeys together, showing cause and consequence.

Abraham saddled his donkey and rode to Mount Moriah to sacrifice Isaac; similarly, the old prophet saddles and rides to retrieve the man of God's body—both journeys involve a profound test of obedience or covenant.
Travel by donkey was the standard mode of transportation for prophets and significant figures in ancient Israel, emphasizing the old prophet's status and the importance of his journey.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, saddling one's own beast indicated either personal urgency or significant status—a person of importance would typically have servants saddle animals for them, but could do it themselves in emergency situations. The old prophet has servants (his sons), yet he commands them to saddle the donkey for him, suggesting he is about to undertake a journey of significant personal importance. Donkeys were the primary means of transport for traveling prophets and holy men in the ancient Levant; they could traverse rough terrain and were reliable over long distances.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8:14-16, Alma rises early to travel, driven by the Spirit's commandment to go back and speak to the people of Ammonihah despite earlier rejection. The old prophet's swift saddling and departure parallel the urgency of those called to fulfill a difficult errand.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 31:5 teaches that 'he who receiveth the word and the testimony of Jesus recordeth it in his heart.' The old prophet is now moved to act on the testimony he received through his own mouth—the word he spoke is now creating the necessity of his action.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The old prophet's willingness to be inconvenienced and to travel to honor the man of God's body reflects the principle that those who hold the priesthood are obligated to minister to one another, even in death.

commentary.christological_typology: The preparation of the donkey for a journey echoes Palm Sunday, when Jesus rode the donkey into Jerusalem—both represent movement toward a confrontation with judgment and death, though in opposite directions (toward and away from the fateful city).
commentary.application: This verse teaches the importance of swift response to moral and spiritual duties. The old prophet heard the news and immediately took action—there was no delay, no excuse-making. When we hear of someone in need, when we become aware of a wrong that needs redressing, when we understand that we bear some responsibility for a tragedy, we should move as quickly as the old prophet did. His sons obeyed without hesitation, suggesting that there was an established pattern of obedience in his household. The lesson is not about the donkey, but about the willingness to set aside comfort and take immediate action when duty calls.

text_kjv: And he went and found his carcase cast in the way, and the ass and the lion standing by the carcase: the lion had not eaten the carcase, nor torn the ass.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet arrives at the scene and discovers the exact conditions that the travelers reported. What is remarkable about this verse is the emphasis on what the lion did NOT do. The Covenant Rendering highlights the double negative: 'The lion had not eaten the body and had not mauled the donkey.' This is theologically significant because it demonstrates that the lion was not acting from natural hunger or predatory instinct. A normal lion, having killed the man of God, would consume the body; a normal lion standing near an unguarded donkey would likely attack it. Instead, the lion stands motionless beside the corpse, having satisfied some divine purpose without indulging in the predatory behavior natural to lions. The preservation of the body and the donkey in this manner signals that this is not random animal violence but a carefully executed judgment.
commentary.narrative_continued: The old prophet's arrival is too late to save the man of God, but not too late to retrieve his body with dignity. The scene remains frozen as the travelers left it—the lion still standing sentinel beside the corpse. The old prophet himself has become a witness to the supernatural restraint of the lion. He now understands with complete clarity that what occurred was not mischance or tragedy, but the enacted word of the LORD. The presence of the old prophet's own donkey alongside the dead man's body and the still-standing lion creates a tableau that emphasizes the old prophet's role: he will now use his donkey to transport the body back to his city for proper burial. The narrative has moved from deception (verse 13) through death (verse 24) through public report (verse 25) through interpretation (verse 26) to now action and witness (verses 27-28).

word_study.meaning: To find, to discover, to come upon; the verb can carry both accidental discovery and deliberate finding.
word_study.significance: The old prophet 'finds' the body as the travelers reported it. The verb matzá emphasizes that the body is still where it fell—it has not been removed, consumed, or disturbed. The old prophet's finding confirms the report.

word_study.meaning: Standing, remaining in place; plural form indicating both the donkey and the lion are in stationary position.
word_study.significance: The repeated use of this word (also in verse 25) emphasizes stillness and restraint. The lion's standing beside prey animals without attacking them is the key indicator that this is supernatural judgment, not natural predation.

word_study.meaning: Had not eaten; negative construction emphasizing what did not occur. The perfect tense indicates a completed action (or in this case, non-action) in the past.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this negative construction. The point is not what the lion did, but what it explicitly did not do. This negative is theologically loaded—it proves the supernatural nature of the judgment.

word_study.meaning: To break, to shatter, to maul; here used of the lion's potential action on the donkey.
word_study.significance: The same verb used in verse 26 to describe what the lion did do to the man of God is here used in the negative to describe what the lion did not do to the donkey. The contrast underscores that the violence was discriminate and purposeful.

cross_references.connection: In Daniel's lion den, the lions do not harm Daniel despite being hungry and dangerous; similarly, the lion here is restrained by divine power from consuming or harming what is not its target.
Verse 24 describes the lion killing the man of God; verse 28 describes the lion not eating the body—together these verses emphasize that the lion was executing judgment, not hunting.

The righteous man experiences God's protection even in death—'Not one of his bones is broken'; the preservation of the man of God's body (not consumed, not torn) reflects divine honor shown even to a covenant-violator's remains.
David describes himself as hunted by Saul and seeks the LORD's judgment; the wild animal (lion) as an instrument of divine will is a recurring motif in biblical accounts of God's direct intervention.

commentary.historical_context: Lions were present in the Levantine wilderness during the Iron Age, though they were becoming less common as human settlement expanded. A lion killing a human would have been noteworthy enough to report, but also plausible within the ancient world's experience. However, a lion that kills but does not consume—a creature that stands guard over its kill—would have been interpreted as extraordinary. Ancient Near Eastern understanding of wildlife was closely tied to theology: unusual animal behavior was read as a sign of divine activity. The old prophet's audience would have understood the lion's restraint as unnatural and therefore as proof of divine judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 28:39, the three Nephites are preserved from death and pain through divine will; similarly, the man of God's body is preserved from defilement through divine restraint. In both cases, the supernatural preservation serves as testimony.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:2 teaches that angelic and divine protection extends even to the preparation of bodies for resurrection; the restraint shown to the man of God's body reflects a broader principle of divine stewardship over the physical remains of the righteous.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept that the body remains sacred even after death, and that proper burial is a covenant obligation, resonates throughout temple theology. The old prophet's recognition of the need to retrieve and bury the man of God's body reflects this principle.

commentary.christological_typology: The lion restraining its hunger parallels the principle that Christ's power over death and all creation is absolute—even predatory forces obey His will. The preservation of the man of God's body anticipates resurrection theology, where the body is honored and preserved for exaltation.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that God's judgments are precise and measured, not indiscriminate. The old prophet and his audience would have understood that the lion's restraint proved the judgment was from the LORD—it was not mere tragedy but divine action with a specific purpose. For us, this teaches that when God judges, He does so with perfect knowledge and perfect justice. We should never assume that God is careless or excessive in His judgments. The supernatural restraint of the lion—an act of not-doing—is as much a sign of divine power as the killing itself. Sometimes God's power is displayed not in what He does, but in what He constrains.

text_kjv: And the prophet took up the carcase of the man of God, and laid it upon the ass, and brought it back: and the old prophet came to his city, to mourn and to bury him.

commentary.narrative: The old prophet now engages in the work of retrieval and restoration. He physically lifts the man of God's body and places it on his donkey. The Covenant Rendering renders the verb 'nasa' ('lifted') to emphasize the dignity and effort of this action—this is not casual handling but reverent care. The old prophet brings the body back to his own city. The phrase "to mourn and to bury him" (lisfod ulqovro) indicates deliberate intention to conduct proper funerary rites. The Covenant Rendering's note is significant: "The verb safad ('to mourn, to beat the breast') indicates genuine grief, not merely ritual obligation. The old prophet mourns the man whose death he caused." This is the crucial moral turning point in the narrative. The old prophet, who deceived the man of God into breaking his covenant with the LORD, now takes full responsibility for retrieving and honoring the body.
commentary.narrative_continued: There is a profound irony at work here. The old prophet brought the man of God to his table with a lie (verse 13); now he brings the man of God's body to his city with truth and intention to honor. The repetition of the command to saddle the donkey creates narrative bookends: the first saddling led to deception, the second leads to restitution. The old prophet does not attempt to hide the body or minimize what occurred. Instead, he brings it to his own city where the death will be known, witnessed, and commemorated. The phrase "his city" emphasizes that the old prophet is claiming responsibility—this is his place, and the dead man will be brought there. The text does not explicitly state that the old prophet repents, but his actions demonstrate something like repentance: he is doing what he can to undo the harm he caused.
