word_study.meaning: After him, in his way, following. The preposition and suffix construct the phrase 'walk after him,' which in covenant language means to be obedient to, to align with, to be a follower of. The phrase is used of covenant loyalty throughout scripture.
word_study.significance: The verb 'follow' (halak acharav) is the language of discipleship and covenant commitment. Joshua urged Israel to 'choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (Joshua 24:15). Elijah's call echoes Joshua's ultimatum. The choice to 'follow' is the choice to align one's entire life with the will and way of the deity.

word_study.term_original: וְלֹא־עָנוּ הָעָם אֹתוֹ דָּבָר (ve-lo anu ha-am oto davar)
word_study.meaning: The people did not answer him a word. The verb anah ('to answer') will become the governing verb of the entire chapter—the central question is which god answers. Here, the people answer Elijah nothing. Their silence is the answer: they are paralyzed, unable to commit.
word_study.significance: The people's failure to answer stands in sharp contrast to the future moment when they will cry out and say, 'The LORD, he is the God' (v. 39). The silence measures the spiritual depth of their apostasy. They have no confession, no commitment, no word. By chapter's end, after witnessing the fire, they will find their voice. The progression from silence to testimony frames the chapter's arc.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's confrontation with the church members at Zarahemla (Alma 4:8–11) diagnoses a similar condition of spiritual paralysis—people nominally belonging to the church but lacking real commitment. Alma compares them to a tree with rotten roots. Mormon's final commentary (Mormon 9) mourns the condition of Israel's descendants who 'stumble because of the stumbling block' (Mormon 9:2), having failed to make the decisive choice Elijah called for. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that genuine conversion requires exclusive loyalty to Christ; compromise and hedging lead to dissolution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:34 states, 'And that wicked one cometh and taketh away light and truth, through disobedience, from the children of men, and because of the tradition of their fathers.' The people's silence—their inability to choose and commit—represents the condition described here: having lost truth through disobedience and tradition, they stand unable to reclaim it. D&C 1:29–30 teaches that the Lord will cause 'the weak things of the world... to break down the mighty and strong ones,' suggesting that Elijah, one man, standing before 450 prophets, embodies this principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants require exclusive loyalty to God and His kingdom. The condition Elijah diagnoses—the people 'limping between two opinions'—would be incompatible with temple commitment. To enter the temple is to renew covenant, to commit fully to the LORD. The silence of the people at Mount Carmel anticipates the moment when, having witnessed divine power, they will confess, 'The LORD, he is the God.' Temple experience moves people from silence and confusion to clear testimony.

commentary.historical_context: In the 9th century BCE, the northern kingdom under Ahab was indeed experiencing religious pluralism. Baal worship, introduced through Jezebel and royal policy, coexisted with whatever remained of Yahwism. For common Israelites, particularly those dependent on agriculture (which Baal was supposed to govern), the appeal of both deities made practical sense—why not invoke both the storm god of Phoenicia and the God of the covenant? This syncretistic impulse was common in the ancient Near East, where peoples often combined elements of different religious systems. However, Israelite covenant theology was inherently exclusive. The first commandment forbade other gods; the golden calf episode (Exodus 32) had already established that even representation of the legitimate God alongside other deities was forbidden. Elijah's binary demand—'either/or, not both'—aligns with the strict monotheism that Israel had formally committed to at Sinai. The people's silence suggests they had never been asked to choose publicly before. As long as both worships were permitted, they could participate in both. Being forced to choose exposed their lack of genuine commitment to either.
commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's call for Israel to choose anticipates Christ's own ultimatum: 'No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Matthew 6:24). Christ, like Elijah, demanded exclusive loyalty and rejected the possibility of partial commitment. The people's silence before Elijah—their inability to confess—contrasts with the future moment when 'every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father' (Philippians 2:11). The silence that paralyzes Israel will be broken only by the power of God revealed at the altar.

text_kjv: Then said Elijah unto the people, I, even I only, remain a prophet of the LORD; but Baal's prophets are four hundred and fifty men.

commentary.narrative: Elijah's statement appears to be factually inaccurate—Obadiah has hidden 100 of the LORD's prophets in caves (1 Kings 18:4, 13). Yet the Covenant Rendering and scholarly commentary clarify that Elijah is not claiming to be absolutely the only prophet alive, but rather 'I alone remain as a [publicly active, openly proclaiming] prophet of the LORD.' Elijah is the only one standing openly in the kingdom, proclaiming the LORD's word. The hidden prophets, though alive and faithful, are silent. Elijah speaks for all of them through his solitary, public witness. This interpretation honors both the text (which says 'I alone remain') and the broader narrative context (which acknowledges the 100 hidden prophets).
commentary.narrative_continued: The statement is also a profound theology of remnant witness. A single prophet authenticated by the LORD outweighs 450 false prophets. Elijah's remark emphasizes that truth is not determined by majority vote, by institutional authority, by royal sponsorship, or by numbers. One man standing on the word of God is sufficient. This principle becomes foundational to Restoration theology: a young man in rural New York, alone in knowledge of the true Church, is more authoritative than the entire ecclesiastical establishment of Christendom. Numbers do not determine truth; truth is truth regardless of how many believe it or deny it.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The contrast—one against 450—is also psychologically strategic. Elijah is openly acknowledging the overwhelming odds. He is not hiding the disparity or pretending it does not matter. Instead, by stating it plainly, he frames the coming test as an unambiguous vindication: if the one triumphs over the 450, it cannot be attributed to advantage or luck. It can only be attributed to the power of the God he represents. The humility of Elijah's position—the radical vulnerability of standing alone—paradoxically becomes the strongest argument for his authenticity. He has nothing to gain but the truth of God; he has everything to lose.
commentary.application: The modern disciple often faces a version of Elijah's position: a conviction that truth lies with a minority position, against prevailing cultural, academic, or even religious consensus. When we believe in the Restoration, we stand numerically against the world's billions of other Christians. When we affirm traditional sexual morality in a sexually permissive age, we are the 'one against 450.' When we commit fully to covenants in an age of shallow commitment, we stand apart. Elijah's example teaches that numbers do not determine truth. The question is not 'How many believe this?' but 'Is this true?' If it is true, then one believer plus God's power equals majority. The test Elijah proposes—'Call on your god, I will call on mine; the one who answers by fire is God'—is still the valid test. We do not debate doctrine in abstracts; we ask which path produces real power, real transformation, real answered prayer. Our testimony is not that we are right because we are many, but that God is true because we have experienced His response. Until we have that experience, we may find ourselves, like Israel, standing silent and paralyzed. Once we have it, we can stand alone with Elijah and declare with absolute conviction: 'The LORD, he is the God.'

cross_references.connection: Obadiah has hidden 100 prophets of the LORD in caves, establishing that Elijah is not the only faithful prophet alive, but is the only one standing openly and publicly proclaiming.

Later, Elijah will claim he alone remains and has not bowed to Baal; yet the LORD will reveal 7,000 in Israel who have not bowed, showing that the remnant is hidden but secure in the LORD's knowledge.
Isaiah later writes of the remnant (she'arit) that the LORD will preserve: the principle of the faithful remnant standing against apostasy becomes a major theme in later prophecy.

Paul applies Elijah's situation typologically, explaining that even in Israel's apostasy, the LORD always preserves a remnant according to grace; Elijah's solitary stand represents the perpetual principle of remnant faithfulness.
The LORD identifies the restored Church as the 'only true and living church,' paralleling Elijah's claim to be the sole remaining true prophet; singular truth persists despite institutional apostasy.

word_study.term_original: אֲנִי נוֹתַרְתִּי נָבִיא לַיהוָה לְבַדִּי (ani notarti navi la-YHWH levaddi)
word_study.meaning: I have remained as a prophet of the LORD, alone. The verb natar ('remain, be left') suggests a survivor, one left standing after others have fallen or disappeared. The adverbial intensifier ani ('I myself, I') and the phrase levaddi ('alone, by myself') emphasize the singularity and solitude. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that Elijah is identifying himself as remaining in active prophetic role.
word_study.significance: The verb 'remain' (natar) echoes language of covenant remnant—those 'left over' who preserve the faith through apostasy. In later biblical and Jewish tradition, the concept of she'arit ('the remnant') becomes central to eschatology. Elijah represents the remnant principle: even when institutional religion has collapsed, the remnant stands. The phrase 'prophet of the LORD' (navi la-YHWH) marks Elijah as possessing divine commission and authorization, not institutional appointment.

word_study.meaning: Prophet, one who speaks on behalf of a god or the deity's representative. The root meaning is debated; some scholars connect it to a word meaning 'to call' or 'to speak.' The navi is characterized by direct communication with the deity and the ability to speak the deity's word with authority.
word_study.significance: The key term of the chapter. The navi is not distinguished primarily by moral superiority or religious knowledge, but by responsiveness to God. The test will ultimately be about which navi ('speaks for a real god') will receive a response. Elijah's self-designation as 'prophet of the LORD' (navi la-YHWH) establishes his identity and claim. The 450 prophets of Baal are also called nevi'im, but the chapter will demonstrate the difference between a prophet who speaks for the living God and prophets who speak for an idol.

word_study.meaning: And the prophets of Baal. The vav ('and') here is not simply a conjunction but a contrastive particle, marking a stark opposition. The grammar places them in a binary relationship: on one side, Elijah; on the other, 450.
word_study.significance: The numerical contrast is emphasized by the grammatical structure. Elijah introduces the point with absolute simplicity: 'I, alone, remain... but Baal's prophets are 450 men.' The flatness of the statement underscores the absurdity of the odds. No rhetorical flourish, no emotional appeal—just the stark fact. This rhetorical restraint is more powerful than any exclamation would be.

word_study.meaning: 450, a specific and considerable number. In ancient contexts, such numbers may or may not be historically accurate, but they convey the idea of a significant organized group.
word_study.significance: The number 450 is mentioned again in verse 19 and will recur when Ahab's forces are destroyed (2 Kings 1:10–14). The precision suggests an official registry—these are state-sponsored prophets, a formal corps of religious officials. The number is also chosen to emphasize the extreme disparity. Fifty men might seem like manageable odds for a powerful prophet; 450 suggests total institutional backing against a solitary voice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Abinadi stands alone before King Noah and his court of priests (Mosiah 12), outnumbered and overpowered, declaring the word of the LORD. Like Elijah, Abinadi is not actually the only faithful believer (Alma becomes converted), but he is the only one standing openly and unafraid to proclaim truth. The parallel teaches that the prophetic witness persists even in apostasy, visible as a solitary figure standing against institutional corruption.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Joseph Smith's experience as the sole witness to the restored priesthood and Church, standing against the entire edifice of institutional Christianity, mirrors Elijah's position. D&C 21:4–6 frames the prophet's word as binding upon the Church, and D&C 1:4–6 speaks of the word of the LORD standing in power despite opposition. The principle is clear: the LORD's word is not dependent on numbers, institutions, or worldly power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the restored covenant, standing as a visible witness in an apostate world. Like Elijah standing at Mount Carmel, the temple stands as a solitary witness to truth amid spiritual confusion. Those who make temple covenants join a remnant, often standing apart from prevailing cultural values, aligned with the word of the LORD.

commentary.historical_context: The 9th century BCE in the northern kingdom saw rapid religious change under Ahab's regime. Elijah's emergence as a prophetic voice represents resistance to state-mandated religious policy. In the ancient Near East, kings controlled religious institutions and could establish or suppress cultic practices. Ahab, under Jezebel's influence, had established Baal worship and attempted to eliminate Yahwistic prophecy (1 Kings 18:4: 'Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD'). Elijah's statement that he 'alone remains' reflects the reality of institutional suppression. The 450 prophets of Baal represent the religious establishment—fed, housed, and protected by the state. Elijah, by contrast, was a hunted man, fed by ravens in the wilderness and sustained by a widow in Zarephath. The institutional advantage was entirely with Baal's prophets. That Elijah would stand against such odds would have seemed not brave but suicidal to contemporaries. His willingness to do so demonstrates either absolute conviction or absolute madness. The narrative is designed to make readers ask: what kind of man stands alone against an entire state religion?
commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's solitary witness anticipates Christ's position: one man against the power of the temple establishment, the Roman state, and the forces of the world. Christ, like Elijah, faced 'twelve legions of angels' worth of disparity in force (Matthew 26:53), yet stood alone on principle. Christ's resurrection vindicated His solitary claim in a way Elijah's fire will vindicate his. The principle is the same: one word from God outweighs all the opposing forces in the world. Hebrews 11:1–2 lists Elijah among the heroes of faith 'who through faith subdued kingdoms,' and faith is defined as 'the evidence of things not seen'—Elijah's faith in what he could not yet see gave him the power to stand alone.

text_kjv: Let them therefore give us two bullocks; and let them choose one bullock for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under: and I will dress the other bullock, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under:

commentary.narrative: Elijah proposes the test, establishing the rules with scrupulous fairness. Two bulls are provided—identical animals, ensuring that the choice of sacrifice is not determined by unequal materials. The prophets of Baal will choose first, giving them the advantage of selection. Both altars will be constructed identically: sacrifice placed on wood. Critically, both prophets and Elijah will 'put no fire under'—this clause is repeated with emphasis. No human agency will kindle the flame. The only variable is prayer. The god who answers by consuming the offering with fire will prove his reality and power. The test eliminates every excuse: equal animals, equal preparation, equal conditions. The only difference will be the name called upon and the god who responds.
commentary.narrative_continued: The design of the test is theologically subtle. Sacrifice was the primary means of communication between Israel and the deity. To call the people to witness a sacrifice contest was to call them to see which god actually receives and accepts offerings. In Israelite theology, the burnt offering (whole burnt offering) was consumed by fire, with the smoke rising to heaven—the consumed offering was a physical sign of divine acceptance. If Baal accepted the offering, the fire would come and consume it. If the fire did not come, Baal's silence would be his judgment: he has rejected the offering. Fire, moreover, was not a neutral medium. Fire was the sign of God's presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), in the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), and in the pillar of fire (Exodus 13:21). Fire was the LORD's medium, His language. By choosing fire as the medium of response, Elijah is choosing the playing field on which the God of Israel has already established His presence.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The physical preparation of the sacrifice—cutting the bull in pieces and laying it on wood—follows the standard procedure for preparing a burnt offering. The Covenant Rendering notes that the verb yinattechuhu ('let them cut it in pieces') uses 'the standard sacrificial term for butchering an offering.' This is not a test of raw power but a test of proper worship. Can Baal receive a correctly prepared offering? Can his fire touch that which is arranged according to the proper forms? The test has an almost perfect fairness that makes its outcome undeniable. When it concludes, no one will be able to claim disadvantage or unfairness.
commentary.application: Elijah's test is designed to be fair and undeniable. There are no excuses, no ambiguities, no room for rationalization. In our own spiritual experience, the equivalent test is simple: call upon God in prayer, with honest heart, in the name of Jesus Christ, and see if He answers. The response may not be fire consuming an altar, but it will be real—a peace that passeth understanding, a confirmation of truth, a changed heart, an answer to a specific prayer. The test Elijah proposed has been administered to every sincere seeker in every generation. God does answer. The question for us is whether we are willing to call upon Him sincerely, and whether we will recognize His answer when it comes. The lesson of this verse is that God's test is fair. He will not handicap you or provide an unfair advantage to your competitors. The playing field will be level, the conditions equal. If you fail to recognize His answer, it will not be because He did not respond, but because you did not recognize His voice. Elijah learned this through forty days of hiding in a cave (1 Kings 19:11–12): the LORD comes not in wind or earthquake or fire, but in a still, small voice. Our responsibility is to prepare the offering (our hearts, our willingness, our faith) and call upon Him, knowing He will answer in His way and time.

cross_references.connection: The procedure for preparing a burnt offering in the Levitical law is mirrored in Elijah's test: the animal is cut into pieces, arranged on wood, and consumed by fire sent from the LORD.
Fire as a sign of divine presence at Mount Sinai establishes fire as the LORD's medium; Elijah's choice of fire as the test criterion draws on this established symbolism.
The burning bush, unconsumed by fire, shows the divine presence; similarly, the fire that consumes the offering at Mount Carmel will manifest the presence and acceptance of the true God.
Elijah will later elaborate the test by adding water to the altar, making ignition even more impossible from any natural source, intensifying the conditions of the test.
Malachi speaks of sacrifices 'pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old,' implying that true sacrifice is characterized by divine acceptance; the fire at Carmel becomes the sign of acceptance.

word_study.meaning: They shall give / they shall choose. The verbs are in third person plural, referred to the prophets of Baal. The volitional tone emphasizes their agency in the selection—they will choose which animal they prefer, giving them the first-mover advantage.
word_study.significance: By allowing Baal's prophets to choose first, Elijah cedes apparent advantage. They can select the finest animal, leaving Elijah with what remains. This generosity serves Elijah's rhetorical purpose: if Baal fails, it cannot be because he was given an inferior offering. The prophets cannot claim, 'We were not given a good bull.' They had the choice.

word_study.meaning: Bulls, male cattle, often of breeding age. The term suggests animals of value, not merely any sacrifice. The parim would be substantial offerings, significant enough to make the test meaningful.
word_study.significance: The choice of bulls (rather than lambs or goats) reflects the magnitude of what is being tested. Baal was worshipped as a storm god and fertility deity, and bulls were symbols of fertility and power in Canaanite religion. A bull is a fitting offering to Baal. By choosing bulls, Elijah is not handicapping Baal; he is offering the god an offering appropriate to his supposed domain.

word_study.meaning: Cut in pieces, butcher, disassemble. The verb nattach is the standard term for preparing an animal for sacrifice, cutting it into parts for burning.
word_study.significance: The use of the standard sacrificial verb emphasizes that this is not a strange or unfamiliar ritual. Both prophets are being asked to do what they have presumably done countless times before in offering to Baal. The familiarity of the procedure makes the subsequent failure even more stark.

word_study.term_english: lay on wood, set no fire
word_study.term_original: שִׂים על־העצים / אש לא / שים (sim al ha-etzim / esh lo / sim)
word_study.transliteration: sim al ha-etzim; esh lo sim
word_study.meaning: Put on the wood / no fire set. The repeated phrase 've-esh lo yasimu / ve-esh lo asim' ('no fire shall they set / no fire shall I set') is the pivot of the test. The wood is prepared, but no human hand will kindle flame.
word_study.significance: The emphatic insistence that no fire will be set establishes that the only agency possible is divine. If fire appears, it cannot be attributed to hidden kindling, to natural ignition, or to any human mechanism. Fire can only come from the god called upon. The repetition of this condition underscores its importance. There is no room for trickery, no ambiguity about natural causation. The fire must be explicitly supernatural.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma and Amulek's test in Ammonihah (Alma 8–14) involves prophetic witness confronting false religion. Though their test is not a sacrificial contest, the principle is similar: prophets offering a clear choice between the living God and false ways, with supernatural confirmation following. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that false prophets cannot produce fruit of the Spirit; they cannot accomplish what they claim.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 68:4 states, 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' The test for a true prophet is whether his word produces fruit—whether God confirms it. D&C 21:4–5 similarly promises that those who follow the prophet will receive the word 'as if from mine own mouth.' The principle is identical to Elijah's test: the true prophet will be confirmed by the response of God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Sacrifice in the temple represented the covenant relationship and the acceptance of the worshiper by God. The placement of hands on the offering, the proper preparation, and the burning by fire all represented the purification and acceptance of the worshiper. The Mount Carmel test, in effect, is asking which altar receives the fire—which represents which covenant is accepted by God. In the latter days, the covenant is not sacrificial but covenantal (the law of sacrifice is fulfilled in Christ). Yet the principle remains: true covenant produces fruit and confirmation. Temple experience should produce spiritual fire—the burning of the Holy Ghost in the heart.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of calling upon gods through sacrifice was universal in the ancient Near East. Hittite, Assyrian, Egyptian, and Canaanite texts all describe sacrificial procedures and divine response. However, most ancient texts do not describe the god sending fire to consume the offering. This is distinctive to Israelite tradition (see the examples of Leviticus, and the later account of David's offerings at the threshing floor of Araunah, 1 Chronicles 21:26, where fire from heaven consumes the offering). The contest format—two priests calling upon competing deities, with a supernatural sign determining the victor—has no direct parallel in known ancient Near Eastern sources, though the conceptual framework (testing which god is real through response to prayer) is recognizable. The use of bulls as offerings was common in Canaanite religion, making Elijah's choice culturally appropriate to Baal worship. The detail about preparing the bull with wood but no fire would be understood by an Iron Age audience as standard sacrificial practice. The innovation is the test itself: taking the normal procedure and creating conditions that make only divine intervention possible.
commentary.christological_typology: The sacrifice consumed by fire prefigures Christ as the ultimate sacrifice. Christ, unlike the bulls at Mount Carmel, is the willing sacrifice, and His offering is received and accepted by the Father (cf. Hebrews 10:10, where Christ's body is offered 'once for all'). The fire that consumes the offering at Mount Carmel becomes, in Christian theology, a type of divine acceptance of the perfect sacrifice. The test itself—that the true God will answer and receive the offering—is answered definitively in Christ, whose sacrifice the Father accepted and vindicated through the Resurrection. Christ is both the answering God (who receives sacrifice) and the sacrifice itself.

text_kjv: And call ye on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the LORD: and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God. And all the people answered and said, It is well spoken.

commentary.narrative: Elijah presents the test as already complete in its essential logic. The pronouncement 'the God that answereth by fire, let him be God' is not speculation but theological principle: godhood itself is defined by responsiveness. A god who does not answer when called is not a god at all. This moves the test beyond mere power-comparison—it becomes a definition of divinity. In Israelite theology, the God of Israel is characterized as the living God, the God who speaks, who acts, who responds to His people. Baal, despite his temples and prophets and royal patronage, may simply be an idol—a dead thing carved of wood or stone, or worse, a demon masquerading as a god. The fire will expose the truth.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase ha-Elohim asher ya'aneh va-esh hu ha-Elohim ('the God who answers by fire—he is the God') appears deceptively simple, but it is the theological thesis of the entire chapter. The verb anah ('to answer, to respond, to hear and reply') becomes the governing verb. It will recur repeatedly: 'Baal's prophets called... but there was no voice, nor any that answered' (v. 26); 'Baal's prophets cried aloud... but there was no voice, nor any that answered' (v. 29); 'Then the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench. And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces: and they said, The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God' (v. 37–39). The chapter is a sustained meditation on the verb 'answer.' A living God answers. A dead idol is silent.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The people's response—'It is well spoken' (tov ha-davar)—breaks their previous silence. They approve the terms of the test. Yet they do not commit to either side. They are spectators, not participants. They will see what happens; they have not yet decided whom to follow. The opening of their mouths marks progress—from verse 21's complete silence to verse 24's verbal approval of the test. But it is still not confession or commitment. The real moment of decision will come after the fire falls, when they see which god actually answers.
commentary.application: The practical application of Elijah's test is available to every person who sincerely seeks to know truth. The test is not reserved for prophets or for moments of dramatic public witness. It is personal and available. If we face a choice between competing paths—the way of the world and the way of the gospel, the way of convention and the way of revelation, the way of immediate gratification and the way of covenant—we can apply Elijah's test. We can call upon God in prayer, with sincere heart and real intent, and ask for confirmation. We can make our offering of faith, time, sacrifice, and then wait for the answer. The answer may come as the burning of the Holy Ghost in our bosom (D&C 8:2–3), as a change of heart (Alma 5:26), as peace in troubled circumstances, as opportunity opening, as light breaking through confusion. God does answer. The people's response—'tov ha-davar'—shows they understand the fairness of the test. We too can approach God with confidence, knowing His test is fair. He will not handicap us. He will not hide Himself. If we call upon Him with full heart, full purpose of heart, with real intent, He will answer. The fire will fall. The question is whether we are willing to call, and whether we will recognize the answer when it comes. Elijah's test stands at the heart of every spiritual experience: Have you called upon God? Has He answered? If yes to both, then you know the truth of what Elijah proclaimed: 'The LORD, he is the God.'

cross_references.connection: Moses asked Israel, 'What nation has gods as close to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call upon him?' This verse encapsulates the definition of the true God: responsiveness to prayer and invocation.
The psalmist describes the LORD as One 'that hearest prayer' and 'that answerest them'—the God who responds to His people, the foundation of all confidence in prayer.

God says, 'I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another... Behold, the former things are come to pass, and new things do I declare,' establishing that the true God is the One who announces and fulfills, who speaks and performs.

John's test for discerning the Spirit of God from false spirits involves discerning which confession and testimony align with truth; Elijah's test of fire parallels this principle of discernment through response.

Moroni's promise that God will manifest the truth of the Book of Mormon through the Holy Ghost is a modern parallel to Elijah's test: call upon God with sincere heart, and He will answer by His Spirit, the living fire of divine confirmation.

word_study.meaning: Call upon, invoke, cry out to by name. The verb qara' ('call, cry out') is fundamental to prayer and worship. To call 'in the name of' (beshem) a deity is to invoke that deity's authority, to address that particular god.
word_study.significance: The invocation of a deity's name was believed to have power in the ancient world. To call a name was to summon that being. Elijah and the Baal prophets will call the names of their respective gods. The names themselves—YHWH versus Baal—represent different theologies, different understandings of reality, different commitments. When Israel later calls upon the name of the LORD (v. 37, 39), they will find He answers.

word_study.meaning: Answers by fire, responds through fire. The verb anah means 'to answer, to respond, to reply, to hear and return an answer.' The medium of answer is fire.
word_study.significance: This is the chapter's pivotal theological word. A god who answers is a living god. A god who does not answer is powerless or nonexistent. Fire is the medium—visible, undeniable, consuming, transformative. The Covenant Rendering notes that anah ('answer') appears in vv. 24, 26, 29, and 37, each time measuring the silence of Baal against the responsiveness of the LORD. To be answerable is to be alive; to be silent is to be dead.

word_study.meaning: He is the God, he shall be recognized as God, he is the real deity. The declaration is not merely that one god defeats another, but that the responder is the true God, worthy of allegiance and worship.
word_study.significance: Godhood itself is on trial. The test is not 'Which is stronger?' but 'Which is the real God?' Strength alone does not confer godhood. Responsiveness, faithfulness, the power to hear and answer—these are the marks of true deity. This is distinctly Israelite theology. The God of Israel is not merely the most powerful god among many; He is the God, the only true God, because He is the one who answers, who speaks, who acts, who is present to His people.

word_study.meaning: Good is the word/proposal. A statement of approval and agreement. The people find the terms of the test acceptable.
word_study.significance: The response 'tov ha-davar' marks the first verbal utterance of the assembled people since their silence in verse 21. They are finding their voice, gaining agency. Yet the approval is of the test structure, not of either deity. They remain unaligned. The next movement will be their confession after witnessing the fire: 'The LORD, he is the God.'

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's testimony to Zeezrom emphasizes the 'witness of the Spirit': 'If ye have experienced a change of heart, and have felt to sing the song of redeeming love, I would ask, can ye feel so now?' (Alma 5:26). This is the modern equivalent of Elijah's test: have you called upon God and received His answer? Can you feel the confirmation? The Book of Mormon repeatedly frames spiritual truth in terms of the Spirit's response—a felt, interior fire that confirms the truth of the gospel.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 8:2–3 promises revelation: 'But, behold, I say unto you, that you must study it out in your mind; then you must ask me if it be right; and if it is right I will cause that your bosom shall burn within you; therefore, you shall feel that it is right.' This is Elijah's test in modern form: study, pray, ask, and God will answer—through the burning of the Holy Ghost in the heart. The fire is interior rather than exterior, but it is undeniable, unmistakable, and available to all who call upon the LORD sincerely.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where heaven and earth meet, where God answers the prayers of His people. Temple recommend holders regularly enter the house of the LORD and experience the peace and confirmation of His presence. The fire that consumes Elijah's offering is paralleled in the transformation of heart that occurs in temple covenants. The work of the temple is the work of response: we offer ourselves to God's purposes, and He confirms His presence and power in our lives.

commentary.historical_context: The theological framework of the Mount Carmel test reflects a particular understanding of deity that was not universal in the ancient Near East. In Egyptian theology, gods were understood as powerful cosmic forces but not necessarily responsive to individual worship. In Mesopotamian religion, the gods were often depicted as distant and capricious. In Canaanite religion, Baal was a weather god whose power might manifest in storm without any sense of personal relationship. But Israelite theology, shaped by the covenant at Sinai and the prophetic tradition, understood God as fundamentally responsive. The God of Abraham heard the cry of Hagar (Genesis 16:11); the God of Israel heard the cry of His people in Egypt and sent a deliverer (Exodus 3:7–8). Prayer was not ritual obligation but genuine communication. This theology of responsiveness shaped Israelite prayer practice and prophetic expectation. When Elijah frames the test in terms of responsiveness ('the god who answers'), he is invoking an already-established Israelite understanding. The innovation is making this abstract theological claim concrete and visible through a public test.
commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate answer to every prayer and every sincere calling upon God. 'No man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). Christ is the fire that consumes the offering of our hearts—the refiner's fire that purges away dross and confirms what is true (Malachi 3:2–3). When the people finally cry out, 'The LORD, he is the God,' they are witnessing to the reality of Christ's atonement—the ultimate sacrifice accepted and confirmed by the Father's fire. Every prayer answered, every confirmation of truth, every burning of the Spirit is ultimately an answer from the God of Israel through the power of the Atonement.

text_kjv: And Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, unto whom the word of the LORD came, saying, Israel shall be thy name.

commentary.narrative:
Elijah's first act at Mount Carmel is theologically profound: he gathers twelve stones, one for each tribe of Jacob. This is not a coincidental detail or a structural convenience. In the divided monarchy, the northern kingdom of Israel (under Ahab, who rules ten tribes) is in conflict with the southern kingdom of Judah. By deliberately selecting twelve stones, Elijah makes a symbolic statement: before God, Israel remains undivided. The reference to Jacob's renaming (Genesis 32:28, 35:10)—when the patriarch was transformed into 'Israel'—reaches back past the political fragmentation of the monarchy to the covenantal foundation at Bethel. Elijah is not merely building an altar; he is rebuilding a theological claim about God's covenant people.

The phrase 'unto whom the word of the LORD came' links this moment to Jacob's encounter with God at Bethel, where the divine promise of multiplication and blessing was established. By invoking that ancient renaming, Elijah suggests that the true identity of God's people transcends the current political split. The altar itself becomes a living testimony that God's covenant encompasses all Israel, not merely the northern or southern kingdom. This is the foundation upon which God's vindication will rest: not tribal favoritism, but covenant unity.

word_study.meaning: Plural of even, 'stone.' In biblical usage, stones often serve as witnesses, markers of covenant, or building blocks of sacred structures. These are not quarried or worked stones but natural rocks, gathered from the earth—reflecting authenticity and simplicity.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering emphasizes that Elijah 'took' these stones, suggesting deliberate collection rather than incidental use. Stones appear throughout Scripture as covenant witnesses (Genesis 28:18, Joshua 4:3-9). Here they anchor the altar to Israel's patriarchal past.

word_study.meaning: Plural of shevet, 'tribe' or 'staff.' A shevet is both a lineage group and a symbol of authority (the patriarchal staff). The twelve shevtim represent the twelve-fold ordering of God's covenant people.
word_study.significance: The use of 'tribes' rather than 'kingdoms' is significant. Elijah avoids contemporary political language and reaches for the older, covenantal vocabulary. He is addressing Israel not as a fractured state but as a people unified by descent from Jacob and covenant with God.

word_study.meaning: A direct echo of Genesis 32:28, where the angel says to Jacob, 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel.' The phrase yihyeh shemekha ('shall be your name') transfers identity. A name in Hebrew thought is not merely a label but the expression of one's true nature and destiny.
word_study.significance: By recalling this moment, Elijah invokes the foundational covenant. The 'name' Israel carries the weight of election, struggle with God (Jacob's wrestling match), and the promise of multiplication. In the context of the drought and apostasy, Elijah's reference reminds the people that their ultimate identity lies not in Ahab's rule but in their covenant as 'Israel.'

cross_references.connection: Jacob's renaming to Israel by the angel at Peniel ('for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men'). Elijah's altar invokes this foundational moment to assert that God's covenant transcends current political division.

The twelve stones taken from the Jordan after Israel's crossing, each stone representing a tribe. Like Joshua's memorial, Elijah's twelve stones mark a covenant moment and serve as a witness to God's faithfulness.
The historical split of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam. Elijah's twelve-stone altar directly confronts this division and implicitly calls for reunion under God's covenant.
The prophecy of the two sticks (representing Judah and Israel) becoming one in God's hand. Elijah's twelve stones embody the same theological vision of restored unity under God's rule.
The Lord's promise that 'all the scattered remnants of Israel shall be brought home.' Elijah's altar anticipates this gathering back to covenant identity and unity.

commentary.historical_context: The divided monarchy (circa 931 BCE onward) created a political reality that gradually eroded the theological unity of 'Israel.' Ahab ruled the northern kingdom (the 'ten tribes'), while the southern kingdom of Judah remained separate. Religious practice diverged markedly: Ahab promoted Baal worship and the Asherah cult, while a more orthodox Yahwism persisted in the south. By the time of Elijah (mid-9th century BCE), the use of twelve as a number referencing all Israel had taken on nostalgic, covenantal significance—it harked back to the united monarchy under David and Solomon, and ultimately to the patriarchal structure itself. Elijah's choice of twelve stones would have resonated with remembrance of that lost unity. Ancient Near Eastern altars varied in construction; some were simply stacked stone, while others (like those at Megiddo) were more elaborate. The simplicity of Elijah's twelve-stone construction contrasts sharply with the elaborate prophetic theater of the Baal cult, suggesting that true worship requires no human embellishment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 19:10, Nephi quotes Isaiah's prophecy about the suffering servant. Like Elijah, Nephi and later Book of Mormon prophets emphasize covenant identity and the gathering of scattered Israel. The Book of Mormon consistently teaches that all descendants of Lehi's family are part of the covenant of Abraham, regardless of political divisions (2 Nephi 30:3-8).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 110:11 describes the appearance of Moses, Elias, and Elijah in the Kirtland Temple, restoring keys pertaining to 'the gathering of Israel from the four parts of the earth, and the leading of the ten tribes from the land of the north.' Elijah's altar symbolically represents this gathering theme—twelve stones as one altar—which becomes central to latter-day covenant restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The twelve stones of the altar echo the twelve stones upon the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28:21), linking tribal covenant to sacred ritual. In temple language, the altar represents the place where heaven and earth meet, where individual tribes (individuals) are unified in covenant relationship with God. Elijah's action prefigures the temple's role as a place of gathering and unification.

commentary.christological_typology: The twelve stones united into one altar foreshadow Christ as the cornerstone who gathers the scattered tribes of Israel (Isaiah 28:16, Romans 9:33). Christ's atonement accomplishes what Elijah's altar symbolizes: the reconciliation of divided Israel into one body. The Savior's teaching that He came 'not to send peace, but a sword' (Matthew 10:34-39) is tempered by His prayer in John 17 for unity among believers—a unity that Elijah's altar likewise calls for. The gathering symbolism also points to Christ as the one who 'shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' (Isaiah 11:12).
commentary.application: This verse invites us to consider what 'twelve stones' might mean in our own covenantal life. Are we, like Elijah, consciously building altars that transcend our divisions—whether generational, cultural, or denominational? The verse challenges modern members of the Church to see beyond the fragmentations that plague community and families and to recognize that all who have entered the covenant are part of one Israel. In personal discipleship, the twelve stones ask: Do I approach God as part of a unified covenant community, or as an isolated individual? Elijah's action suggests that our worship is strongest when it is rooted in covenantal identity and includes explicit acknowledgment of our place in God's gathered people.

text_kjv: And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD: and he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed.

commentary.narrative:
Elijah now constructs the altar from the twelve stones. The phrase 'in the name of the LORD' is crucial: the altar is not built for ritual mechanics or human honor, but as a deliberate act of devotion to Yahweh. This construction happens in the shadow of Baal's altar on the same mountain, making the theological claim audible even through the act itself. The sanctuary is established by speech act (in the name of the LORD) and physical building.

But the truly unusual detail is the trench. Altars did not normally have trenches running around them. This is Elijah's preparation for the test: he will later soak the sacrifice and wood with water, and this trench will collect that water, making the eventual ignition by fire humanly impossible. The trench is thus a guarantee of divine authentication. The measurement—'as great as would contain two measures of seed' (ke-veit sa'atayim zera, literally 'like a house of two seahs of seed')—indicates substantial dimensions. A seah is approximately 22 liters; two seahs would cover an area of roughly one-third of an acre's perimeter when planted. The trench, then, is not a small groove but a significant channel around the altar. Every detail has been calibrated to remove natural explanation from the coming miracle.

word_study.meaning: To build, construct, erect. In biblical usage, banah can refer to building physical structures but also to establishing dynasties, covenants, or relationships. The word suggests permanence and intention.
word_study.significance: Elijah does not merely pile stones; he 'builds' them. This is constructive action, not accidental assembly. The use of banah invokes the solidity and lasting nature of what he is establishing—a true altar, not a temporary structure.

word_study.term_english: in the name of the LORD
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in/by the name of YHWH.' In Hebrew thought, to do something 'in the name' of God means to do it as His representative, under His authority, and for His glory. The name carries the character and presence of the named one.
word_study.significance: This phrase distinguishes Elijah's altar from the Baal altar. Whereas the Baal prophets are prophets of a false god, Elijah's entire action is explicitly authorized by and dedicated to Yahweh. The altar's legitimacy derives from its dedication to the true God.

word_study.meaning: A channel, watercourse, or ditch. The root suggests something dug out or carved, as opposed to a natural formation. Te'alah appears in contexts of irrigation (1 Kings 18:32, 35) and can refer to the channels that bring water.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering emphasizes that the trench is 'large enough to hold two seahs of seed,' underscoring that this is not decorative but functional—designed to hold water. The trench is Elijah's guarantee that no natural cause can explain the fire.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'a house of two seahs of seed.' A seah is a dry measure (approximately 22 liters or 7.3 quarts). 'A house of two seahs of seed' means the area of ground that would require two seahs of seed to plant. This is an agricultural measurement, not a linear one.
word_study.significance: The use of an agricultural measurement—rather than a simple linear dimension—grounds the narrative in practical, observable reality. Anyone hearing this story would understand immediately how large the trench was, because they knew how much seed was required to plant a given field. This makes the miracle even more tangible and verifiable.

cross_references.connection: Abram built an altar 'in the name of the LORD.' The same formula appears here, linking Elijah's action to the patriarchal foundation of Yahweh worship in covenant history.

God's instruction that altars should be built of unhewn stone: 'If thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone.' Elijah's twelve natural stones conform to this ancient law, emphasizing authenticity and covenant compliance.

Instructions for the perpetual fire on the altar of burnt offering in the tabernacle. The fire represents God's acceptance; in Elijah's test, the descent of fire will authenticate his altar and his prayer.

God declares that all things are created 'for my glory.' Elijah builds the altar explicitly 'in the name of the LORD,' making clear that the ensuing miracle exists to glorify God, not to prove Elijah's power.

In the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple, the Lord's house is dedicated 'in the name of Jesus Christ.' Like Elijah's altar, sacred spaces are built under divine authority and for the advancement of God's kingdom.

commentary.historical_context: Altars in the ancient Near East took various forms. Some were simple stone stacks, while others (particularly in larger temples) were more elaborate structures with foundations, drainage systems, and channels for blood and libations. The trench is, in fact, not entirely without parallel—some Levantine altars did include channels to manage the flow of liquid offerings. However, the depth and capacity of Elijah's trench (large enough to hold two seahs of water—roughly 44 liters) is exceptional and deliberate. Mount Carmel, being at the crossroads between the coastal plain and the interior, was home to sanctuaries dedicated to various deities, including Baal. The Baal altar on Carmel would have been a well-known structure in the region. The fact that both altars stand on the same mountain makes the test a direct competition for recognition—not in some neutral location, but on what the Baal worshipers considered sacred ground.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 11:3-12, King Noah builds altars and sanctuaries for idolatrous worship, explicitly engaging in covenant violation. In contrast, Alma 2:24-37 describes Alma's people building altars and gathering to worship God. The contrast between true and false altars runs throughout the Book of Mormon, much as it does in 1 Kings 18. True altars are built 'in the name' of God and reflect covenant commitment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:119 describes the house of the Lord as a place 'prepared in all things, and replenished with all manner of precious things.' The attention to detail in Elijah's altar—the twelve stones, the precise trench dimension—parallels the specificity with which God directs temple building and the building up of His kingdom. Both require careful attention to covenant requirements.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The altar is the central focal point of temple worship, representing the place where mortals approach God and where God's presence is manifest. Elijah's trench, which will be filled with water in verse 35, parallels the water and blood that flow from temple ordinances. The dimensions given for the trench suggest precise, sacred measurements—just as temple architecture involves careful proportion and symbolic measurement.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's altar built 'in the name of the LORD' prefigures Christ as the true and living altar. Hebrews 13:10 speaks of 'an altar whereof they have no right to eat which serve the tabernacle.' Christ is that altar—the sacrifice and the place of atonement in one. The trench designed to hold water foreshadows the water and blood that flow from Christ's pierced side (John 19:34), waters that sanctify and cleanse. The fire that will descend on Elijah's altar parallels the Holy Ghost fire that purifies believers through Christ's atonement (Matthew 3:11).
commentary.application: Modern disciples are invited to ask: What 'altars' am I building in my life, and are they explicitly 'in the name of the LORD'? Elijah's careful preparation—with the trench as a guarantee of divine validation—suggests that true worship requires both faith and foresight. We prepare ourselves through repentance, covenant keeping, and deliberate spiritual practice, positioning ourselves for God's grace to flow. The trench also reminds us that we should not ask God to perform miracles carelessly; we should come with preparation and intentionality. Just as the trench removes natural explanation for the fire, our preparation removes the excuse of unreadiness when God desires to manifest His power in our lives.

text_kjv: And he put the wood in order, and cut the bullock in pieces, and laid him on the wood, and said, Fill four barrels with water, and pour it on the burnt sacrifice, and on the wood.

commentary.narrative:
Elijah now methodically prepares the sacrifice itself. He arranges the wood, cuts the bull into pieces, and arranges these pieces on the wood—all the standard preparation for a burnt offering. This is not novel; it follows the pattern established in Levitical law (see Leviticus 1:6-8). What is extraordinary is what comes next: he commands that water be poured over the entire offering and wood, not once, but multiple times.

The pouring of water is the narrative's crucial mechanism for eliminating natural explanation. During a severe drought (Israel had been without rain for three and a half years, per 1 Kings 17:1), water would have been desperately scarce. The act of pouring water—not just sprinkling, but filling jars and pouring them out—over a sacrifice is unprecedented and wasteful by any ordinary standard. Moreover, it makes ignition impossible. A wood fire requires dry material; Elijah ensures the sacrifice is completely waterlogged. The repetition ('Fill four barrels... Do it a second time... Do it a third time') creates a drumming rhythm of excess: twelve jars of water in total (four jars × three times). This is not a pragmatic action but a prophetic gesture, designed to make the eventual miracle undeniable.

word_study.meaning: To arrange, order, or set in a row. In the context of sacrifice, it means to stack the wood in the proper configuration for a burnt offering. Arak suggests deliberate arrangement according to pattern.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes careful preparation. This is not haphazard but methodical, following the correct form of sacrifice. Elijah's adherence to proper sacrifice procedure authenticates his action as legitimate Yahweh worship.

word_study.meaning: To cut, divide, or sever. In sacrifice, the animal is cut into specific pieces according to ritual law. Nitach emphasizes the deliberate division of the whole into its parts for sacrifice.
word_study.significance: Like arak, nitach emphasizes correct procedure. Elijah is not improvising; he is following the laws of burnt offering, which lends authenticity and divine authorization to his action.

word_study.meaning: Plural of kad, a water jar or vessel. Kadi are ceramic or wooden containers used for storing and carrying water. The use of 'four barrels' indicates large quantities of water, not a casual sprinkling.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering maintains 'jars' rather than 'barrels,' emphasizing portable containers. The point is that water is being actively brought and deliberately poured—this is not passive or incidental moisture.

word_study.meaning: A burnt offering or whole offering. The olah is a sacrifice in which the entire animal is burned on the altar, with nothing reserved for human consumption. It represents complete devotion and consecration.
word_study.significance: The burnt offering is the most basic and fundamental sacrifice, representing complete surrender to God. By preparing a proper olah, Elijah is making an act of total consecration—his entire effort and the entire offering are given wholly to God.

cross_references.connection: The law of the burnt offering specifies how the animal shall be cut into pieces and arranged on the wood for burning. Elijah follows this precise protocol, demonstrating that his altar and sacrifice are legitimate under covenant law.

Elijah's declaration of the drought: 'As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.' The water Elijah now pours out is particularly precious in light of this declared drought.

Abraham's preparation of the sacrifice on Mount Moriah, with wood arranged and the animal laid upon it. Elijah's preparation mirrors Abraham's, linking the two prophets in acts of covenantal devotion and submission to God's word.
A vow of burnt offerings: 'I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings.' The psalmist's commitment to offering whole sacrifices parallels Elijah's total devotion in this moment.
The epistle contrasts the repetition of OT sacrifices with Christ's one offering. Elijah's single, carefully prepared burnt offering prefigures the efficacy of Christ's singular sacrifice.

commentary.historical_context: Burnt offerings were the most common sacrifice in ancient Israel, performed daily at the Jerusalem temple (Exodus 29:38-42) and at local altars throughout the land. The preparation Elijah follows—arranging wood, cutting the animal into pieces, and placing it on the wood—is precisely the method outlined in Leviticus 1:6-8. What is extraordinary is the addition of water. In the ancient Near Eastern world, water was precious, especially during drought. Archaeological evidence from Carmel and other Levantine sites shows that water management and storage were critical concerns. The deliberate waste of water on a sacrifice would have been shocking—and, to the onlooking crowd, clearly designed to prove that only divine fire could ignite such a thoroughly soaked offering. The repetition of the watering (three times) mirrors other covenant ceremonies in which actions are repeated for emphasis and solemnity (see Naaman's seven-fold washing in 2 Kings 5:10).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 9:7, the Savior 'breaketh the bands of death, that the grave shall have no victory, and that death should have no sting.' The preparation and offering of the sacrifice in verse 33 parallels how Christ prepared Himself for sacrifice—fully aware of the cost, methodically moving toward the cross. Alma 34:10 notes that the Savior 'shall be led, like a lamb before the shearer, and as a lamb to the slaughter.' Both Elijah's sacrifice and Christ's emphasize willing, conscious preparation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 135:3 records Joseph Smith's final words: 'I am going like a lamb to the slaughter; but I am calm as a summer's morning; I have a conscience void of offense towards God and towards all men.' Elijah's calm, methodical preparation of the sacrifice reflects this same courage and acceptance of God's will, even in the face of apparent danger.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The preparation of the sacrifice in verse 33 mirrors the preparation of the temple ordinances, where careful arrangement and sequence matter. Just as Elijah arranges wood and animal according to covenant law, temple work unfolds according to divine pattern. The four jars of water poured three times may also echo the use of water in temple washing and anointing.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's bull sacrifice prefigures Christ as the Lamb of God. Isaiah 53:6-7 describes the Servant: 'The LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all... he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter.' Like the bull, Christ is prepared, cut off (in death), and offered wholly for the sin of the world. The water poured over the sacrifice anticipates the water and blood from Christ's side (John 19:34), waters that cleanse and sanctify all who believe. The burnt offering's complete consumption in fire foreshadows the total, once-for-all nature of Christ's sacrifice, leaving nothing undone or incomplete.
commentary.application: Elijah's methodical preparation invites reflection on how we approach covenant action and sacrifice. Do we prepare with care and attention to detail, or do we approach God's work haphazardly? The pouring of water—a precious commodity—over the sacrifice teaches us about radical commitment: true consecration may cost us what we treasure most. In modern terms, this might mean time, resources, or comfort. Elijah's action also teaches us to make our faith visible and verifiable. He did not secretly prepare the sacrifice in hopes of a hidden miracle; he did it before witnesses, removing any possibility of ambiguity or natural explanation. This challenges us to live our faith openly and to make choices that clearly demonstrate our commitment to God.

text_kjv: And he said, Do it the second time. And they did it the second time. And he said, Do it the third time. And they did it the third time.

commentary.narrative:
This verse completes the water-pouring sequence that began in verse 33. After the first four jars are poured out, Elijah commands the action a second time, and the servants obey. Then a third time. In total, twelve jars of water have been poured over the sacrifice, the wood, and into the trench (four jars per round × three rounds). The repetition serves multiple purposes. First, it ensures complete saturation—no dry wood remains that might catch fire from an overlooked spark. Second, it creates a dramatic buildup: with each repetition, the action becomes more absurd by worldly standards. Why would anyone pour water on a sacrifice intended to burn? The repetition makes the eventual ignition even more miraculous. Third, the repetition emphasizes Elijah's authority. He commands, and the people obey without question. This establishes him as a figure of spiritual authority, in stark contrast to the false authority of the Baal prophets, whose elaborate rituals and hours of screaming have achieved nothing.

The structure of verse 34—'He said... and they did... He said... and they did'—creates a rhythmic pattern. The parallelism is almost ceremonial, as though this is itself a kind of ritual action. The people are not merely obeying orders; they are participating in a covenant act. By pouring water on Elijah's altar, they are literally investing in his prayer and God's vindication. The verse is brief but dense with implication: obedience, repetition, escalation, and the approaching climax of divine response.

word_study.meaning: Imperative forms derived from the numbers two and three, used as verbs. 'Shenu' literally means 'do a second time'; 'shalleshu' means 'do a third time.' This is an idiomatic way of commanding repetition without explicitly saying 'repeat' each time.
word_study.significance: The use of numeric verbs creates a rhythmic, almost liturgical quality. The TCR rendering ('Do it a second time') makes the repetitive command explicit, emphasizing that this is not a natural or casual action but a deliberate, ceremonial repetition.

word_study.meaning: Third-person plural past tense of 'asah, 'to do' or 'to make.' The simple, repeated use of this verb emphasizes swift, unquestioning obedience.
word_study.significance: The absence of hesitation or question in 'they did' underscores that Elijah's word is being received as authoritative. There is no debate, no delay, no second-guessing—just immediate compliance. This contrasts sharply with the Baal prophets, who have screamed all day with no response.

cross_references.connection: The immediate context: after the third watering, Elijah prays, and fire falls from heaven, consuming not only the sacrifice but even the water in the trench. The repetition makes this miracle more spectacular and undeniable.

Joshua commands Israel to march around Jericho seven times on the seventh day. Repetition of a commanded action, done in faith, leads to God's intervention. Like Joshua's marches, Elijah's repeated water-pourings prepare the way for divine action.

Naaman is commanded to dip seven times in the Jordan for healing. Repetition of an act, especially involving water, becomes the occasion for God's grace. Both Elijah and Naaman's stories teach that exact obedience, even when it seems illogical, invites divine power.

In Gethsemane, Jesus prays three times, asking that the cup pass from Him. The repetition of prayer in crisis—and the acceptance of God's will—parallels Elijah's preparatory actions leading to his own plea in verse 36.

The dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple emphasizes that petitions made with faith and exactness will be heard. Elijah's precisely repeated water-pouring, done with full faith in God's word, exemplifies the kind of exactness the Lord honors.

commentary.historical_context: The phenomenon of ritual repetition appears throughout the ancient Near East and in biblical tradition. The number three (and sometimes seven, or multiples thereof) carries ceremonial weight. In Egyptian religious practice, repetition of ritual actions was understood as magically efficacious—a belief the biblical text rejects by making clear that Israel's God responds to covenant faithfulness and direct address, not ritual mechanics. However, ritual structure and repetition are not themselves rejected; rather, they are subordinated to covenant relationship. The fact that 'they did it' suggests Elijah has developed sufficient authority with the assembled crowd that they will carry out his commands without question. This would have been remarkable given that Ahab, the king, is presumably present (see verse 41), and Ahab is hostile to Elijah.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 12:47, the Savior teaches, 'And if ye shall ask the Father in my name, asking for that which is right, he shall give unto you.' The three-fold repetition of water-pouring, done at Elijah's word and in preparation for his prayer, reflects the principle that preparation and exact obedience align us with God's will. In Alma 32, Alma teaches that faith is 'an experiment upon the word' (Alma 32:27)—the people's three-fold obedience is an experiment, a test of whether God's word (through Elijah) is true.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:27-28 states: 'I require all things to be done in mine own way... and let all things be done with order.' Elijah's three-fold, ordered command-and-obedience sequence reflects God's requirement for order and precision in covenant work. The repetition itself mirrors the principle that important actions in God's kingdom are done with deliberate, repeated confirmation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple ordinances, certain words and actions are repeated at different points for emphasis and power. Elijah's command, obeyed three times, parallels the structure of temple worship, where repetition and witness combine to seal covenants. The three-fold watering also echoes the baptism ceremony, which may be performed multiple times in certain contexts.

commentary.christological_typology: The three-fold repetition may foreshadow Christ's three-fold resurrection manifestations in the New Testament accounts, or His three days in the grave. More broadly, the obedience of the people to Elijah's commands prefigures the obedience that Christ calls for from all disciples (Matthew 28:20, 'Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you'). The willingness of the people to 'waste' water on the sacrifice—to act in apparent foolishness in faith—parallels the foolishness of faith in the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18-25).
commentary.application: Verse 34 teaches the power of exact obedience and the value of preparation. Elijah does not ask the people to 'help if they feel like it'; he commands precise action, repeated. Modern disciples are invited to consider: Are we willing to follow prophetic direction with the same exactness that these people followed Elijah? Are we willing to do 'illogical' things (like the earlier water-pouring) because God's word demands it, trusting that God's purposes will be vindicated? The verse also invites reflection on preparation. Just as Elijah does not expect fire to descend on dry wood and a casual sacrifice, so we should not expect God's blessings without deliberate preparation and obedience. The repetition teaches that spiritual power is not a one-time event but the result of sustained, faithful action.

text_kjv: And the water ran round about the altar; and he filled the trench also with water.

commentary.narrative:
After the three rounds of water-pouring, the narrative pauses to confirm the effect: the water has thoroughly saturated the entire scene. Water 'ran round about the altar,' flowing in every direction from the soaked wood and sacrifice. The trench, prepared in verse 32 for precisely this purpose, is now 'filled with water.' The scene is complete: the sacrifice is waterlogged, the wood is drenched, and water surrounds the entire structure. At this moment, ignition by any natural means—spark, hidden coals, or human trickery—is impossible.

This verse is transitional. It marks the completion of Elijah's preparation and the readiness for God's response. The narrative slows momentarily to let the reader absorb what has been done: every possible natural explanation for the subsequent fire has been systematically eliminated. The burning of the sacrifice will be undeniably divine action. The verse also creates dramatic tension. The Baal prophets have been screaming all day with no response. Elijah has now set up the most impossible circumstance imaginable. What will happen? The reader is positioned on the edge of witnessing a miracle or a complete vindication of Baal. The water-filled trench is Elijah's guarantee: if fire comes, it will be God alone.

word_study.meaning: Past tense of halak, 'to go' or 'to walk.' When used with water, it means to flow or run. The word suggests movement and continuation, not static pooling.
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes that the water was still moving, actively flowing around the altar. This is not stagnant water but living, moving water, reinforcing the saturation of every crevice and gap.

word_study.meaning: To fill, satisfy, or complete. Milla carries the sense of making full or complete, leaving no empty space.
word_study.significance: The trench is not merely 'moistened' or 'dampened' but 'filled'—completely full of water. This emphasizes the impossibility of natural ignition and the completeness of Elijah's preparation.

cross_references.connection: God separates the waters and gathers them together. Elijah's water, gathered in the trench, is an instrument of God's power, much as the waters in Genesis are.

Moses stretches out his hand, and God divides the Red Sea. Later, God brings the waters back together. Elijah's water, about to be overcome by fire, demonstrates God's power over the elements, just as Moses' experience did.
'My cup runneth over.' The abundant provision of the Lord. Similarly, Elijah's trench overflows with water—an abundance designed to manifest God's power.

'When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee... they shall not overflow thee.' Though fire (not water) is the immediate element in Elijah's case, the principle holds: God's protection and purpose transcend the elements.

In the Book of Mormon, Jesus appears in fire and in cloud. Fire and water are both instruments of God's manifestation. Elijah's test demonstrates that fire, not water, is the sign of God's acceptance.

commentary.historical_context: The saturation described in verse 35 would have been particularly striking in the context of a three-and-a-half-year drought (1 Kings 17:1, 18:1). Water was more precious than gold. The Levantine region, especially during dry seasons, was acutely aware of water's value. Archaeological evidence from Mount Carmel and surrounding areas shows that water collection and storage were critical concerns throughout the year. The visual of water running and filling the trench would have been an astounding sight to the assembled crowd—not just because of the waste (by their standards), but because it demonstrated absolute confidence in divine response. No one would destroy that much water for a failed ritual.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 15:32-36, Nephi describes the 'filthy water' of the doctrine of the devil, contrasting it with the living waters of Christ. Elijah's water here, though literal and abundant, represents the preparation for a theophany. In the Book of Mormon, abundance of water often signals God's blessing and provision (see Alma 26:35, 'Behold, waters do come forth from the wilderness and the day spring breaketh forth upon the mountains').
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14 describes how God's word shall 'go forth out of my mouth... unto the ends of the earth.' Elijah's preparation, complete and overflowing, is his moment of readiness to speak God's word (verse 36). The preparation in verse 35 sets the stage for the petition in verse 36.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Water is a central symbol in temple ordinances, representing purification and preparation for divine encounter. Elijah's water-filled trench, though literal and functional, parallels the spiritual cleansing that precedes approach to God's presence. The abundant water also echoes the water fonts and baptismal washings that prepare the soul.

commentary.christological_typology: The water filling the trench may prefigure the floods of judgment through which Christ passes in the Father's behalf. Psalm 42:7 speaks of 'all thy waves and thy billows' passing over the psalmist. Christ submitted to the 'waters' of judgment and death, emerging to give 'living water' to all who believe (John 7:37-38). Elijah's water-filled trench, overcome by fire, prefigures Christ's triumph over death through resurrection fire.
commentary.application: Verse 35 invites us to examine the completeness of our preparation before asking God for intervention. Elijah did not pray for fire until he had done everything in his power to make natural explanation impossible. Modern believers are challenged to ask: Before we petition God for miracles in our lives, have we done the spiritual equivalent of filling the trench? Have we repented, prepared, studied, prayed, fasted, and made ourselves ready? Have we removed excuses and prepared the ground for God's grace to fall? The verse teaches that preparation is not lacking in faith; it is the prerequisite for faith to be efficacious. We demonstrate faith not by avoiding preparation but by preparing thoroughly and then trusting God to provide what only He can.

text_kjv: And it came to pass at the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that Elijah the prophet came near, and said, LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel, and that I am thy servant, and that I have done all these things at thy word.

commentary.narrative:
After all the preparation, after the twelve stones, the trench, the sacrifice, and the thrice-poured water, Elijah finally prays. The prayer comes 'at the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice'—the ninth hour of the day, the appointed time when the daily burnt offering was made in the Jerusalem temple. By timing his petition at this moment, Elijah aligns his individual prayer with the corporate worship of Israel, reaching back to patriarchal covenant and forward to the temple's daily rhythms. His prayer is strikingly brief. The Baal prophets screamed for hours; Elijah speaks in measured, controlled language.

The prayer has three parts. First, the invocation: 'LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel.' This reaches back beyond the monarchy, beyond the conquest, to the patriarchs. 'Israel,' not 'Jacob,' invokes the renewed name (as referenced in verse 31). The God Elijah addresses is not merely the God of the current moment but the God of covenant continuity. Second, the petition: 'Let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel.' This is the central request—not merely that fire fall, but that through fire, God's identity and power be made known. Third, the assertion of relationship and authority: 'I am thy servant' and 'I have done all these things at thy word.' Elijah claims no power of his own; everything he has done derives from God's direction. The phrase 'at thy word' (u-bidvarekha) is crucial: Elijah is not acting on personal initiative but as God's messenger.

Notice what Elijah does NOT ask for. He does not ask for vindication of himself. He does not ask for honor or recognition. He does not even explicitly ask for fire. He asks that God be known. This is the difference between true prophecy and false prophecy. The Baal prophets are invested in their own status; Elijah is invested in God's glory. This prayer epitomizes biblical prophecy: the prophet's role is to make God known, not to promote himself.

word_study.term_english: at the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice
word_study.meaning: 'Alah, 'to go up' or 'to offer up'; minha, 'grain offering' or 'evening offering.' The phrase literally means 'at the going up of the offering,' referring to the moment when the priest's hand lifts the offering toward heaven.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering interprets this as 'the evening offering' specifically. The timing—evening prayer, the moment of the temple sacrifice—links Elijah's petition to the formal worship of Israel. This is not a private, improvised moment but a deliberate alignment with covenant practice.

word_study.meaning: To draw near, approach, or come forward. In religious contexts, nigash often refers to approaching God's presence, especially at an altar or in prayer.
