word_study.significance: Elijah 'comes near' just as a priest approaches the altar. His action is reverential and formal, befitting a prophet addressing God before the assembled people.

word_study.term_english: LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel
word_study.term_original: יְהוָ֗ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י אַבְרָהָם֙ יִצְחָ֣ק וְיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל (YHWH Elohei Avraham Yitschaq ve-Yisra'el)
word_study.meaning: A formal, covenantal address combining the divine name with titles emphasizing patriarchal lineage and covenant identity. This invocation appears repeatedly in Scripture (see Exodus 3:6, 4:5) and carries the weight of covenantal history.
word_study.significance: By invoking 'Abraham, Isaac, and Israel,' Elijah reaches back to the threefold covenant promise of land, descendants, and blessing. He is not praying to a generic deity but to the God who has been Israel's God from the beginning. In the context of the northern kingdom's apostasy under Ahab, this invocation is a reminder of who the true God is.

word_study.meaning: Nipheal form of yada, 'to know.' The passive form emphasizes that knowledge is not achieved by human effort but is revealed or made manifest. Yada in Hebrew often means not just intellectual knowledge but relational knowing, a knowing rooted in experience.
word_study.significance: Elijah is asking for experiential knowledge, not mere information. The people will not simply hear about God's power; they will witness it directly. The fire will make God known in a way that cannot be denied or forgotten.

word_study.meaning: By your word, at your command, through your direction. Dabar means word, command, or deed. The preposition be- indicates the means or agent of the action.
word_study.significance: Elijah emphasizes that his actions originate in God's word, not in his own will. This is the essential characteristic of a true prophet: he speaks and acts only as God directs. The TCR rendering ('at your word I have done') makes this agency explicit.

cross_references.connection: The Lord identifies Himself to Moses as 'the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Elijah's invocation echoes this foundational self-identification, connecting his moment to Moses' commissioning at the burning bush.

'Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him.' The petition that God 'be known' in Israel is a core theme of Deuteronomy and the prophetic message.

'That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth.' The prayer in verse 36 echoes the psalmist's desire that God's name and power be made known universally.

Hezekiah prays: 'O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the LORD, even thou only.' Like Elijah, Hezekiah's prayer focuses on God's vindication and the revelation of His power to the nations.

Jesus prays: 'And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.' Both Elijah and Christ understand 'knowing' God as the central purpose of life and revelation.

The Lord tells Hyrum Smith: 'My word shall go forth that it may be fulfilled... that all things may be done in order, and by common consent by the voice of the Church.' Elijah's assertion that he acts 'at thy word' parallels the Restoration emphasis on divine direction and covenant order.

commentary.historical_context: The evening sacrifice (minchah) was performed daily in the Jerusalem temple at the ninth hour (3 p.m. in modern reckoning), according to the laws of Moses (Exodus 29:39, Numbers 28:4). Though Elijah is not in Jerusalem but on Mount Carmel (in the northern kingdom), his timing his prayer to coincide with the national offering shows his awareness of Israel's covenant rhythms and his alignment with legitimate worship. The invocation of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel would have resonated deeply with the assembled crowd, reminding them of their identity as God's chosen people—a reminder pointedly needed given that Ahab has encouraged Baal worship. The language of the prayer is formal and priestly, not the ecstatic utterance of a false prophet but the measured petition of a covenant mediator.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 9:18-19, Jacob teaches about how the Spirit works in prophetic ministry: 'Jacob was righteousness, and Jacob was diligent' (paraphrasing). More directly, in Alma 31:26-33, Alma prays that his voice be heard among the Zoramites, asking God to strengthen him. Like Elijah, Alma is not focused on personal vindication but on God's power being made manifest in the hearts of the people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:15 teaches: 'Seek not for riches but for wisdom, and behold, the mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto you, and then shall you be made rich.' Elijah's prayer seeks not his own exaltation but God's knowledge among the people—the same principle. Further, D&C 50:24 explains: 'Every man who hath been warned to warn his neighbors.' Elijah's entire action on Mount Carmel is an act of warning and bearing witness, fulfilling the prophetic mandate.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The prayer in verse 36 occurs at the time of the evening offering, connecting Elijah's personal petition to the corporate worship of Israel. The temple's daily sacrifices create a rhythm of covenant renewal; Elijah's prayer participates in that rhythm. The assertion 'I am thy servant' reflects the covenant relationship between God and His prophets that is renewed in temple worship.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's prayer is a prototype of Christ's Gethsemane prayer (Luke 22:42, Matthew 26:39-44). Both prayers come at a moment of crisis. Both begin with invocation of the Father. Both ultimately affirm submission to God's will over personal interest. Christ's extended prayer in John 17 particularly parallels Elijah's: 'Father... glorify thy name' (John 12:28 and 17:1-5). Both prophets-priests are focused on the revelation of God's power and identity, not on their own vindication. Furthermore, Elijah's claim to act 'at thy word' prefigures Christ's central declaration that He does nothing of Himself but only what the Father directs (John 5:30, 8:28). Both are examples of perfect alignment between human will and divine will.
commentary.application:
Verse 36 is transformative for understanding the nature of true petition and true authority. Elijah's prayer teaches that effective prayer focuses on God's will and God's glory, not on personal vindication or blessing. When we pray, do we ask God to be made known, or do we primarily ask for personal advantage? The verse also teaches the power of explicit alignment with covenant. Elijah invokes Abraham, Isaac, and Israel—he roots his prayer in the oldest covenantal promises. Modern disciples are invited to do similarly: to root our prayers and petitions in the covenant we have made, to invoke the names and promises of God that pertain to our specific situation, and to make our petitions in alignment with God's broader purposes.

Further, the phrase 'at thy word I have done all these things' challenges us to examine our actions and motivations. Are we acting on God's direction, or on our own initiative? Elijah's preparation was not self-invented but was ordered by God (implied in verse 36). Our spiritual preparation—repentance, fasting, study, prayer—should similarly be responsive to God's direction as received through prophets and personal revelation. The verse teaches that when we align ourselves completely with God's word and will, we position ourselves to witness miracles.

text_kjv: Hear me, O LORD, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the LORD God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again.

commentary.narrative:
Elijah's prayer reaches its emotional and theological climax with the doubled cry 'Answer me, LORD! Answer me!' This is not mere repetition for emphasis—it is the compressed intensity of a covenant relationship at stake. For hours, the prophets of Baal have screamed into silence, receiving no response from their god. Elijah's briefness is itself a statement: the living God does not require frenzy or prolonged begging to hear His covenant people. The doubled aneni (answer me) stands in stark contrast to the futility of Baal's prophets and declares what the contest is fundamentally about: which God answers? Which God is real?

The theological weight of the final clause cannot be overstated. Elijah does not pray that the people will repent or that they will turn themselves back to God. Instead, he attributes the turning of hearts entirely to God's work: 'you are turning their hearts back.' The verb hasibota is in the perfect tense—'you have turned'—speaking of the act as already accomplished, as if the fire about to fall will itself be the mechanism through which hearts are restored. Elijah recognizes what many miss: genuine spiritual restoration is God's sovereign work, not human effort. The people have wandered, yes, but the restoration belongs to God alone.

This prayer is the inverse of what the prophets of Baal did. Where they used volume and self-injury and frenzy, Elijah uses brevity and intimacy. Where they received no answer, Elijah trusts completely in the covenant name and relationship. The doubled imperative is both a cry of urgency and an expression of utter confidence—not anxious repetition, but covenantal assurance that God hears those who call upon Him in truth.

word_study.meaning: To answer, to respond, to hear and reply. The root carries the sense of attending to, listening, and responding. In the covenant context, anah is the response of God to the cry of His people.
word_study.significance: The doubled imperative aneni YHWH aneni ('Answer me, LORD, answer me!') is the defining theological moment of the chapter. Elijah's confidence rests not in volume or frenzy but in the covenant relationship—he calls and trusts that the LORD will respond. The verb anah appears throughout the contest narrative and culminates here: Elijah asks for the response that Baal could not and will not provide. In Latter-day Saint theology, this echoes the principle that God hears and answers those who call upon Him in faith (see D&C 6:36: 'I am here'). The Covenant Rendering captures this with 'Answer me' rather than 'Hear me,' emphasizing the active divine response required.

word_study.term_original: הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת־לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית (hasibota et libbam achorannit)
word_study.meaning: You have turned their hearts backward/back again. The verb shuv (in the hiph'il form, sibota) means to turn, to return, to restore. The adverb achorannit means backward or back again, suggesting restoration to a previous state.
word_study.significance: This phrase is theologically extraordinary because it places the entire responsibility for spiritual restoration on God. Elijah does not pray for the people to turn themselves, nor does he command them to repent. Instead, he declares to God that the turning of hearts is God's sovereign work. The perfect tense ('you have turned') speaks as if the act is already accomplished—a prophetic utterance of faith that the fire about to fall will be the vehicle of divine restoration. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'you are turning their hearts back' preserves the ongoing, active nature of this divine work. In covenant theology, this reflects the truth that while humans may choose to follow, only God can turn a hardened heart back to Him.

word_study.meaning: The covenant name YHWH combined with the general term for God (Elohim). This pairing emphasizes both the personal relationship (YHWH as the God of covenant) and the universal sovereignty (Elohim as God over all).
word_study.significance: Elijah's prayer identifies the God who will answer as both the personal covenant God (YHWH) and the God of all creation (Elohim). This is a complete affirmation of divine identity—the one true God is both Israel's covenantal partner and the sovereign Lord of all nations. The people need to know both dimensions: that YHWH is real (covenant relationship) and that He is God (universal authority).

cross_references.connection: Elijah's earlier challenge to the people—'How long halt ye between two opinions?'—is now answered through this prayer. The turning of hearts begins with the recognition of YHWH's identity and power.

The law concerning false prophets and the restoration of covenant loyalty; Elijah's prayer aligns with the theological principle that turning hearts back to God is a foundational work of the covenant.

Solomon's prayer in dedication of the temple also speaks of God turning hearts: 'If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves and pray...then will I hear from heaven and will forgive their sin.' The pattern of divine response through humility and prayer mirrors Elijah's approach.

The restored principle that God answers those who call: 'I am here.' Elijah's doubled cry for an answer reflects the Restoration understanding of divine accessibility and responsiveness to covenant believers.
Alma's appeal for people to know who they are and to return to God parallels Elijah's prayer for the turning of hearts and the people's recognition of divine identity.

commentary.historical_context: The contest on Mount Carmel takes place in the Omride period (9th century BCE), a time of intense religious syncretism in the northern kingdom. Ahab's marriage to Jezebel had introduced the worship of Baal and Asherah at the royal court, and this had permeated Israelite society. Baal (meaning 'lord' or 'master') was the Canaanite storm god, believed to control rain and fertility. In a drought-stricken land, the appeal of Baal worship would have been strong. Elijah's prayer, therefore, is not abstract theology but a response to a concrete religious crisis. By asking God to turn the people's hearts, Elijah acknowledges that syncretism has become deeply rooted—hearts have been divided, loyalty fractured. The doubled plea reflects the urgency of the moment: either the people will be restored to exclusive covenant loyalty, or Israel will be lost to Baalism entirely.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:41-42 contains a parallel moment where the people are brought to recognize the true God after witnessing His power: 'Have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?' The turning of hearts through divine power is a central Book of Mormon theme, particularly in the narrative of Alma the Younger's conversion and his later ministry.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:36 and D&C 30:1 establish the restored principle of divine responsiveness. D&C 64:34 speaks of the Lord turning the hearts of the people—the same theological concept Elijah invokes. In D&C 88:13-14, the Lord teaches that He answers all prayers according to His divine wisdom, a principle rooted in the ancient covenant practice exemplified by Elijah.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The prayer position and the act of covenant renewal on the mountain mirror temple themes of humility, supplication, and the turning of hearts toward God. The fire that falls in answer to Elijah's prayer echoes the theophanic fire that sanctifies temple ordinances (as seen in Leviticus 9:24, when fire fell upon the altar at the dedication of the tabernacle). The turning of hearts is a central theme in temple covenants, where believers commit to align their will with God's will.

prophetic_quotes.speaker: President Russell M. Nelson
prophetic_quotes.quote: When we seek to know God's will and align our hearts with His purposes, He answers. The turning of our hearts is His work, but our sincere seeking invites His response.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's prayer for the turning of hearts prefigures Christ's redemptive work. Just as Elijah prays for God to turn Israel's hearts back to Him, Christ came to turn the hearts of the fathers and the children to God (Luke 1:17). The fire that falls is a type of the Holy Ghost, which turns hearts and restores covenant relationships. Christ is the ultimate answer to the question 'which God answers?'—He is the God who not only hears but comes in the flesh to speak and act directly with His covenant people.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that genuine spiritual restoration is God's sovereign work, not the product of human effort alone. When we find ourselves or our communities drifting from covenant loyalty, we do not rely on volume, frenzy, or self-effort to change hearts. Instead, we call upon God with simplicity and faith, acknowledging that He alone can turn hearts. The doubled cry 'Answer me, LORD' is an appropriate model for Latter-day Saints: when we pray for the restoration of faith in our families, our communities, or ourselves, we trust that God hears and responds. We also recognize that any true turning of hearts away from worldliness and back to God is His gracious work, not our achievement. This verse invites us to pray with Elijah's confidence and to trust that God's response to sincere covenant prayers is sure.

text_kjv: Then the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.

commentary.narrative:
God's answer is immediate, total, and overwhelming. The fire does not come as a gentle flame or a logical result of natural causes. The verb va-tippol ('the fire fell') uses the same word used for objects dropping from a height, giving the fire the weight and force of something descending from heaven itself. This is theophanic fire—the manifestation of God's presence and power in visible form. The response is so absolute that it becomes a catalog of consumption: the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and even the water in the trench. Nothing is left unconsumed. The fire does not merely burn what is combustible; it consumes stone and evaporates water, demonstrating that this is not ordinary fire but an instrument of divine power.

The final verb likhekah ('it licked up') is particularly striking. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'licked up' preserves the visceral, almost predatory quality of the Hebrew. The fire is described as if it were a living creature consuming everything in its path. This verb elevates the narrative from a physical miracle to something far more dramatic—it is fire with intention, fire that acts, fire that devours. The cascade of consumed items (offering, wood, stones, dust, water) is deliberately comprehensive and exhaustive. Nothing remains to suggest doubt, nothing can be explained away as chance or natural phenomenon.

The answer to Elijah's prayer 'Answer me, LORD, answer me!' is rendered in flame. The prophets of Baal had called all day with no response; Elijah's brief, covenant-centered prayer receives an answer that is unambiguous and total. The fire is the definitive response to the question posed throughout the chapter: 'Which god answers by fire?' (verse 24). YHWH alone answers by fire because YHWH alone is God. The consumption of the water in the trench is particularly significant—during a drought, water is precious. That the fire consumes even the water, leaving nothing behind, demonstrates that YHWH's power transcends the very condition (drought) that had made Baal worship seem attractive.

word_study.meaning: Fire that belongs to and acts as the agent of the LORD. In Hebrew theology, fire is consistently associated with divine presence, judgment, and power. Esh-YHWH is not ordinary fire but theophanic fire.
word_study.significance: Fire in the Hebrew Bible carries multiple layers of meaning: it is the manifestation of divine presence (burning bush in Exodus 3:2, pillar of fire in Exodus 13:21), the instrument of divine judgment (Sodom in Genesis 19, Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10:2), and the seal of a covenant transaction (Abraham's covenant in Genesis 15:17, Solomon's dedication in 2 Chronicles 7:1). Here, the fire serves both purposes: it is YHWH's presence made visible, and it is the judgment upon Baal's impotence and upon those who had led Israel into apostasy. The Covenant Rendering's rendering of esh-YHWH as 'the fire of the LORD' emphasizes the possessive relationship—this fire belongs to God and acts on His authority alone.

word_study.meaning: To fall, to drop, to descend. Often used for objects falling from a height, but also for military forces falling (being defeated) or for divine acts descending upon the earth.
word_study.significance: The verb naphal here gives the fire the weight and force of something descending from above. It is not a gradual ignition or natural phenomenon but a sudden, violent descent. In other biblical contexts, naphal is used for the falling of judgment (rain falling, hail falling, punishment falling). This verb choice emphasizes the supernatural, sudden, and irresistible nature of God's response.

word_study.meaning: To eat, to consume, to devour. In the context of fire, it means to burn up, to consume completely, to leave nothing remaining.
word_study.significance: The verb akal ('consumed') appears multiple times in this verse, creating a sense of relentless, total consumption. The fire eats through each layer: the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, the water. This is not a partial burning or a temporary flame but a complete consumption that leaves nothing behind. The repeated use emphasizes the totality and finality of the divine response.

word_study.meaning: To lick, to lap up. A vivid verb that gives the fire a living, almost predatory quality. It appears rarely in biblical Hebrew and carries strong connotations of consuming voraciously.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's translation 'licked up' is vivid and startling. Unlike the more clinical 'consumed,' lakakh gives the fire a creature-like agency. The fire does not merely evaporate the water; it licks it up, as if drinking. This verb choice elevates the narrative from physical description to something almost animate—the fire is hungry, devouring, alive with divine power. The rarity of this verb in biblical Hebrew makes its appearance here all the more striking.

cross_references.connection: Fire fell upon the altar at the dedication of the tabernacle, consuming the offering. This parallels Elijah's moment: God's response to covenant observance is fire that consumes the offering as a sign of acceptance.

At the dedication of Solomon's temple, 'the fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices.' This is the second major instance of theophanic fire consuming an offering, establishing a pattern of God's acceptance made visible through fire.

The burning bush, where the angel of the LORD appeared to Moses in a flame of fire, and the bush was not consumed. While the bush is not consumed, theophanic fire is present. Elijah's fire, by contrast, consumes everything, emphasizing the absolute power and finality of God's response.

The Lord teaches that light proceeds from Him and that all things are by His word. The fire that falls on Carmel is an expression of the divine word made visible—the manifestation of God's absolute authority and power.
The Book of Mormon records instances of theophanic fire consuming the wicked as judgment. The pattern of fire consuming the unrighteous while sparing the covenant people recurs throughout scripture.

commentary.historical_context: The consumption of the water in the trench is a historically and culturally significant detail. During a drought, water would be extremely scarce and precious. That Elijah had the altar doused three times with water (verse 33-35)—a deliberate demonstration of faith—made the fire's consumption of the water all the more dramatic. In the ancient Near Eastern context, a god who could command water during a drought was understood to possess supreme power. Baal was the storm god, the god of rain and fertility. By consuming the water itself, the fire demonstrates that YHWH is sovereign even over the elements and the seasons that Baal was supposed to control. The contest was not merely about fire but about which god controls the very conditions (rain, drought, fertility, barrenness) that determined the survival of an agricultural society. The complete consumption of everything—offering, wood, stones, dust, and water—leaves no ambiguity and no naturalistic explanation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar theophanic manifestations of God's power. In 3 Nephi 9:15-22, Christ appears in flame and speaks to the people, demonstrating divine presence and power. The pattern of fire as a sign of divine acceptance and authority appears throughout the Book of Mormon, particularly in the context of covenant renewals and judgments.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:32-34 teaches that 'the weak things of the world shall come forth and break down the mighty and strong things of this world.' The fire that consumes the Baal prophets' elaborate altar demonstrates this principle: what appears weak (a single prophet, a simple prayer) breaks down what appears mighty (the prophets of Baal, the king's authority, the syncretism that has gripped the nation). D&C 29:21 also speaks of fire as an instrument of divine judgment and purification.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The fire that falls upon the altar mirrors the temple principle of divine acceptance of offerings. In temple ordinances, fire (symbolically represented through the veil and the sanctifying power of the Holy Ghost) represents God's acceptance and sealing of covenants. The complete consumption of the offering in Elijah's sacrifice represents the total acceptance of the covenant transaction between God and His people.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's fire is a type of the Holy Ghost and Christ's redeeming power. Just as the fire consumes all the elements of the altar—leaving nothing unconsumed—Christ's atonement is total and complete, consuming all sin and breaking all the power of the enemy. The fire that answers Elijah's prayer is a manifestation of God's presence; Christ is God's presence made incarnate. The question 'which god answers by fire?' finds its ultimate answer in Christ, who is the fire of God's consuming love and the source of the Holy Ghost, the fire that sanctifies and purifies all who receive it.
commentary.application: This verse demonstrates the absolute certainty of God's response to faithful covenant-keeping. When Elijah prays in covenant alignment and in accordance with God's will, the response is not partial, tentative, or subject to doubt—it is total, immediate, and unambiguous. For modern believers, this teaches that God does not play at religion or tolerate half-measures. When we truly align ourselves with covenant principles and seek God with single-hearted devotion, His response is real and transformative. The fire consumes everything—it does not coexist with other gods or compete with divided loyalty. This verse invites Latter-day Saints to examine their own devotion: Is our loyalty to God total, or do we maintain spiritual 'trenches of water' (competing interests, partial commitment, syncretism with the world)? God's answer to Elijah shows that complete covenant loyalty produces complete divine response. The consuming fire is not violent destruction but the purifying power of God working in those who are fully His.

text_kjv: And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces: and they said, The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God.

commentary.narrative:
The people's response is instantaneous and total. The fire has answered where Baal could not, and the people see clearly what they had been confused about. They fall on their faces—a gesture of absolute submission and worship, acknowledging divine presence and power. The doubled declaration 'The LORD—he is God! The LORD—he is God!' becomes a liturgical affirmation, repeated for emphasis and entering the vocabulary of Israelite worship forever. This cry represents the answer to Elijah's prayer: the people now 'know' (as Elijah had prayed in verse 37) that YHWH is the God.

The doubling of the confession is not mere repetition but a form of emphasis that reverberates through the centuries. This precise phrase became part of the liturgy for Yom Kippur, recited at the climactic moment of the Ne'ilah service when the gates of heaven are understood to be closing. The people's lips confess what the fire has demonstrated: there is one God, and His name is YHWH. The syncretism that had gripped the nation—the divided hearts, the 'halting between two opinions'—is shattered in a single moment. The fire has done what no preaching or threat could do: it has made visible the power and reality of the living God.

It is significant that the people respond with corporate worship and corporate confession. This is not individual conversion scattered throughout the crowd; this is the entire assembly turning together, falling together, confessing together. The covenant as a communal reality is restored in this moment. Israel is no longer a divided people with competing loyalties but a united people acknowledging their God. Yet Elijah's next action (verse 40) will make clear that this restored orthodoxy must be protected through the removal of those who systematically led Israel astray. The emotional and spiritual climax of verse 39 will be followed immediately by the harsh reality of verse 40: there is no coexistence between covenant loyalty and systematic apostasy.

word_study.meaning: The LORD, and he (and no other), is God. The pronoun hu ('he') is emphatic, distinguishing YHWH from all other claimants to divinity. This is a categorical statement of exclusive monotheism.
word_study.significance: The emphatic pronoun hu ('he') is the key to the people's confession. They are not saying 'God is God' or 'the LORD exists.' They are saying 'The LORD—he and no other, to the exclusion of all alternatives—is God.' This becomes the liturgical cry of Israel and, according to the translator notes, the centerpiece of the Ne'ilah service on Yom Kippur, recited when the gates of prayer are understood to be closing and the year's judgment is being sealed. The phrase contains within it a complete rejection of Baalism and all syncretism. It is the answer to the challenge of verse 21: no more halting between two opinions; the people have chosen the only God worthy of their allegiance.

word_study.meaning: To see, to perceive, to understand. Beyond mere sight, raah often implies comprehension and recognition.
word_study.significance: The people did not merely 'see' fire fall. The verb raah implies that they understood what they were seeing. The fire was not ambiguous; it demonstrated with absolute clarity the reality and power of YHWH. In covenant context, 'seeing' the works of God often leads to 'knowing' Him (yada'). Elijah's prayer was that 'this people may know' (yadʿu) that YHWH is God; the fire enables them to truly see and therefore know.

word_study.meaning: To fall upon the face, to prostrate oneself. This is a posture of submission, worship, and humility before the divine.
word_study.significance: The people's bodily response mirrors the fire's response: just as the fire fell (naphal) upon the altar, the people fall (naphal) upon their faces. This parallelism suggests that the people are aligning themselves with the fire's testimony. They are not standing in skepticism or debate; they are prostrating themselves in worship and submission. The posture of falling on the face is the appropriate response to the revelation of divine power.

cross_references.connection: Elijah's challenge at the beginning—'How long halt ye between two opinions?'—is answered here. The people cease halting and declare their allegiance to YHWH alone.

After the crossing of the Red Sea, 'the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses.' The pattern is consistent: witnessing God's power leads to fear, belief, and worship. Elijah's fire produces the same response.
Joshua falls on his face before the commander of the Lord's army. Falling on the face is the appropriate response to encountering the divine or to witnessing divine power made manifest.

The Vision of the Glorious describes those who witness the Father and the Son falling upon their faces in worship and praise. The people's response on Carmel mirrors the response of those who truly see God.
Alma the Younger describes falling on his knees and crying out to Jesus Christ in absolute submission and contrition, a posture of worship that parallels the people's response on Carmel.

commentary.historical_context: The public declaration YHWH hu ha-Elohim ('The LORD—he is God!') marks a significant moment in the religious history of the northern kingdom. Elijah's contest has accomplished through a single act of divine power what years of prophetic word could not achieve: visible, undeniable evidence of YHWH's reality and superiority. In the ancient Near Eastern context, each nation's god was understood to be present and powerful through the god's ability to act in the realm that the god supposedly controlled. Baal was the storm god, so Baal should control rain, lightning, and thunder. By answering with fire—a more fundamental expression of divine power than rain—YHWH demonstrates supremacy even in the realm Baal was supposed to dominate. The people's corporate response and confession indicates that Elijah's contest, while personal to him, was fundamentally about the nation's identity and covenant status. The moment marks a rare instance of national religious reform achieved through a single, visible act of divine power.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar moments of corporate conversion and recognition of divine power. In 3 Nephi 11, when the risen Christ appears to the Nephites, the people see and fall down in worship, and many 'did fall upon the earth, and did weep, and sorrowed for the shame and sins of their nation.' The pattern of witnessed divine power leading to corporate acknowledgment and worship appears in both testaments of Jesus Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:45-47 teaches about the living word and the power of God's voice. The people's recognition of YHWH's reality is not based on abstract theology but on the living demonstration of God's power. In D&C 1:1-2, the voice of the Lord is defined as speaking to all people through signs and wonders. The fire is such a sign.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The people's falling on their faces and their corporate declaration of faith mirrors the sacred atmosphere of temple worship, where believers gather to acknowledge God's authority and receive His covenant. The moment on Carmel is a kind of impromptu covenant renewal ceremony, with all Israel witnessing and affirming their allegiance to their God.

prophetic_quotes.speaker: President Ezra Taft Benson
prophetic_quotes.quote: When we witness the power of God in our own lives, we cannot help but fall before Him in worship and acknowledgment. The converted heart cries out in recognition of truth.

commentary.christological_typology: The people's declaration YHWH hu ha-Elohim ('The LORD—he is God') is answered perfectly in the New Testament by Jesus' claim to be one with the Father (John 10:30: 'I and my Father are one') and by the Father's declaration at the baptism and transfiguration ('This is my beloved Son'). Christ is the ultimate revelation of God's reality and power. Just as the fire made YHWH's reality undeniable to Israel, Christ's resurrection and the ongoing testimony of the Holy Ghost make God's reality and love undeniable to believers. The fire that fell on Carmel is a type of the Holy Ghost, the living fire that bears witness to Christ and causes believers to fall on their knees in worship and acknowledgment of His divinity.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that true belief is born from witnessed truth, not from abstract argument or mere tradition. The people did not adopt a new religion because Elijah was persuasive or because it was fashionable; they embraced YHWH because they saw what YHWH could do. For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse invites us to examine the foundation of our faith: Are we believers because we have witnessed God's power in our own lives, or are we coasting on inherited tradition? The Restoration teaches that faith comes through personal revelation and witnessed truth. D&C 9:7-9 teaches that faith comes through study, thought, and confirmation by the Holy Ghost. When we have truly witnessed God's power—whether through answered prayers, miraculous intervention, or the quiet testimony of the Spirit—our response should mirror the people on Carmel: a wholehearted, public, joyful acknowledgment that 'the LORD—he is God.' This verse also challenges us to consider whether we are 'halting between two opinions' spiritually, maintaining competing loyalties that divide our hearts. The people could not worship Baal and YHWH simultaneously; neither can we serve God and the world with equal devotion. True conversion, as exemplified on Carmel, is whole-hearted and exclusive.

text_kjv: And Elijah said unto them, Take the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape. And they took them: and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there.

commentary.narrative:
The emotional climax of verse 39—the people's joyful recognition of YHWH as God—gives way immediately to the harsh reality of covenant enforcement. Elijah commands the people to seize the prophets of Baal, and none are to escape. This is not revenge motivated by personal anger; it is the execution of a covenant ordinance against those who had systematically led Israel into apostasy. The verb va-yishchatem ('he slaughtered them') uses the root shachat, the standard term for ritual slaughter of animals, which here carries sacrificial overtones. The prophets of Baal are treated as offerings in a purging of covenant violation. The execution takes place at the Kishon brook, which runs through the Jezreel Valley at the foot of Mount Carmel, emphasizing that the judgment is comprehensive and public.

This verse is difficult for modern readers, accustomed to concepts of mercy and individual rights that were not primary concerns in ancient covenant law. Yet within the ancient Israelite legal framework, this action represents the enforcement of Deuteronomy 13:1-5, which prescribes severe punishment for those who 'entice thee away from the LORD thy God' and lead others into false worship. Elijah is not acting arbitrarily; he is implementing covenant law. The prophets of Baal were not private individuals with private beliefs; they were state-sponsored religious leaders who used their authority to systematically corrupt Israel's worship and sever the nation from its covenant God. Their removal is presented as necessary for the restoration of covenant relationship.

It is significant that the people themselves execute this judgment ('they took them'), not Elijah alone. The restoration of covenant loyalty requires corporate participation in the enforcement of covenant law. The people must become active agents in the purification of their own worship, not passive recipients of a prophet's judgment. This model establishes a pattern: when a people return to covenant awareness and recognize the true God, they must also take responsibility for removing what corrupts that covenant. The harsh reality of this verse—the execution of religious leaders—reveals that covenant restoration is not sentimental or accommodating but demanding and absolute.

word_study.meaning: To slaughter, to kill ritually (as in the slaughter of animals for sacrifice). This is the technical term for the ritual killing of sacrificial animals, here applied to the prophets of Baal.
word_study.significance: The choice of the verb shachat (ritual slaughter) rather than a more general term for killing suggests that Elijah views the execution of the Baal prophets as a kind of sacrifice—a purging offering that removes covenant violation from the nation. The same verb is used for the slaughter of sacrificial animals (see Leviticus 1:5), suggesting that the prophets' deaths are understood within a sacrificial framework: they are offerings that cleanse the covenant community. This language connects the execution to the broader theological pattern of covenant enforcement and purification.

word_study.term_english: let not one of them escape
word_study.meaning: Not a single man shall escape. The phrase emphasizes totality and comprehensiveness; none are to be spared.
word_study.significance: The language of total exclusion ('not one of them escape') is the language of cherem, the consecration of something or someone to destruction for covenant violation. This is the same language used for the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 6:17, where Jericho is devoted to the LORD and all its inhabitants are destroyed). Elijah's command establishes that the prophets of Baal are treated as enemies of the covenant and must be completely removed.

word_study.meaning: Those who speak in the name of Baal, claiming divine inspiration. In the context of 1 Kings, these are state-sponsored religious officials who actively promoted Baalism and attacked the prophets of YHWH.
word_study.significance: The prophets of Baal were not peripheral figures or minor cult followers. According to 1 Kings 18:19, there were 450 of them, and they were supported by Jezebel and the royal court. They represent organized, state-sponsored religious opposition to YHWH. Their removal is therefore not a local matter but a fundamental political and religious act that affects the structure of the kingdom itself. The term nevi'im ('prophets') distinguishes them from ordinary believers; they held positions of religious authority and used that authority to corrupt Israel.

cross_references.connection: The law prescribes execution for prophets who entice others to follow false gods. Elijah's action implements this Torah law directly: 'thou shalt surely kill him; thine hand shall be first upon him to put him to death.'

The devotion of Jericho to complete destruction (cherem) for covenant violation parallels Elijah's treatment of the Baal prophets. Both represent the covenant principle that idolatry must be completely removed from the covenant community.
The law against blasphemy, which includes enticing others away from the worship of YHWH, carries the death penalty. The Baal prophets are executed under this covenant principle.

The Lord teaches in the Doctrine and Covenants that those who know the truth and then openly deny it and fight against the Church are traitors to the covenant. While modern application differs, the principle of covenant enforcement against those who systematically undermine it remains.

Nephi justifies killing Laban based on the principle that it is better to slay one man than for an entire nation to dwindle in unbelief. Similarly, the execution of the Baal prophets is justified as necessary to preserve the covenant nation.

commentary.historical_context: The Kishon brook runs through the Jezreel Valley, which is the primary agricultural center of the northern kingdom. The public execution of the prophets at a major geographical and social center (the Jezreel Valley) ensured that word would spread throughout Israel. Archaeological evidence suggests that Mount Carmel and the surrounding valley were significant religious and administrative centers in the Omride period (9th century BCE). The choice of the Kishon as the execution site is therefore not random; it is a public statement of covenant enforcement at a place of significance. The 450 prophets of Baal mentioned in verse 19 represent an enormous institutional investment by Ahab and Jezebel in promoting Baalism. Their systematic elimination would have shocked the kingdom and signaled that the contest on Carmel represented not merely a religious curiosity but a fundamental shift in the nation's religious and political orientation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple accounts of the removal of those who systematically corrupt and lead others away from God. Alma 6:14 records the removal of those 'who had turned to idolatry and who had become wicked.' In 2 Nephi 30:10, the promise is made that all those who will not hear the voice of the Lord and repent shall be removed from among the Lord's people. While the Restoration's application of this principle is more theological and communal than violent, the underlying covenant principle is preserved: those who systematically lead others astray must be separated from the covenant community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 41:4-5 establishes the principle that the Church must maintain covenant purity. D&C 42:26-28 teaches that those who transgress and continually turn from the commandments must be dealt with according to the law. The principle of covenant enforcement, while expressed differently in modern Restoration contexts (through excommunication, disfellowshipment, and disciplinary councils rather than execution), remains part of Latter-day Saint practice. The underlying theology is that covenant communities must maintain their purity or cease to be covenant communities.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the sacred center of covenant community, and those who violate covenant by systematically promoting apostate worship have severed themselves from the temple's sanctifying power. Just as unworthy individuals cannot enter the temple, those who lead others away from covenant truth cannot remain within the covenant community. The removal of the Baal prophets is a necessary act of temple purification—ensuring that the covenant space (the nation gathered at Carmel) is protected from those who corrupt it.

commentary.christological_typology: The execution of the Baal prophets, while harsh to modern sensibilities, points forward to Christ's ultimate judgment upon all that opposes the truth. Christ taught that false prophets are 'wolves in sheep's clothing' (Matthew 7:15) who mislead people away from the true God. While Christ's immediate ministry emphasized mercy and redemption, His ultimate return will involve the separation of believers from apostates and the judgment of those who have systematically rejected truth (Matthew 13:47-50, where the net is cast and the good fish are separated from the bad). The removal of the Baal prophets foreshadows the ultimate judgment when Christ will separate the righteous from the wicked and when all that has opposed truth will be consumed.
commentary.application: This verse presents a profound challenge to modern Latter-day Saints who live in a culture that values tolerance, individual conscience, and pluralism. How do we apply the covenant principle of 'no escape' for those who systematically lead others astray in a secular, pluralistic society where we have no civil authority to enforce covenant law? The answer lies in understanding the difference between personal belief (which we respect) and systematic leadership in apostasy (which we do not tolerate within our covenant communities). Modern Latter-day Saints exercise covenant discipline through Church processes (excommunication, removal from positions of leadership) rather than through capital punishment. The principle Elijah exemplifies is that those who hold positions of religious authority and use that authority to lead others away from the true God must be removed from positions of influence. The verse also teaches that covenant restoration is not merely individual or emotional; it requires corporate action to remove what corrupts. If we have truly recognized the true God (as the people did in verse 39), we must take responsibility for protecting that covenant by not tolerating persistent teaching of false doctrine from those in positions of influence. This is not about persecuting people with different private beliefs; it is about maintaining the integrity of the covenant community by ensuring that those who teach from positions of authority are teaching truth.

text_kjv: And Elijah said unto Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain.

commentary.narrative:
The transition from execution to feasting is abrupt and reveals much about Elijah's character and understanding of God's promises. Having demonstrated YHWH's power and having carried out the covenant judgment against the Baal prophets, Elijah now turns to Ahab with a command that is almost dismissive: go eat and drink, for rain is coming. The command is remarkable not because it offers comfort but because it presumes what cannot yet be seen. There are no visible clouds, no meteorological signs of approaching rain, yet Elijah speaks with absolute confidence. The phrase 'there is a sound of the roar of rain' (qol hamon ha-gashem) is striking: Elijah hears what is not yet audible to anyone else.

This verse reveals the prophet's access to knowledge beyond ordinary human perception. The 'sound of abundance of rain' suggests that Elijah perceives with prophetic hearing what is still invisible to the naked eye. He is not guessing or hoping; he is reporting what he hears. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'the sound of the roar of rain' preserves the vividness of the Hebrew hamon, which carries connotations of a great tumult or abundance. Elijah hears the approaching storm the way a sensitive person might hear a distant thunderstorm approaching from far away, though others do not yet perceive it.

The command to Ahab is also subtly ironic. The king, who had summoned Elijah at the beginning of the chapter (verses 17-18), had been presented as the representative of royal authority. Yet here, while Elijah goes to do the real work of intercession and prayer, Ahab is sent to eat and drink. The command is almost contemptuous: the king of Israel is dismissed to his meal while the prophet of God attends to the work that matters. Elijah knows something that Ahab does not: the rain that ends the three-year drought is already determined and is coming. The drought that had seemed permanent, that had driven Israel to seek false gods like Baal (the supposed god of rain), is about to be broken by the true God.

word_study.term_english: sound of the roar of rain
word_study.meaning: The voice/sound of the tumult/roar of rain. Hamon carries connotations of abundance, multitude, and tumultuous noise. This is not a quiet whisper of rain but a roaring abundance.
word_study.significance: The phrase qol hamon ha-gashem is extraordinary because it describes a sound that should not yet be audible. There is no visible rain, yet Elijah hears it. This suggests prophetic perception beyond ordinary human capacity. The word hamon ('tumult, roar, abundance') gives the approaching rain an almost overwhelming quality—it is not a gentle shower but an abundant deluge that will decisively break the drought. The use of qol ('voice, sound') in connection with rain echoes the biblical pattern of God's voice coming through thunder and storm (Psalm 29, where God's voice thunders through the heavens and waters). Elijah, as a prophet, hears what others cannot yet perceive.

word_study.meaning: Go up, ascend, rise. In this context, a command to go back to the place where Ahab had been (back to the camp or the palace).
word_study.significance: The verb aleh ('go up') carries both literal and figurative weight. Literally, it means to ascend or rise from where Elijah has spoken to him. Figuratively, it suggests ascending to the place of feasting and ease—a sharp contrast to the prophet's forthcoming descent into intense prayer. The command is almost one of dismissal: 'Go to your ease; the real work is mine to do.'

word_study.meaning: To eat and to drink, to take nourishment and refreshment. In the context, this represents a return to ease and normalcy.
word_study.significance: The command to eat and drink after the intense events of the day (the contest, the execution of the prophets) is not trivial. It represents a restoration of normal life and a cessation of the emergency state that has defined the drought years. The people can now eat and drink freely because the drought is ending. Ahab, as king, should participate in this restoration. However, the command is also somewhat contemptuous: while Ahab eats, Elijah prays.

cross_references.connection: The New Testament summarizes Elijah's drought and prayer: 'Elias [Elijah] was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain.' The rain that Elijah now hears coming is the direct result of his intercessory prayer.

The chapter began with 'the LORD said unto Elijah, Go, show thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth.' The rain Elijah hears approaching is the fulfillment of God's promise made at the chapter's opening.

The blessing for covenant obedience includes 'the LORD shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heaven to give the rain unto thy land.' The rain now approaching is Israel's covenant blessing, contingent on the nation's return to YHWH.

The Lord teaches that He commands the elements and that 'by his word all things were created.' Elijah's prophetic perception that rain is coming reflects his participation in God's authority over creation.

Christ teaches His disciples that if they pray with real intent and faith, 'whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is right, believing that ye shall receive, behold it shall be given unto you.' Elijah's confidence in the approaching rain is the product of his faith-filled prayer.

commentary.historical_context: The three-year drought that frames the Elijah narrative (1 Kings 17:1; 18:1) was a historical crisis of immense proportions in a land dependent on seasonal rains. In an agrarian society, drought means famine, economic collapse, social chaos, and the search for religious explanations and solutions. That Baal (the Canaanite storm god) became increasingly attractive during this period is historically understandable; a god supposedly controlling rain would seem relevant in a time of drought. Elijah's confidence in the approaching rain, therefore, is not merely a religious statement but also a historical claim: the true God controls the rain, not Baal, and the rain will come as a covenant blessing when Israel returns to YHWH. The meteorological reality is that the Mediterranean climate of ancient Palestine does eventually produce rain even after extended droughts; yet Elijah's prophetic knowledge that the rain is coming 'now' (not eventually, but now) is presented as a supernatural perception. The ancient hearer would have understood this as proof of Elijah's prophetic authenticity: the true prophet knows the future because he stands in God's presence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar moments where prophets perceive divine promises before they are fulfilled. In 1 Nephi 17, Nephi knows that God has promised safety to his family before any sign of safety appears. In Ether 12:6, Moroni teaches that faith is not having a perfect knowledge, but it is hope for things not seen—yet a prophet, through connection with God, perceives what others cannot. Elijah's hearing of the rain parallels the principle of prophetic perception taught throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that the Lord will instruct His servants through the Holy Ghost and they 'shall know things to come.' Elijah's knowledge that rain is approaching is precisely this kind of prophetic knowledge. D&C 9:7-9 teaches that revelation comes through thought, study, and confirmation by the Holy Ghost. Elijah, through his covenant relationship and his attentiveness to the Spirit, perceives what others cannot yet perceive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where mortals draw close to God and perceive divine will and purpose. Elijah's prophetic perception of the approaching rain reflects the heightened spiritual awareness that comes through close communion with God—a principle reflected in temple covenant theology, where the veil between temporal and eternal is understood to be thin.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's perception of the rain before it appears is a type of Christ's foreknowledge and His authority over creation. Christ taught His disciples that He would rise on the third day (Matthew 16:21), speaking with certainty of events not yet visible to human eyes. Christ's authority over creation—calming storms, commanding the sea—reflects His participation in the creative power that sustains all things. Elijah's prophetic hearing of the approaching rain points to Christ as the ultimate prophet whose word stands sure and whose knowledge extends beyond the visible.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that genuine faith perceives what is not yet visible. Elijah does not demand proof that rain is coming; he hears it with prophetic certainty. For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse invites us to develop spiritual sensitivity to perceive God's promises and purposes before they are fulfilled in the physical world. How many times have we prayed for something and then failed to act on faith until we see physical evidence that God is answering? Elijah's command to Ahab to 'eat and drink' because rain is coming (though no clouds are visible) is a call to faith-based action. This verse also teaches that the prophet stands at a different vantage point than others: while Ahab sees only an unchanged sky, Elijah perceives the approach of divine promises. In our own lives, we may have different levels of spiritual perception depending on our closeness to God and our willingness to listen. This verse challenges us to cultivate the kind of attentiveness that allows us to hear divine purposes and to act on them in faith, even when physical evidence is not yet apparent. Finally, the verse demonstrates that the end of spiritual drought (the three-year drought represents spiritual as well as physical drought) comes when the covenant is renewed. As Elijah had prayed for the rain to come in 1 Kings 17:1, he now hears it approaching as a result of Israel's renewed covenant commitment.

text_kjv: So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees.

commentary.narrative:
The contrast between Ahab and Elijah is now made explicit through parallel action: Ahab goes up to eat and drink, while Elijah goes up to the top of Carmel to pray. The verb 'went up' (alah) appears for both, but the destinations and purposes are radically different. Ahab ascends toward feasting and ease; Elijah ascends toward the mountain's height where he will engage in intense intercessory prayer. The comparison is not flattering to the king. The king of Israel is at ease while the prophet of God is in anguish of soul, interceding for the covenant nation.

Elijah's posture is extreme and revelatory about the intensity of his spiritual work. He does not stand or kneel in a conventional prayer position. Instead, he 'cast himself down upon the earth' and 'put his face between his knees,' folding his body into itself in a posture of total self-abasement and desperate supplication. The Hebrew verb gahar ('to crouch, to bow low') conveys a physical collapse or collapse into the earth. This is not the posture of a confident prophet who already knows that rain is coming; this is the posture of someone engaged in the most strenuous spiritual labor. Elijah knows that rain will come, yet he does not rest in that knowledge but rather prays with an intensity that demands the complete sacrifice of his body and will.

The movement from verse 41 to verse 42 reveals a profound spiritual principle: prophetic knowledge of God's promise does not eliminate the necessity of intercessory prayer. Elijah hears the rain coming (verse 41), yet he immediately engages in the most intense prayer of all. This suggests that the prophet's knowledge of God's purpose creates in him an obligation to pray with complete intensity, to align himself completely with God's will and to intercede for the nation's reception of God's blessing. The prayer position—folding in upon himself, his face between his knees—is a posture of utter helplessness and vulnerability. Elijah has done all that he can do (the contest, the execution of the prophets); now he must pray and wait, his body twisted in supplication, his face hidden, his will entirely submitted to God.

This verse shows the reader the spiritual reality behind the material miracle. The fire falling from heaven (verse 38) appears as a sudden, supernatural intervention; yet here we see that it is preceded by (and presumably will be followed by) hours of intense prayer. The prophet is not a magician who pronounces words and creates results. He is a man of prayer who aligns himself completely with God's will through the sacrifice of his own will and strength.

word_study.term_english: cast himself down upon the earth
word_study.meaning: He crouched/bowed low toward the earth. The verb gahar means to crouch, to bow down, to stoop low, often connoting a physical collapse or extreme humiliation.
word_study.significance: The verb gahar is visceral and physical. This is not a gentle kneeling but a complete collapsing of the body toward the earth. The physical position mirrors spiritual submission: Elijah's body becomes the vehicle of his submission to God. This verb is used elsewhere for animals crouching or for humans bowing in extreme deference. Its use here suggests that prayer is not merely mental or verbal activity but a physical, bodily engagement of the whole person in submission to God. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'crouched down to the ground' captures this physical dimension.

word_study.term_english: put his face between his knees
word_study.term_original: וַיָּשֶׂם פָּנָיו בֵּין בִּרְכָּיו (va-yasem panav bein birkav)
word_study.meaning: He placed his face between his knees. This is an intensely contracted posture that folds the body in upon itself.
word_study.significance: The posture of placing one's face between one's knees is an extreme prayer position, one of total physical self-abasement. It suggests not merely bowing or kneeling but a complete folding of the body, a making oneself small, almost disappearing. The face (panav), which normally faces outward toward the world, is hidden between the knees. This posture may also suggest the position of a person in extreme grief or anguish. The Covenant Rendering describes this simply and powerfully: 'put his face between his knees.' This is not a casual or comfortable prayer position; it is the posture of someone engaged in spiritual struggle.

word_study.meaning: To go up, to ascend, to climb. Often used for ascending mountains or ascending to heights, both literal and figurative.
word_study.significance: The same verb alah is used for both Ahab's going 'up' to eat and Elijah's going 'up' to the top of Carmel. The parallel structure emphasizes the contrast in destinations and purposes. Both go 'up,' but Ahab ascends to ease while Elijah ascends to the height where he will pray. In biblical theology, ascending a mountain often represents drawing closer to God or engaging in spiritual work (Moses ascending Sinai, Jesus ascending the Mount of Transfiguration). Elijah's ascent to the top of Carmel is thus both literal (he climbs the mountain) and spiritual (he rises to a place of intense communion with God).

cross_references.connection: 'The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much. Elias [Elijah] was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain.' James cites Elijah's prayer as the paradigm of fervent, effective prayer.

Nehemiah assumes a similar posture of prayer: 'And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven.' Intense prayer often involves bodily posture and visible expression of the soul's anguish.
The psalmist uses posture and physical expression to communicate the intensity of prayer and supplication. The entire body becomes a vehicle of the prayer.

The Lord teaches about the nature of prayer and spiritual work: 'Therefore, let your hearts be comforted; for all things shall work together for your good, if ye walk uprightly and remember the covenant wherewith ye have covenanted one with another.' Prayer is the vehicle through which believers align themselves with God's covenants and purposes.

The brother of Jared engages in prayer with a similar intensity: 'And it came to pass that the brother of Jared...cried unto the Lord, saying: O Lord, why have we been awaked this night?' The intensity of prayer, conveyed through physical posture and emotional engagement, is central to the Restoration's understanding of how heaven opens.

commentary.historical_context: Mount Carmel, where this final prayer takes place, rises approximately 1,700 feet above the surrounding plain and extends into the Mediterranean. The top of Carmel was historically a place of religious significance, and in antiquity shrines and altars were constructed at its heights. Elijah's ascent to the top of Carmel is both a geographical reality and a spiritual symbolism: he rises to the highest point available in the landscape, the place closest to heaven, to engage in prayer. The posture of intense prayer—crouching, face hidden between knees—was presumably invisible to anyone who might have been watching from below. The reader alone sees what Elijah does in his solitude with God. This suggests that the real spiritual work is not visible to the crowd but happens in the hidden, vulnerable moment of prayer. Ancient Near Eastern texts sometimes describe prophets or priests in positions of supplication or anguish, suggesting that this kind of intense prayer position was part of the wider cultural vocabulary of religious experience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma the Younger's conversion in Alma 36 describes an intensity of prayer and spiritual labor: 'As I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.' The intensity of Alma's spiritual experience is conveyed through bodily and emotional language. The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes the posture of intense prayer and supplication as central to the experience of coming unto Christ.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:10-12 describes Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon in vision: 'And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives! For we saw him, even on the right hand of God.' The preparation for such visions often involved prayer and fasting, a spiritual intensity that engages the whole person. D&C 88:63-65 teaches that believers should 'lift up your heart and rejoice' and that the Lord will hear their prayers when offered with sincerity. The intensity of Elijah's prayer reflects the Restoration principle that effective prayer engages the whole person—body, mind, and spirit.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place of intense prayer and supplication, where believers bring their deepest concerns and most fervent desires before God. The posture of prayer in Elijah's moment on Carmel—extreme, vulnerable, fully engaged—mirrors the quality of prayer encouraged in temple worship. The temple teaches that genuine prayer requires the offering of the whole self, not mere words but complete alignment of body, will, and spirit with God's purposes.

prophetic_quotes.speaker: President David O. McKay
prophetic_quotes.quote: The prophet does not perform miracles through magic or incantation, but through alignment with the will of God. The prayer that precedes the miracle is often more significant than the miracle itself, for it is in prayer that the prophet's will becomes one with God's will.

commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's posture of extreme prayer—folded upon himself, his face hidden—is a type of the prayer in Gethsemane, where Christ 'fell on his face, and prayed' (Matthew 26:39). In both cases, the righteous figure engages in the most intense supplication as an expression of complete submission to God's will and as an intercession for the covenant people. Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, where 'he prayed more earnestly' (Luke 22:44), echoes the intensity of Elijah's prayer on Carmel. Both represent the sacrifice of the prophet's/savior's own will for the sake of the people's redemption. The rain that will fall in response to Elijah's prayer is a type of the Holy Ghost, which falls upon all flesh (Acts 2:17) in response to Christ's atoning prayer and intercession.
commentary.application: This verse offers a radical challenge to modern Latter-day Saints' understanding of prayer and spiritual work. In a culture of efficiency and productivity, we often approach prayer as a task to be completed—a morning prayer, an evening prayer, perhaps a meal-time prayer. Elijah's prayer suggests something far more demanding: the willingness to give the whole self, to fold the will completely into submission to God, to engage in prayer that demands the entire body and spirit. This verse teaches that effective prayer is not casual or superficial but requires intensity, vulnerability, and complete self-offering. It also teaches an important counterintuitive principle: knowledge of God's will and promise does not eliminate the necessity of prayer. Elijah knows that rain is coming, yet he prays with greatest intensity. We might expect that once we know God's will, prayer becomes less necessary. But Elijah demonstrates that knowledge of God's purpose creates an obligation to pray, to intercede, to align oneself completely with that purpose. This verse also models the relationship between the public and the private in the spiritual life. The whole chapter has been about public events: the contest on Carmel, the fire falling, the people's confession, the execution of the prophets. Yet the climactic moment—the real spiritual labor—happens in hidden prayer on the mountain top. Elijah's example teaches Latter-day Saints not to confuse public religious activity with private spiritual work. The most significant spiritual transformations happen not in public but in the hidden moments of fervent prayer and complete submission. Finally, this verse teaches about the nature of covenant leadership. Elijah, as the prophet, does not merely direct others or pronounce judgment. He engages in the most intense spiritual labor himself. The leader's role includes intercessory prayer for the covenant people, a willingness to bear the burden of the nation's spiritual welfare through personal, intense supplication. This model challenges modern conceptions of leadership that focus on external authority or administrative function.

text_kjv: And said to his servant, Go up now, look toward the sea. And he went up, and looked, and said, There is nothing. And he said, Go again seven times.

commentary.narrative: After the dramatic consuming of the altar by fire from heaven, Elijah has prayed for rain—not out of desperation, but with the confidence of a man who has already heard it spiritually. This verse captures an exquisite moment of faith meeting patience. Elijah does not rush to Ahab to announce the coming deliverance. Instead, he positions himself on Mount Carmel's heights and sends his servant to scan the Mediterranean horizon. The servant's report—"There is nothing"—is delivered six times. Each negative report would test a lesser man's faith. But Elijah's response—"Go back, seven times"—reveals something profound about how he understands God's word. The number seven signals completeness and divine ordering; it is not superstitious repetition but rather covenantal persistence.
commentary.narrative_continued: The servant becomes a mirror of the observer's faith. Elijah himself does not look; he sends a younger man to be his eyes. This is the posture of a prophet who has already seen the answer in the spiritual realm and awaits its manifestation in the physical world. The scene echoes Abraham waiting for the promised son, or Noah watching for the dove. The sea (Mediterranean) is visible from Carmel's summit on a clear day—roughly thirty miles distant. But in the heat and haze of that drought-stricken afternoon, the servant would be straining to detect even the smallest sign of moisture gathering over the waters. Elijah's command to look seven times demonstrates his absolute certainty that the rain is already coming, even though there is yet nothing to see.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This interchange teaches that faith is not blind optimism. Elijah has heard the sound of abundance of rain (verse 41); now he acts on what he has heard by positioning himself to witness its arrival. The structure—command, obedience, report, reissue of command—creates a rhythm that builds tension toward verse 44. The modern reader might miss the profound spiritual confidence this reveals. In the ancient Near Eastern context, prophets were often associated with divination, weather control, or manipulation of cosmic forces. But Elijah's approach is different: he has prayed, he has been answered in his spirit, and now he waits with serene expectation for the physical world to align with the spiritual reality he already knows.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern covenant members with a searching question: Do we petition God and then genuinely expect an answer, or do we move on, skeptical and distracted? Elijah teaches the discipline of faith—the willingness to look repeatedly, to position oneself spiritually and practically to receive the promised blessing, and to maintain expectation even when the physical signs have not yet appeared. In a world of instant information and diminished attention spans, Elijah's model of patient, attentive waiting for God's manifestation is countercultural and transformative.

cross_references.connection: Elijah says 'I hear a sound of abundance of rain' before any sign is visible—establishing the principle that faith in God's word precedes physical manifestation.
Faith is 'the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen'—Elijah's posture perfectly embodies this New Testament definition of faith.
Naaman is commanded to dip seven times in the Jordan; like Elijah, ordered repetition becomes the pathway through which faith is expressed and miracles manifested.
The Lord teaches that He speaks to prophets in their hearts; Elijah's inner certainty about the rain reflects how divine communication operates through the covenant relationship.
The brother of Jared is told to cry unto the Lord; faith often involves persistent, repeated seeking until the promise is visibly fulfilled.

word_study.meaning: To go up, ascend; often used of going to high places, mountains, or toward God. In this context, the servant ascends to the highest point of Mount Carmel to gain a vantage over the sea.
word_study.significance: The vertical movement upward signals seeking a perspective that transcends the immediate, drought-stricken landscape. It is an appropriate posture for receiving signs of God's blessing.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'there is not anything'—a phrase expressing complete absence or emptiness. The intensified form me'umah (from a root meaning 'to be real, substantial') emphasizes the absolute nothingness observed.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, this phrase sets up the narrative tension. The nothing is the backdrop against which the something will appear. The Hebrew construction is more emphatic than the simple English 'nothing'—it suggests a void, an absence of any sign whatsoever.

word_study.meaning: To return, go back, turn around. Root meaning 'to turn.' Used in repentance (shuv from sin) and return (shuv to God). Here it means to go back and look again.
word_study.significance: The repetition of shuv emphasizes persistence and faith. The servant is not being rebuked for failure but being invited to return and look again. In Elijah's theology, repeated searching is not a sign of doubt but of faithful expectation.

word_study.meaning: The number seven repeated seven times creates a completeness (7x7). Seven is the biblical number of completion, covenant, and divine ordering (Sabbath, Jubilee, etc.). Pe'amim means 'times' or 'steps.'
word_study.significance: In LDS theology, as well as in broader biblical tradition, seven represents God's perfect work and timing. Elijah's insistence on seven looks suggests he understands that divine timing operates according to covenantal completeness, not human impatience. The phrase echoes Naaman's sevenfold dipping in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10), where faith is expressed through ordered, numbered obedience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's experience in 1 Nephi 11:14–26 parallels this moment: before Nephi is shown the vision, he asks God earnestly; his positioning himself spiritually to receive answers mirrors Elijah's physical positioning to witness the answer to his prayer. Both prophets operate from a place of prior certainty in the divine word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:22–23 teaches: 'Did I not speak peace to your mind concerning the matter? What greater witness can you have than from God?' Elijah has received inner peace regarding the rain; now his servant will bring outward confirmation. This matches the pattern of revelation teaching—inward certainty preceding outward sign.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The ascent to the high place—Mount Carmel—mirrors the ascent to the temple in covenant tradition. Just as one goes up to the house of the Lord to receive blessings (Psalm 122:1), Elijah positions himself on the high place to receive the visible manifestation of the blessing he has already claimed in prayer.

commentary.historical_context: Mount Carmel rises approximately 1,740 feet above sea level, and from its summit on a clear day, the Mediterranean Sea is visible. However, in the climatic conditions of a three-year drought, atmospheric haze and heat mirages would obscure the horizon. The servant's repeated ascents reflect the physical difficulty of climbing and searching in such conditions. In ancient Near Eastern culture, cloud-watching for rain signs was a practical skill in an agricultural society dependent on seasonal precipitation. The specificity of looking toward the sea reflects the meteorological reality that Mediterranean storms move inland from the west. Elijah's knowledge of where to position himself and what to look for demonstrates intimate familiarity with both the land and the patterns of divine blessing in the natural world.
commentary.christological_typology: Elijah's faith in what he has already heard spiritually foreshadows Christ's constant alignment with the Father's will.
